Lupus nephritis from detection to pregnancy planning

Intermittent flank pain in a child
Confusion and extreme hyperglycemia in an older man

items.stemHtml: A 20-year-old woman has had burning on urination and urinary frequency for 2 days. She became sexually active with a new partner 3 weeks ago. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), and there is mild suprapubic tenderness without flank tenderness. Urinalysis shows leukocyte esterase and many white blood cells; the nitrite test is negative. Urine culture grows gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase positive, coagulase negative and grow normally around a novobiocin disk. Which of the following is the most likely organism?
items.explanationHtml:
Catalase-positive, coagulase-negative staphylococci that are resistant to novobiocin (they grow up to the disk) are S. saprophyticus, the second most common cause of cystitis in young, sexually active women. It does not reduce nitrate, so the nitrite test is often negative.

Takeaway: coagulase-negative staphylococcal cystitis in a young sexually active woman with novobiocin resistance is S. saprophyticus.

whyNot.A: Enterococci are catalase negative and grow in chains or pairs, not clusters.
whyNot.B: S. aureus is coagulase positive; in urine it usually signals bacteremia seeding the kidney.
whyNot.C: S. epidermidis is also coagulase negative, but it is novobiocin sensitive and causes catheter or device infections rather than cystitis in healthy women.
whyNot.E: Group B streptococci are catalase negative and form chains; they cause bacteriuria mainly in pregnancy and older adults with diabetes.

items.objective: Identify Staphylococcus saprophyticus from its setting and laboratory features (coagulase negative, novobiocin resistant).

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has fever of 39.2°C (102.6°F), chills and right flank pain 4 days after symptoms of cystitis began. There is right costovertebral angle tenderness. Urine culture grows a lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod. Molecular typing of the isolate shows a gene encoding an adhesin that binds galactose-containing glycolipids on uroepithelial cells of the renal pelvis. Which of the following virulence factors does this gene encode?
items.explanationHtml:
The patient has acute pyelonephritis due to uropathogenic E. coli. P (pyelonephritis-associated) fimbriae bind the galactose-containing P blood-group glycolipids on uroepithelium, letting the organism resist urine flow and ascend to the kidney. Type 1 fimbriae, which bind mannose, matter more for bladder colonisation.

Takeaway: P fimbriae are the E. coli adhesin most linked to ascending pyelonephritis.

whyNot.A: The K1 capsule protects E. coli from phagocytosis and complement and is the key factor in neonatal meningitis; it is not an adhesin.
whyNot.C: Shiga-like toxin is made by enterohemorrhagic E. coli and causes bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome.
whyNot.D: Heat-labile toxin is the enterotoxigenic E. coli toxin of traveler's diarrhea; it raises cAMP in enterocytes.
whyNot.E: Lipid A drives septic shock through TLR4 signalling but does not mediate attachment to uroepithelium.

items.objective: Link P fimbriae of uropathogenic E. coli to ascending pyelonephritis.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with a long-term indwelling urethral catheter after spinal cord injury has had three urinary tract infections in a year. Urine pH is 8.5. Abdominal radiography shows a large branching radiopaque calculus filling the left renal pelvis and calyces. Urine culture grows a gram-negative rod that spreads in waves across the agar plate. Which of the following enzymes produced by this organism is most responsible for the calculus?
items.explanationHtml:
A swarming gram-negative rod in a catheterised patient is Proteus mirabilis. Its urease splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide; ammonia makes urine strongly alkaline, and in alkaline urine magnesium, ammonium and phosphate precipitate as struvite, which can grow into a staghorn calculus. The stone shelters bacteria, so infection recurs until the stone is removed.

Takeaway: alkaline urine plus a staghorn calculus means a urease-producing organism and struvite.

whyNot.A: Beta-lactamase gives antibiotic resistance but does not change urine chemistry or form stones.
whyNot.B: Catalase protects bacteria from hydrogen peroxide; it has no role in stone formation.
whyNot.C: Coagulase is a Staphylococcus aureus enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
whyNot.D: Nitrate reductase gives a positive urine nitrite test but does not alkalinise urine.

items.objective: Explain how urease-producing organisms such as Proteus cause struvite staghorn calculi.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, chills, nausea and left flank pain. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). There is left costovertebral angle tenderness. Which of the following findings on urine microscopy most specifically shows that the infection involves the kidney rather than only the bladder?

options.label: A
options.html: Bacteria seen on an unspun specimen

options.label: B
options.html: More than 10 white blood cells per high-power field

options.label: C
options.html: Red blood cells with a normal shape

items.explanationHtml:
Casts are moulds of the tubular lumen made of Tamm-Horsfall glycoprotein. White blood cell casts therefore form only when neutrophils are inside renal tubules, which places the inflammation in the kidney (pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis). Pyuria, bacteriuria and hematuria occur with cystitis as well.

Takeaway: white blood cell casts localise a UTI to the kidney.

whyNot.A: Bacteriuria occurs with infection at any level of the urinary tract and with contamination.
whyNot.B: Pyuria shows inflammation somewhere in the urinary tract but does not tell bladder from kidney.
whyNot.C: Normally shaped red cells suggest bleeding below the glomerulus, which occurs with hemorrhagic cystitis too.
whyNot.D: Squamous cells mean the specimen is contaminated by vaginal or skin cells.

items.objective: Use white blood cell casts to localise urinary infection to the kidney.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man who moved from a rural region abroad 10 years ago has had painless intermittent hematuria and urinary frequency for 4 months. He has lost 3 kg. Urinalysis shows many white blood cells and red blood cells on repeated samples, but routine bacterial urine cultures are negative three times. He has not taken antibiotics. Intravenous urography shows irregular, moth-eaten calyces in the right kidney and a narrowed right ureter. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Acid-fast culture and nucleic acid testing of first-morning urine samples

options.label: B
options.html: Serum antinuclear and anti-double-stranded DNA antibody titres

options.label: C
options.html: Microscopy of a midday urine sample for eggs with a terminal spine

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat bacterial urine culture on chocolate agar in carbon dioxide

options.label: E
options.html: Urine eosinophil count using a Hansel stain

items.explanationHtml:
Sterile pyuria with hematuria, calyceal destruction and ureteral stricture is the picture of genitourinary tuberculosis, which reaches the kidney by hematogenous spread, often many years after primary infection. Bacilli are shed intermittently, so several first-morning urine samples are sent for mycobacterial culture and nucleic acid testing. Caseating granulomas are seen if tissue is obtained.

Takeaway: sterile pyuria plus hematuria and a deformed collecting system points to renal tuberculosis.

whyNot.B: Lupus nephritis causes active sediment with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts, not calyceal destruction or ureteral strictures.
whyNot.C: Schistosoma haematobium eggs cause terminal hematuria with bladder-wall granulomas and calcification; the infection centres on the bladder, not on destruction of the renal calyces with sterile pyuria.
whyNot.D: Fastidious organisms such as Haemophilus would not produce this destructive chronic picture.
whyNot.E: Urine eosinophils are a weak test for drug-induced interstitial nephritis, which does not deform the calyces.

items.objective: Recognise genitourinary tuberculosis as a cause of sterile pyuria and choose mycobacterial urine testing.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man who grew up farming irrigated land along a river in North Africa has painless gross hematuria. Cystoscopy shows a fungating mass on the posterior bladder wall surrounded by thickened, calcified mucosa. Biopsy of the surrounding wall shows granulomas around calcified ova that carry a terminal spine. Which of the following is the most likely histologic type of the bladder mass?
items.explanationHtml:
Eggs with a terminal spine in the bladder wall are Schistosoma haematobium. Chronic egg-driven inflammation causes squamous metaplasia of the urothelium, and the cancer that follows is typically squamous cell carcinoma. Other chronic irritants (long-term catheters, stones) do the same.

Takeaway: chronic bladder irritation, classically schistosomiasis, leads to squamous metaplasia and squamous cell carcinoma.

whyNot.A: Bladder adenocarcinoma arises mainly from a urachal remnant at the dome or with bladder exstrophy.
whyNot.B: Clear cell carcinoma is the common renal cortical cancer, not a bladder tumour linked to parasites.
whyNot.C: Small cell carcinoma of the bladder is rare and is not linked to schistosomiasis.
whyNot.E: Urothelial carcinoma is the commonest bladder cancer overall, linked to smoking and aromatic amines, but chronic schistosomal inflammation shifts the type to squamous.

items.objective: Associate Schistosoma haematobium infection with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman has 3 months of malaise, low-grade fever, left flank pain and a 6-kg weight loss. She has had recurrent urinary infections with Proteus mirabilis. CT shows an enlarged, nonfunctioning left kidney containing a staghorn calculus and several low-density masses replacing the parenchyma. Nephrectomy is performed. Microscopy of the yellow masses shows sheets of macrophages with abundant foamy cytoplasm mixed with plasma cells and neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.html: Renal malakoplakia confined to the bladder

items.explanationHtml:
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a destructive chronic infection of an obstructed kidney, usually with a staghorn stone and Proteus or E. coli. Lipid-laden (foamy) macrophages form yellow nodules that can look like a tumour on imaging and grossly. The kidney is usually nonfunctioning, and nephrectomy is the usual treatment.

Takeaway: staghorn stone, chronic infection and foamy macrophages replacing the kidney is xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis.

whyNot.A: Angiomyolipoma contains fat, smooth muscle and thick-walled vessels; it is a benign tumour, often with tuberous sclerosis, not an infection.
whyNot.B: Clear cell carcinoma cells contain glycogen and lipid, but they are malignant epithelial cells in nests with delicate vessels, not macrophages with plasma cells and neutrophils.
whyNot.C: Malakoplakia shows macrophages with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies (calcified inclusions) and usually involves the bladder; it does not explain the replaced kidney and staghorn stone.
whyNot.D: Renal tuberculosis forms caseating granulomas with epithelioid macrophages, and routine cultures are negative.

items.objective: Recognise xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis from its setting and histology.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman received a kidney transplant 9 months ago and takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone. Her serum creatinine has risen from 1.2 to 2.1 mg/dL over 6 weeks. She feels well. Urine cytology shows tubular epithelial cells with enlarged nuclei containing homogeneous basophilic inclusions. Allograft biopsy shows tubulointerstitial inflammation and the same intranuclear inclusions, which stain for SV40 large T antigen. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
items.explanationHtml:
Intranuclear inclusions in tubular cells ("decoy cells" in urine) staining for SV40 antigen mean BK polyomavirus nephropathy, which reactivates when immunosuppression is intense. No antiviral is reliably effective, so the core step is to reduce immunosuppression (typically lowering or stopping the antimetabolite and lowering the calcineurin inhibitor) while watching for rejection.

Takeaway: BK virus nephropathy in a kidney graft is treated by reducing immunosuppression.

whyNot.A: Ganciclovir treats cytomegalovirus; it has no meaningful activity against BK polyomavirus.
whyNot.B: More calcineurin inhibitor would deepen immunosuppression and allow more viral replication.
whyNot.D: Pulse steroids treat acute cellular rejection; giving them for BK nephropathy would worsen the infection.
whyNot.E: Acyclovir is for herpes simplex and varicella zoster and does not act on polyomaviruses.

items.objective: Recognise BK polyomavirus nephropathy in a kidney transplant recipient and reduce immunosuppression.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has had dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency for 1 day. She has no fever, flank pain or vaginal discharge, and she is not pregnant (urine hCG negative). She has had no antibiotics in the past year and no drug allergies. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). There is mild suprapubic tenderness and no costovertebral angle tenderness. Urine dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrite. Her eGFR is above 90 mL/min/1.73 m². Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Pelvic examination with nucleic acid testing before any treatment

options.label: E
options.html: Urine culture, with antibiotics only if the culture is positive

items.explanationHtml:
This is acute uncomplicated cystitis: a healthy, nonpregnant woman with typical lower-tract symptoms, no fever or flank pain and no complicating features. A first-line agent such as nitrofurantoin for 5 days (or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 3 days where resistance is low, or single-dose fosfomycin) is appropriate without a culture.

Takeaway: treat typical uncomplicated cystitis empirically with a first-line agent; culture is for complicated, recurrent or atypical cases.

whyNot.B: Fluoroquinolones work but are reserved for pyelonephritis or when first-line agents cannot be used, because of adverse effects and resistance.
whyNot.C: Without vaginal discharge or irritation, sexually transmitted urethritis or vaginitis is unlikely, and treatment need not wait.
whyNot.D: Imaging has no role in a first episode of uncomplicated cystitis.
whyNot.E: Culture is unnecessary for a first typical episode, and waiting 2 days for it delays relief.

items.objective: Treat acute uncomplicated cystitis empirically with a first-line agent.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 13 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit. She has no urinary symptoms. A screening urine culture grows more than 100,000 colony-forming units/mL of Escherichia coli, susceptible to cephalexin, nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. She has no allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: No treatment, because she has no symptoms

options.label: B
options.html: Oral cephalexin for 5–7 days, then a follow-up urine culture

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat the urine culture at 28 weeks' gestation

items.explanationHtml:
In pregnancy, asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated, because about a third of untreated women develop pyelonephritis, which is linked to preterm birth and low birth weight. A short course of a pregnancy-safe agent guided by susceptibility, such as cephalexin, is appropriate, followed by a test-of-cure culture and periodic rescreening.

Takeaway: screen once early in pregnancy and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic.

whyNot.A: Pregnancy is the main exception to the rule of not treating asymptomatic bacteriuria.
whyNot.C: Fluoroquinolones are generally avoided in pregnancy when safer options exist.
whyNot.D: Tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal tooth discoloration and bone effects).
whyNot.E: Waiting leaves her at risk of pyelonephritis in the meantime.

items.objective: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman who lives in a nursing home and has moderate dementia is evaluated because a urine culture, sent after staff noticed her urine was cloudy and malodorous, grew more than 100,000 colony-forming units/mL of Klebsiella pneumoniae. She has no fever, change in mental status, dysuria, new incontinence or abdominal pain. Vital signs are normal. Examination shows no suprapubic or costovertebral angle tenderness. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Oral antibiotic for 7 days based on susceptibilities

items.explanationHtml:
This is asymptomatic bacteriuria, which is common in older adults, especially in long-term care. Cloudy or smelly urine is not a symptom of infection. Treatment does not reduce symptomatic infection or mortality and does cause adverse drug events, C. difficile infection and resistant organisms, so the right step is no antibiotics.

Takeaway: outside pregnancy and planned urologic procedures, do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

whyNot.A: Prophylaxis is for recurrent symptomatic UTI, not bacteriuria without symptoms.
whyNot.C: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults gives harm without benefit.
whyNot.D: Routine surveillance cultures lead to unnecessary treatment.
whyNot.E: Even a single dose is unnecessary and selects for resistance.

items.objective: Avoid treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, chills, nausea and right flank pain. She is not pregnant. She vomited once yesterday but has kept down fluids and food today. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse 98/min and blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg. There is right costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows pyuria, bacteriuria and white blood cell casts. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. Local fluoroquinolone resistance among E. coli is below 10%. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the abdomen and pelvis before any antibiotic

options.label: E
options.html: Urine culture, then oral ciprofloxacin for 7 days

items.explanationHtml:
She has acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis and is stable and able to take oral fluids, so outpatient treatment is appropriate. Send a urine culture before antibiotics, then give an oral fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin for 7 days, or levofloxacin for 5 days) where local resistance is low, and adjust to susceptibilities.

Takeaway: stable pyelonephritis: culture, then an oral fluoroquinolone (or susceptible trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole); admit only for sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy or obstruction.

whyNot.A: Imaging is for severe illness, suspected obstruction or no response after 48–72 hours, and it should not delay antibiotics.
whyNot.B: She is not septic and can take oral drugs; a carbapenem would be broader than needed.
whyNot.C: Nitrofurantoin does not reach adequate kidney tissue levels and should not be used for pyelonephritis.
whyNot.D: Fosfomycin as a single dose is for cystitis and is not adequate for pyelonephritis.

items.objective: Manage stable acute pyelonephritis with a urine culture and an oral agent that reaches renal tissue.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man has 1 day of severe left flank pain radiating to the groin, followed by fever and rigors. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), pulse 118/min and blood pressure 96/58 mm Hg after 2 L of intravenous crystalloid. There is left costovertebral angle tenderness. Leukocyte count is 19,500/mm³ and serum creatinine 1.6 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. Blood and urine cultures are drawn, and intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam is started. Noncontrast CT shows a 7-mm stone in the proximal left ureter with moderate hydronephrosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue antibiotics and wait for spontaneous stone passage

options.label: C
options.html: Start tamsulosin and discharge with oral antibiotics

options.label: D
options.html: Ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy and stone extraction today

options.label: E
options.html: Urgent decompression with a ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy

items.explanationHtml:
An infected, obstructed kidney with sepsis is a urologic emergency. Antibiotics cannot sterilise a closed, pressurised collecting system, so the kidney must be decompressed urgently, by retrograde ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy, alongside antibiotics and resuscitation. Definitive stone treatment is delayed until the infection has resolved.

Takeaway: stone plus obstruction plus infection means drain first, treat the stone later.

whyNot.A: Waiting with an obstructed, infected kidney risks worsening septic shock and loss of the kidney.
whyNot.B: Shock wave lithotripsy in active infection can worsen sepsis, and it does not drain the system quickly.
whyNot.C: Medical expulsive therapy is for uncomplicated stones without infection; he is septic and needs admission.
whyNot.D: Definitive stone surgery during sepsis raises the risk of bacteremia; drainage alone is the safer first step.

items.objective: Decompress an obstructed, infected kidney urgently before definitive stone treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (hemoglobin A1c 10.8%) has had 4 days of fever, right flank pain and vomiting. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F), pulse 112/min and blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg. Serum glucose is 386 mg/dL and creatinine 1.9 mg/dL. Urine culture is pending. Intravenous ceftriaxone and fluids are started. CT of the abdomen shows gas within the right renal parenchyma extending into the perirenal space, without a ureteral stone or hydronephrosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step, in addition to antibiotics and glucose control?

options.label: C
options.html: No intervention; continue intravenous antibiotics alone for 6 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Percutaneous catheter drainage of the right kidney

items.explanationHtml:
Gas in the renal parenchyma in a patient with diabetes is emphysematous pyelonephritis, a necrotising infection usually caused by E. coli or Klebsiella. When gas extends beyond the parenchyma, antibiotics alone have high mortality; the standard is antibiotics with percutaneous drainage, with emergency nephrectomy if she does not improve or has extensive disease with shock.

Takeaway: emphysematous pyelonephritis needs source control (percutaneous drainage, or nephrectomy) plus antibiotics.

whyNot.A: Retrograde pyelography evaluates the collecting system; there is no obstruction, and it would not drain parenchymal gas.
whyNot.B: Hyperbaric oxygen is not a standard treatment for this condition and would delay source control.
whyNot.C: Antibiotics alone are reserved for gas limited to the collecting system; extension beyond the kidney needs drainage.
whyNot.E: Waiting a week in a septic patient with a necrotising infection is unsafe.

items.objective: Recognise emphysematous pyelonephritis and arrange source control.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman has had four culture-confirmed episodes of acute cystitis in the past 12 months, each with E. coli and each resolving with a short course of nitrofurantoin. Between episodes she is well, and urinalysis between episodes shows no blood. Post-void residual volume is 30 mL. Pelvic examination shows pale, thin vaginal mucosa with loss of rugae; there is no prolapse. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce recurrences?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent uncomplicated cystitis in a postmenopausal woman with genitourinary atrophy is driven partly by low estrogen, which lets lactobacilli fall and uropathogens colonise. Vaginal estrogen restores the vaginal flora and reduces recurrences, with minimal systemic absorption. Low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis is an alternative if this fails, using a first-line agent rather than a fluoroquinolone.

Takeaway: for recurrent UTI after menopause with atrophy, start vaginal estrogen.

whyNot.A: Upper-tract imaging is not needed for recurrent uncomplicated cystitis without hematuria, stones, Proteus or other atypical features.
whyNot.B: Cystoscopy is not indicated without hematuria or another atypical feature.
whyNot.C: Fluoroquinolones are a poor choice for long-term prophylaxis because of adverse effects and resistance.
whyNot.D: Systemic hormone therapy does not reduce UTIs and carries cardiovascular and breast risks.

items.objective: Prevent recurrent UTI in a postmenopausal woman with vaginal estrogen.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man has had an indwelling urethral catheter for 5 weeks because of urinary retention after a stroke. Today he has a temperature of 38.7°C (101.7°F), new confusion and suprapubic discomfort. Blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg. There is no cough, diarrhea or wound. Urinalysis from the catheter bag shows pyuria and bacteriuria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step before starting antibiotics?

options.label: A
options.html: Collect urine from the drainage bag for culture

options.label: B
options.html: Irrigate the existing catheter with saline

options.label: C
options.html: Replace the catheter and send a urine culture from the new catheter

items.explanationHtml:
He has a symptomatic catheter-associated UTI. A catheter in place for more than about 2 weeks is coated with biofilm; cultures from it reflect colonisation, and the biofilm protects organisms from antibiotics. The catheter should be removed or replaced, and urine for culture collected from the fresh catheter before antibiotics start. Then reassess whether he still needs a catheter at all (intermittent catheterisation may be possible).

Takeaway: in catheter-associated UTI, replace a long-dwelling catheter and culture from the new one before antibiotics.

whyNot.A: Bag urine is contaminated and overgrown; it should never be used for culture.
whyNot.B: Irrigation does not clear biofilm infection and is not recommended.
whyNot.D: Imaging is not routine unless there is suspected obstruction, poor response or severe sepsis.
whyNot.E: Bladder irrigation with antibiotics is not effective treatment for catheter-associated UTI.

items.objective: Manage catheter-associated UTI by replacing the catheter and culturing from the new one.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 22 weeks' gestation has had fever, chills and right flank pain for 1 day. She vomited three times today. Temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F), pulse 108/min and blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg. Fetal heart rate is 160/min. There is right costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows pyuria, bacteriuria and white blood cell casts. Urine and blood cultures are sent. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Discharge with oral amoxicillin for 3 days

options.label: D
options.html: Discharge with oral nitrofurantoin for 7 days

options.label: E
options.html: Observe without antibiotics until culture results return

items.explanationHtml:
Pyelonephritis in pregnancy carries risks of sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome and preterm labour, so it is treated in hospital with an intravenous beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone, adjusted to culture results and switched to oral therapy once she has been afebrile for 24–48 hours.

Takeaway: pyelonephritis in pregnancy means admission and IV beta-lactam therapy.

whyNot.B: Fluoroquinolones are avoided in pregnancy when safer agents exist.
whyNot.C: Oral amoxicillin has poor activity against many E. coli strains, and 3 days is far too short for pyelonephritis.
whyNot.D: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve kidney tissue levels and cannot treat pyelonephritis; she is also vomiting.
whyNot.E: Withholding antibiotics in a febrile pregnant patient with pyelonephritis risks sepsis and preterm labour.

items.objective: Admit and treat pyelonephritis in pregnancy with an intravenous beta-lactam.

items.stemHtml: The patient was admitted and treated with intravenous ceftriaxone. Urine culture grew pan-sensitive E. coli. She became afebrile after 36 hours, was switched to oral cephalexin and completed a 14-day course. She is now at 25 weeks' gestation, feels well, and a repeat urine culture is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the rest of her pregnancy?

options.label: A
options.html: Low-dose daily antibiotic suppression until delivery

options.label: B
options.html: No further urine cultures unless symptoms recur

options.label: C
options.html: Renal ultrasonography every 4 weeks until delivery

options.label: D
options.html: A repeat 14-day course of cephalexin each trimester

items.explanationHtml:
Pyelonephritis recurs in a meaningful share of pregnant women. A common approach is low-dose suppressive antibiotic therapy (for example nitrofurantoin or cephalexin at bedtime) for the rest of the pregnancy, with periodic urine cultures; close surveillance with repeat cultures is an accepted alternative.

Takeaway: after pyelonephritis in pregnancy, prevent recurrence with suppression or close culture surveillance until delivery.

whyNot.B: Waiting for symptoms misses recurrent bacteriuria, which can progress to another pyelonephritis.
whyNot.C: Serial imaging does not prevent recurrence; mild dilation of the right collecting system is normal in pregnancy.
whyNot.D: Repeated full treatment courses expose her to more antibiotic than low-dose suppression without added benefit.
whyNot.E: Weekly parenteral antibiotics are not a standard or practical suppression strategy.

items.objective: Prevent recurrent pyelonephritis in pregnancy with suppression or culture surveillance.

items.stemHtml: A 21-year-old man notices dark red urine the day after a sore throat and fever begin. He had a similar episode 2 years ago that cleared on its own. Blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows red blood cells, many of them dysmorphic, a few red cell casts and 1+ protein. Serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. Serum C3 is normal. A kidney biopsy is performed. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on immunofluorescence?

options.label: A
options.html: Granular IgG and C3 in large subepithelial deposits

options.label: B
options.html: Granular IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q in subendothelial deposits

options.label: C
options.html: Linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane

options.label: D
options.html: Mesangial deposits that stain mainly for IgA

items.explanationHtml:
Gross hematuria that starts within a day or two of an upper respiratory infection (synpharyngitic), recurs, and comes with normal complement is IgA nephropathy, the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. Immune complexes of galactose-deficient IgA1 lodge in the mesangium, where they cause mesangial proliferation.

Takeaway: hematuria during a mucosal infection with normal C3 means mesangial IgA deposits.

whyNot.A: Large subepithelial humps with granular IgG and C3 are post-infectious GN, which follows the infection by weeks and lowers C3.
whyNot.B: A "full house" pattern in subendothelial deposits is lupus nephritis, which usually lowers C3 and C4 and occurs with systemic features.
whyNot.C: Linear IgG is anti-GBM disease, which causes rapidly progressive kidney failure rather than self-limited recurrent episodes.
whyNot.E: Pauci-immune GN (ANCA vasculitis) usually causes a rapidly progressive course with systemic symptoms, not brief recurrent hematuria in a young man.

items.objective: Recognise IgA nephropathy from synpharyngitic hematuria with normal complement and predict mesangial IgA deposits.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy has had microscopic hematuria since early childhood. He now has 2+ protein on dipstick and serum creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL. Audiometry shows bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Slit-lamp examination shows a conical bulge of the anterior lens surface. His maternal uncle began dialysis at age 30. Electron microscopy of a kidney biopsy shows a glomerular basement membrane that is irregularly thickened and thinned, with splitting of the lamina densa into a layered pattern. A defect in which of the following proteins is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.html: Alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen

items.explanationHtml:
Hematuria from childhood, progressive kidney failure in a male, sensorineural hearing loss, anterior lenticonus, an affected maternal uncle and a split, "basket-weave" GBM are Alport syndrome. The most common form is X-linked, from variants in COL4A5, which encodes the alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen; the same collagen network is found in the cochlea and lens capsule.

Takeaway: hematuria, deafness and eye lesions with a split GBM point to an inherited type IV collagen defect (Alport syndrome).

whyNot.B: Fibrillin-1 defects cause Marfan syndrome, with lens dislocation and aortic root dilation but no glomerular disease.
whyNot.C: Nephrin variants cause congenital nephrotic syndrome in infancy with heavy proteinuria, not hematuria and deafness.
whyNot.D: The phospholipase A2 receptor is the target antigen in membranous nephropathy, an acquired adult nephrotic disease.
whyNot.E: Polycystin-1 defects cause autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, with enlarged cystic kidneys rather than a split GBM.

items.objective: Recognise Alport syndrome as an inherited defect of type IV collagen.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has new ankle edema and blood pressure of 152/96 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts and a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 2.6 g/g. Serum creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 1.5 mg/dL over 2 months. A kidney biopsy shows endocapillary proliferation in more than 60% of glomeruli and thickened, rigid-appearing capillary loops. Electron microscopy shows large electron-dense deposits between the endothelium and the basement membrane. Which of the following laboratory findings would best reflect the activity of this process?

options.label: A
options.html: High anti-dsDNA antibody titre with low serum C3 and C4

options.label: B
options.html: High anti-histone antibody titre with normal complement

options.label: C
options.html: High anti-Ro (SSA) antibody titre with low C4 only

options.label: D
options.html: Positive anti-phospholipid antibodies with a prolonged aPTT

options.label: E
options.html: Positive anti-Smith antibody with a normal C3

items.explanationHtml:
Diffuse proliferation with subendothelial ("wire-loop") deposits is class IV lupus nephritis. The deposits contain DNA-anti-DNA immune complexes that activate the classical pathway, so rising anti-dsDNA titres and falling C3 and C4 parallel nephritis activity. Anti-Smith antibody is very specific for lupus but does not track activity.

Takeaway: in lupus nephritis, anti-dsDNA and complement levels follow disease activity.

whyNot.B: Anti-histone antibodies point to drug-induced lupus, which rarely involves the kidney.
whyNot.C: Anti-Ro antibodies are linked to neonatal lupus and Sjögren overlap, not to the activity of nephritis.
whyNot.D: Antiphospholipid antibodies cause thrombotic microangiopathy and clotting, a different kidney lesion.
whyNot.E: Anti-Smith antibody is specific for lupus but its level does not change with disease activity.

items.objective: Use anti-dsDNA titres and complement levels to follow activity of class IV lupus nephritis.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old girl has had edema, hypertension and tea-colored urine for 3 weeks. She had no preceding infection. Serum C3 is 28 mg/dL (N = 90–180) and C4 is 30 mg/dL (N = 15–45). Antistreptolysin O and anti-DNase B are not elevated, and anti-dsDNA is negative. Kidney biopsy shows a membranoproliferative pattern; immunofluorescence shows bright C3 staining with little or no immunoglobulin. Serum studies show an IgG autoantibody that binds the alternative-pathway C3 convertase. Which of the following best describes the effect of this antibody?

options.label: A
options.html: It blocks C1 esterase inhibitor and activates the classical pathway

options.label: B
options.html: It cleaves C5 into C5a and C5b directly

options.label: C
options.html: It inactivates factor H so that C4b2a is degraded

options.label: D
options.html: It prevents C3 from binding to bacterial surfaces

options.label: E
options.html: It stabilises C3bBb and prolongs its half-life

items.explanationHtml:
Low C3 with normal C4, no streptococcal evidence and dominant C3 staining define C3 glomerulopathy. A common driver is C3 nephritic factor, an autoantibody that stabilises the alternative-pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb), protecting it from factor H-mediated decay so that C3 is consumed continuously and deposits in the glomerulus.

Takeaway: C3 nephritic factor stabilises C3bBb, giving persistent alternative-pathway activation, low C3 and C3-dominant GN.

whyNot.A: Loss of C1 esterase inhibitor function causes angioedema with low C4; it does not cause C3-only deposits.
whyNot.B: C5 convertases cleave C5; an antibody that cleaved C5 itself is not the mechanism of this disease.
whyNot.C: C4b2a is the classical-pathway convertase; C4 is normal here, so the classical pathway is not involved.
whyNot.D: Preventing C3 binding would reduce, not increase, C3 consumption and deposition.

items.objective: Explain how C3 nephritic factor causes C3 glomerulopathy by stabilising the alternative-pathway convertase.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old Black man with HIV infection who stopped antiretroviral therapy 3 years ago has 2 months of leg swelling. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 9.1 g/g, serum albumin is 2.2 g/dL and creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL. CD4 count is 85/mm³. Ultrasonography shows large, echogenic kidneys. Kidney biopsy shows glomerular capillaries collapsed by wrinkled basement membranes, with overlying swollen, proliferating podocytes and microcystic tubular dilation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Untreated HIV with heavy proteinuria, rapid loss of function and large echogenic kidneys, and a biopsy showing collapsed capillary tufts with hyperplastic podocytes and microcystic tubules, is HIV-associated nephropathy: the collapsing variant of FSGS. It is strongly linked to two APOL1 risk variants, which are common in people of West African ancestry. Antiretroviral therapy is the key treatment.

Takeaway: HIV, Black ancestry, nephrotic-range proteinuria and big echogenic kidneys mean collapsing FSGS.

whyNot.B: Nodular glomerulosclerosis needs long-standing diabetes and shows mesangial nodules, not collapsed tufts.
whyNot.C: Immune-complex MPGN occurs with hepatitis C or B and shows a nephritic, hypocomplementemic picture with double contours.
whyNot.D: Membranous nephropathy shows thickened capillary walls with subepithelial deposits and usually preserved function at first.
whyNot.E: Minimal change disease has normal light microscopy and rarely causes this degree of kidney failure.

items.objective: Recognise HIV-associated nephropathy as collapsing FSGS linked to APOL1 risk variants.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome from membranous nephropathy (serum albumin 1.9 g/dL) has sudden left flank pain and gross hematuria. Serum creatinine rose from 1.1 to 1.8 mg/dL over 2 days, and serum LDH is elevated. CT venography shows a filling defect in the left renal vein. Which of the following best explains his increased tendency to thrombosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Increased urinary loss of factor VIII

items.explanationHtml:
In nephrotic syndrome, small anticoagulant proteins such as antithrombin (and proteins C and S) are lost in the urine, while the liver, stimulated by low oncotic pressure, makes more large procoagulant proteins (fibrinogen, factors V and VIII) that are too big to be filtered. The balance shifts towards clotting, and renal vein thrombosis is most common with membranous nephropathy.

Takeaway: nephrotic hypercoagulability comes from urinary antithrombin loss plus increased hepatic procoagulant synthesis.

whyNot.A: Hepatic antithrombin synthesis does not rise enough to offset losses; increased synthesis would protect against clotting.
whyNot.B: Factor VIII is a large protein that is not filtered; its level rises in nephrotic syndrome.
whyNot.D: Fibrinogen synthesis increases, not decreases, in nephrotic syndrome.
whyNot.E: Hypoalbuminemia increases platelet aggregability rather than reducing it.

items.objective: Explain the hypercoagulable state of nephrotic syndrome and its link to renal vein thrombosis.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis for 25 years, poorly controlled despite several drugs, has 3 months of leg swelling. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 7.8 g/g and serum albumin 2.4 g/dL. Urine sediment is bland. Kidney biopsy shows acellular, pale, homogeneous material expanding the mesangium and capillary walls. With Congo red staining, the material shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light. The precursor of this material is most likely which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
Congo red-positive deposits with apple-green birefringence are amyloid. In long-standing, poorly controlled chronic inflammation such as rheumatoid arthritis, the liver makes large amounts of the acute-phase reactant serum amyloid A, which is cleaved and deposits as AA amyloid, with the kidney the main target organ.

Takeaway: chronic inflammatory disease plus nephrotic syndrome and Congo red-positive deposits means AA amyloidosis.

whyNot.A: Beta-2 microglobulin amyloid builds up in people on long-term dialysis and affects joints and carpal tunnels.
whyNot.B: Light-chain (AL) amyloid comes from a plasma cell clone; chronic inflammation without a paraprotein points to AA.
whyNot.D: Transthyretin amyloid mainly affects the heart and nerves (wild-type in older men, or hereditary forms).
whyNot.E: Type IV collagen is a normal basement-membrane protein and does not form amyloid.

items.objective: Link chronic inflammation to AA amyloidosis of the kidney.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man has had type 2 diabetes for 15 years. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 420 mg/g and eGFR is 58 mL/min/1.73 m². A kidney biopsy for an unrelated reason shows mesangial expansion with round, acellular, PAS-positive nodules and hyaline thickening of both afferent and efferent arterioles. He is started on lisinopril. Which of the following best explains how this drug slows the progression of his kidney disease?

options.label: A
options.html: Afferent arteriolar constriction that lowers renal blood flow

options.label: B
options.html: Dilation of the efferent arteriole that lowers glomerular capillary pressure

options.label: C
options.html: Increased aldosterone secretion that raises sodium reabsorption

options.label: D
options.html: Increased permeability of the glomerular basement membrane to albumin

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of sodium-glucose cotransport in the proximal tubule

items.explanationHtml:
The biopsy shows diabetic nephropathy with Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules. Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole more than the afferent, raising glomerular capillary pressure and driving hyperfiltration, proteinuria and sclerosis. ACE inhibitors and ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, lower intraglomerular pressure and reduce albuminuria. A small, stable rise in creatinine after starting them reflects this expected fall in filtration pressure.

Takeaway: RAS blockade protects the diabetic kidney by lowering intraglomerular pressure through efferent dilation.

whyNot.A: ACE inhibitors do not constrict the afferent arteriole; afferent constriction is how NSAIDs (by blocking vasodilator prostaglandins) reduce GFR.
whyNot.C: ACE inhibitors lower aldosterone, which is why they can raise potassium.
whyNot.D: Greater permeability to albumin would worsen, not slow, the disease; RAS blockade reduces albuminuria.
whyNot.E: Blocking proximal sodium-glucose cotransport is the action of SGLT2 inhibitors, which act on the afferent side through tubuloglomerular feedback.

items.objective: Explain how ACE inhibitors protect the diabetic kidney through efferent arteriolar dilation.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man is treated with intravenous nafcillin for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia. Twelve days later he has fever and a diffuse maculopapular rash. Serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.6 mg/dL. Leukocyte count is 9,800/mm³ with 11% eosinophils. Urinalysis shows white blood cells, white cell casts and 1+ protein; urine culture is negative. Which of the following best describes the main immune mechanism of this kidney injury?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibody to the glomerular basement membrane (type II hypersensitivity)

options.label: B
options.html: Circulating immune complexes deposited in glomeruli (type III hypersensitivity)

options.label: C
options.html: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation (type I hypersensitivity)

options.label: D
options.html: Nonimmune direct tubular toxicity of the drug

options.label: E
options.html: T cell-mediated interstitial inflammation (type IV hypersensitivity)

items.explanationHtml:
Fever, rash, eosinophilia, sterile pyuria with white cell casts and a rising creatinine 1–2 weeks after a beta-lactam is drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis. The drug or a hapten bound to tubular proteins triggers a delayed, T cell-mediated (type IV) reaction, with lymphocytes, macrophages and eosinophils in the interstitium.

Takeaway: drug-induced AIN is mainly a type IV hypersensitivity reaction in the interstitium.

whyNot.A: Anti-GBM antibodies cause crescentic glomerulonephritis with red cell casts, not drug-related interstitial inflammation.
whyNot.B: Immune-complex GN gives a nephritic sediment with red cell casts and often low complement.
whyNot.C: IgE mast cell reactions cause immediate urticaria and anaphylaxis; the 12-day delay and interstitial infiltrate fit a T cell reaction.
whyNot.D: Direct tubular toxicity (as with aminoglycosides) causes acute tubular necrosis with muddy brown casts, without rash or eosinophilia.

items.objective: Identify drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis as a type IV hypersensitivity reaction.

items.stemHtml:
A 71-year-old woman has 6 weeks of fatigue, arthralgia, a 4-kg weight loss and decreasing urine output. Blood pressure is 158/92 mm Hg. Lung examination is normal, and chest radiography is clear. Laboratory results:

TestResult
Serum creatinine (6 weeks ago)0.9 mg/dL
Serum creatinine (today)3.8 mg/dL
UrinalysisDysmorphic red cells, red cell casts, 2+ protein
C3 and C4Normal
Anti-myeloperoxidase (MPO) ANCAStrongly positive
Anti-proteinase 3 (PR3) ANCANegative
Anti-GBM antibodyNegative
Antinuclear antibodyNegative

A kidney biopsy is scheduled for tomorrow. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Begin hemodialysis and await the biopsy

options.label: C
options.html: Begin plasma exchange alone and await the biopsy

options.label: D
options.html: Prescribe an ACE inhibitor and recheck in 4 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat the ANCA test before any treatment

items.explanationHtml:
A rising creatinine over weeks with red cell casts, normal complement and a positive MPO-ANCA means rapidly progressive, pauci-immune GN from microscopic polyangiitis. Kidney function is at stake, so induction with glucocorticoids plus rituximab (cyclophosphamide is the alternative) should start without delay; the biopsy still proceeds to confirm the diagnosis and grade chronicity.

Takeaway: ANCA-positive rapidly progressive GN is treated at once with glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide; do not wait for the biopsy.

whyNot.B: She has no urgent indication for dialysis (no refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, overload or uremic complications), and dialysis does not treat the vasculitis.
whyNot.C: Plasma exchange is an adjunct in selected severe cases; it is not induction therapy on its own.
whyNot.D: Supportive therapy alone allows irreversible glomerular scarring over the next weeks.
whyNot.E: A strongly positive immunoassay in this picture is reliable; repeating it only delays treatment.

items.objective: Start immediate induction therapy for ANCA-associated rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy has puffy eyelids, swollen ankles and brown urine for 2 days. Three weeks ago he had crusted, honey-colored sores on his legs that healed without treatment. Blood pressure is 138/90 mm Hg (above the 95th percentile for his age and height). There is mild pitting edema. He is alert and has no headache or visual change. Urinalysis shows red cells, red cell casts and 1+ protein. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL (baseline about 0.5 mg/dL), potassium 4.8 mEq/L, C3 is low and C4 is normal. Anti-DNase B is elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Kidney biopsy before starting any treatment

options.label: D
options.html: Restriction of sodium and fluid with a loop diuretic

options.label: E
options.html: Ten days of intravenous penicillin to clear the glomeruli

items.explanationHtml:
Edema, hypertension and hematuria with red cell casts 3 weeks after impetigo, with low C3, normal C4 and a raised anti-DNase B, is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. It is self-limited in most children, so treatment is supportive: restrict sodium and fluid and give a loop diuretic for the volume overload and hypertension, adding another antihypertensive if needed. C3 should normalise within about 8 weeks.

Takeaway: post-streptococcal GN is managed supportively; immunosuppression and biopsy are not routine.

whyNot.A: Glucocorticoids do not change the course of typical post-streptococcal GN.
whyNot.B: Biopsy is reserved for atypical courses, such as low C3 beyond about 8 weeks or rapidly worsening function.
whyNot.C: Cytotoxic therapy has no role in this self-limited immune-complex disease.
whyNot.E: Antibiotics treat any ongoing streptococcal infection but do not reverse the glomerular immune complexes; the skin lesions have already healed.

items.objective: Manage post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis supportively with salt and fluid restriction and a loop diuretic.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man had kidney biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy diagnosed 3 months ago. He takes no medicines. Blood pressure today is 136/88 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL (eGFR 70 mL/min/1.73 m²), potassium 4.4 mEq/L, and the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 1.4 g/g. The biopsy showed mesangial proliferation without crescents and little scarring. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: ACE inhibitor titrated to the maximal tolerated dose

options.label: C
options.html: Dietary protein restriction to 0.4 g/kg/day alone

items.explanationHtml:
All patients with IgA nephropathy and proteinuria get optimised supportive care: an ACE inhibitor or ARB at the highest tolerated dose, a blood pressure target below about 120–130 mm Hg systolic as tolerated, an SGLT2 inhibitor when eGFR allows, salt restriction and cardiovascular risk control. Persistent proteinuria above about 0.5–1 g/day despite this marks high risk, and immunosuppressive or newer targeted therapy is then considered.

Takeaway: first-line treatment for IgA nephropathy with proteinuria is maximal RAS blockade with blood pressure control (plus an SGLT2 inhibitor).

whyNot.B: Cyclophosphamide is reserved for rapidly progressive, crescentic IgA nephropathy, which he does not have.
whyNot.C: Very low protein diets risk malnutrition and are not the main treatment; protein intake of about 0.8 g/kg/day is advised in CKD.
whyNot.D: Plasma exchange has no role in IgA nephropathy without rapidly progressive disease.
whyNot.E: Tonsillectomy is not standard treatment in most populations and does not replace RAS blockade.

items.objective: Start maximal RAS blockade as first-line therapy for IgA nephropathy with proteinuria.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man who has smoked 1 pack a day for 45 years has 2 months of leg swelling and a 6-kg weight loss. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 8.2 g/g, serum albumin 2.3 g/dL and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. Urine sediment is bland. Hepatitis B and C, HIV, ANA and serum free light chains are normal or negative, and serum anti-PLA2R antibody is negative. Kidney biopsy shows diffusely thickened capillary walls with granular IgG and C3 in subepithelial deposits; glomerular staining for PLA2R is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Observation, since one third remit spontaneously

items.explanationHtml:
The biopsy shows membranous nephropathy. Negative serum and tissue PLA2R in an older heavy smoker with weight loss raises concern for secondary membranous nephropathy from a solid tumour, most often lung or gastrointestinal cancer. Before immunosuppression, he needs a malignancy evaluation, starting with chest CT given his smoking history, plus age-appropriate colorectal screening. Treating the tumour can lead to remission of the nephropathy.

Takeaway: PLA2R-negative membranous nephropathy in an older adult should prompt a search for a secondary cause, especially cancer.

whyNot.A: Immunosuppression before ruling out cancer could worsen an occult tumour and would not address the cause.
whyNot.C: Repeating the biopsy adds nothing; the diagnosis is made, and the missing step is finding the cause.
whyNot.D: Watchful waiting is reasonable for low-risk primary disease, but red flags for cancer must be investigated first.
whyNot.E: IgG4-related disease can cause membranous nephropathy but is far less likely than lung cancer in this smoker with weight loss.

items.objective: Evaluate for malignancy in PLA2R-negative membranous nephropathy with red flags.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy diagnosed 1 month ago (serum albumin 2.0 g/dL) has sudden right flank pain and visible blood in her urine. She has had no trauma. Temperature is 37.2°C (99°F) and blood pressure 134/82 mm Hg. There is right costovertebral angle tenderness. Serum creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 1.6 mg/dL, and LDH is elevated. Urinalysis shows many red cells without casts. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Contrast CT venography of the renal veins

items.explanationHtml:
Sudden flank pain, gross hematuria, a rising creatinine and a raised LDH in a patient with membranous nephropathy and very low albumin suggest renal vein thrombosis. The diagnosis is confirmed by imaging the veins, usually CT venography (MR venography or Doppler ultrasonography are alternatives). Confirmed thrombosis is treated with anticoagulation.

Takeaway: acute flank pain and hematuria in a nephrotic patient means renal vein thrombosis until venous imaging says otherwise.

whyNot.B: Cystoscopy evaluates bladder sources of bleeding and would miss a venous clot.
whyNot.C: Intravenous pyelography is outdated and does not show the renal vein.
whyNot.D: Biopsy carries a high bleeding risk and does not diagnose venous thrombosis.
whyNot.E: Without fever or pyuria, infection is unlikely, and delaying venous imaging risks propagation and pulmonary embolism.

items.objective: Diagnose renal vein thrombosis in nephrotic syndrome with venous imaging.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed 2 years ago comes for follow-up. Her joint symptoms are controlled with hydroxychloroquine. She has no complaints. Blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg (previously 116/72). Urinalysis shows 2+ protein, dysmorphic red cells and occasional red cell casts. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 1.6 g/g. Serum creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL (0.7 mg/dL 6 months ago). C3 and C4 are low, and anti-dsDNA titre has risen. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Add an ACE inhibitor and recheck urine protein in 3 months

options.label: E
options.html: Start high-dose prednisone and stop hydroxychloroquine

items.explanationHtml:
Proteinuria above 0.5 g/day with an active sediment and a rising creatinine in lupus means lupus nephritis is likely, and a kidney biopsy is needed: the class and the activity and chronicity scores decide treatment.

Takeaway: in lupus, proteinuria of 0.5 g/day or more, an active sediment or a rising creatinine is an indication for kidney biopsy.

whyNot.A: An ACE inhibitor helps proteinuria but does not treat active proliferative nephritis, and waiting 3 months risks permanent damage.
whyNot.B: Hydroxychloroquine is continued at standard weight-based dosing; higher doses raise retinal toxicity without treating nephritis.
whyNot.D: Ultrasonography shows kidney size and excludes obstruction but cannot classify the glomerular lesion.
whyNot.E: Hydroxychloroquine should be continued in all patients with lupus, and treatment choice depends on the biopsy class.

items.objective: Biopsy the kidney when a patient with lupus develops proteinuria with an active sediment.

items.stemHtml: The biopsy shows class IV lupus nephritis with active lesions and little chronic scarring. She continues hydroxychloroquine. Which of the following is the most appropriate induction treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Class III or IV lupus nephritis needs combined induction: glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate mofetil or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide, with add-on belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor used in many patients, plus hydroxychloroquine and RAS blockade. Mycophenolate is often preferred in young women because cyclophosphamide threatens fertility.

Takeaway: induct class III or IV lupus nephritis with glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate (or low-dose cyclophosphamide).

whyNot.B: Plasma exchange has not shown benefit in typical lupus nephritis.
whyNot.C: Glucocorticoids alone are less effective and cause more toxicity than combination therapy.
whyNot.D: Methotrexate helps lupus arthritis and skin disease but is not an induction agent for proliferative nephritis.
whyNot.E: Rituximab is used for refractory disease, not as standard first-line monotherapy.

items.objective: Choose glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate for induction of class IV lupus nephritis.

items.stemHtml: Eighteen months later her nephritis is in complete remission on low-dose prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil and hydroxychloroquine. She and her partner want to have a child within the next year. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to her treatment before she tries to conceive?

options.label: B
options.html: Replace mycophenolate with azathioprine and continue hydroxychloroquine

items.explanationHtml:
Mycophenolate is teratogenic (miscarriage and malformations of the ear, face and heart) and should be replaced at least several weeks before conception. Azathioprine is compatible with pregnancy and maintains remission. Hydroxychloroquine is continued because stopping it raises the risk of flares, and it is safe in pregnancy. Pregnancy should be planned after at least about 6 months of quiescent disease.

Takeaway: before pregnancy in lupus nephritis, switch mycophenolate to azathioprine and keep hydroxychloroquine.

whyNot.A: Continuing mycophenolate exposes the fetus to a known teratogen, and stopping hydroxychloroquine increases flare risk.
whyNot.C: Cyclophosphamide is teratogenic and gonadotoxic.
whyNot.D: Methotrexate is a teratogen and abortifacient and is contraindicated in pregnancy.
whyNot.E: Stopping all therapy invites a flare of nephritis, which harms both mother and fetus.

items.objective: Switch mycophenolate to azathioprine and continue hydroxychloroquine before pregnancy in lupus nephritis.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man was started on omeprazole 8 weeks ago for dyspepsia. Routine laboratory tests now show serum creatinine of 2.3 mg/dL; it was 1.0 mg/dL 3 months ago. He feels well and has no rash or fever. He takes no NSAIDs. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, and he is euvolemic. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein, white blood cells and a few white cell casts; urine culture is negative. Kidney ultrasonography is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Increase fluid intake and recheck in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
A rise in creatinine with sterile pyuria and white cell casts after starting a proton pump inhibitor suggests drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis. Proton pump inhibitor AIN is often subtle, without rash, fever or eosinophilia. The first step is to stop the drug (an H2 blocker can replace it). If creatinine does not improve within several days, or the injury is severe, biopsy and glucocorticoids are considered.

Takeaway: suspected drug-induced AIN: stop the culprit drug first.

whyNot.A: He has no indication for dialysis.
whyNot.C: He is not volume depleted, and continuing the drug lets the inflammation progress to fibrosis.
whyNot.D: Cyclophosphamide is not a treatment for AIN.
whyNot.E: Sterile pyuria and a negative culture do not suggest bacterial infection, and sulfonamides can themselves cause AIN.

items.objective: Stop the culprit drug as the first step in proton pump inhibitor-induced interstitial nephritis.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of the worst headache of his life, followed by vomiting and neck stiffness. He has had hypertension since age 25. His father required dialysis from age 52. Examination shows bilateral, nontender, irregular abdominal masses extending from the flanks toward the pelvis. Noncontrast CT of the head shows blood in the basal cisterns. Which of the following vascular lesions most likely caused the bleeding?

options.label: A
options.html: Arteriovenous malformation of the cerebral cortex

options.label: B
options.html: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm of a lenticulostriate artery

options.label: D
options.html: Mycotic aneurysm of a distal cerebral artery

options.label: E
options.html: Saccular aneurysm at a circle of Willis branch point

items.explanationHtml:
Enlarging bilateral flank masses, early hypertension and a parent on dialysis point to autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. ADPKD weakens the arterial wall (polycystins are expressed in vascular smooth muscle), and saccular (berry) aneurysms form at branch points of the circle of Willis. Rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage, shown here by blood in the basal cisterns.

Takeaway: ADPKD plus subarachnoid hemorrhage means a ruptured berry aneurysm.

whyNot.A: Arteriovenous malformations are developmental lesions not linked to ADPKD, and they usually bleed into the brain parenchyma.
whyNot.B: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms cause deep intraparenchymal (for example basal ganglia) hemorrhage from chronic hypertension, not blood in the basal cisterns.
whyNot.C: Vertebral dissection presents with neck pain and posterior circulation stroke after trauma or neck manipulation.
whyNot.D: Mycotic aneurysms come from septic emboli, usually in infective endocarditis, and sit at distal branches.

items.objective: Recognise subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm as an extrarenal complication of ADPKD.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease has an eGFR that has fallen from 78 to 61 mL/min/1.73 m² over 3 years, and MRI shows total kidney volume far above the expected value for her age. She is started on a drug that slows the growth of her kidneys. She reports marked thirst, polyuria and nocturia after starting it. Which of the following best describes how this drug slows cyst growth?

options.label: A
options.html: It activates the calcium-sensing receptor on tubular cells

options.label: B
options.html: It blocks aldosterone binding to its nuclear receptor

options.label: C
options.html: It blocks vasopressin V2 receptors and lowers cAMP in tubular cells

options.label: D
options.html: It inhibits mTOR signalling in cyst epithelial cells

options.label: E
options.html: It inhibits the sodium-glucose cotransporter in the proximal tubule

items.explanationHtml:
Tolvaptan is a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist. In ADPKD, loss of polycystin function lowers intracellular calcium, and the resulting rise in cAMP drives cyst cell proliferation and fluid secretion. Vasopressin acting on V2 receptors in the collecting duct is a major stimulus for cAMP, so blocking it slows cyst growth and loss of GFR. Blocking V2 also prevents water reabsorption, causing aquaresis: thirst, polyuria and nocturia.

Takeaway: tolvaptan slows ADPKD by cutting vasopressin-driven cAMP in cyst epithelium.

whyNot.A: Calcium-sensing receptor agonists (calcimimetics) lower PTH in hyperparathyroidism and are not ADPKD therapy.
whyNot.B: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists treat hyperaldosteronism and heart failure; they do not cause aquaresis or slow cyst growth.
whyNot.D: mTOR inhibitors shrink angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis but did not slow kidney decline in ADPKD trials.
whyNot.E: SGLT2 inhibitors cause glycosuria and natriuresis; they are not the drug that targets ADPKD cyst growth.

items.objective: Explain how vasopressin V2 antagonism slows cyst growth in ADPKD.

items.stemHtml: A male newborn is delivered at 36 weeks' gestation after a pregnancy complicated by severe oligohydramnios. He has respiratory distress, a flattened nose, a recessed chin and bilateral clubfoot. Both flanks contain large, smooth masses. Ultrasonography shows symmetrically enlarged, diffusely echogenic kidneys. His parents are healthy, and their renal ultrasounds are normal. If he survives the neonatal period, which of the following liver abnormalities is he most likely to have?

options.label: A
options.html: Congenital hepatic fibrosis with portal hypertension

options.label: E
options.html: Multiple large hepatic cysts with normal liver function

items.explanationHtml:
Large echogenic kidneys from fetal life, oligohydramnios and the Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, facial flattening, limb deformities) with unaffected parents fit autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (PKHD1, fibrocystin). The same ciliary defect causes a ductal plate malformation in the liver, so every patient has congenital hepatic fibrosis, which leads to portal hypertension, varices and cholangitis in childhood.

Takeaway: ARPKD pairs collecting duct cysts with congenital hepatic fibrosis.

whyNot.B: Hepatic adenomas are linked to oral contraceptives, anabolic steroids and glycogen storage disease, not ARPKD.
whyNot.C: Hemangiomas are common benign vascular liver tumours unrelated to cystic kidney disease.
whyNot.D: Hepatoblastoma is linked to Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis, not ARPKD.
whyNot.E: Multiple large liver cysts with preserved function are the typical liver finding in the dominant (adult) form, ADPKD.

items.objective: Associate autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease with congenital hepatic fibrosis and the Potter sequence.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman has had seizures since childhood. Examination shows reddish papules over the nose and cheeks, several hypopigmented oval macules on the trunk and a raised, rough plaque over the lower back. CT of the abdomen shows several masses in both kidneys that contain areas of fat density. Biopsy of one mass shows mature adipose tissue, smooth muscle bundles and thick-walled blood vessels. Loss of function of the protein encoded by the mutated gene most directly causes which of the following?

options.label: C
options.html: Increased Ras activity from loss of a GTPase-activating protein

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of a ciliary calcium channel in tubular cells

options.label: E
options.html: Unrestrained activity of the MET receptor tyrosine kinase

items.explanationHtml:
Facial angiofibromas, ash-leaf macules, a shagreen patch, seizures and bilateral angiomyolipomas define tuberous sclerosis complex. Hamartin (TSC1) and tuberin (TSC2) form a complex that inactivates Rheb and so keeps mTORC1 in check. Loss of either protein leaves mTORC1 constitutively active, driving cell growth in hamartomas throughout the body; this is why the mTOR inhibitor everolimus shrinks these tumours.

Takeaway: tuberous sclerosis = loss of the hamartin-tuberin brake on mTORC1.

whyNot.B: Failure to degrade HIF is the mechanism of von Hippel-Lindau disease, which causes clear cell renal carcinoma and hemangioblastomas.
whyNot.C: Loss of the Ras GTPase-activating protein neurofibromin causes neurofibromatosis type 1.
whyNot.D: Loss of ciliary polycystin calcium channels causes ADPKD, which produces cysts rather than fat-containing tumours.
whyNot.E: Activating MET mutations cause hereditary papillary renal cell carcinoma.

items.objective: Link renal angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis complex to loss of TSC1/TSC2 control of mTORC1.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman has a 3-cm right renal mass found on CT done for abdominal pain. She has no other medical problems. Which of the following features on the CT would most strongly indicate that the mass is a benign tumour rather than a renal cell carcinoma?

options.label: A
options.html: A central area of lower density

options.label: B
options.html: Areas with attenuation below that of water, matching fat

options.label: C
options.html: Bright enhancement in the arterial phase

items.explanationHtml:
Macroscopic fat (negative attenuation values, below that of water) within a renal mass is the imaging signature of angiomyolipoma, a benign tumour of fat, smooth muscle and thick-walled vessels. Renal cell carcinomas very rarely contain visible fat, so this finding usually ends the work-up for cancer.

Takeaway: fat in a renal mass on CT means angiomyolipoma.

whyNot.A: A central low-density area can be the stellate scar of an oncocytoma, but carcinomas also have central necrosis, so it does not separate benign from malignant.
whyNot.C: Avid arterial enhancement is typical of clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
whyNot.D: Tumour thrombus in the renal vein is a feature of renal cell carcinoma.
whyNot.E: Calcification is seen in cystic carcinomas and other lesions; it does not prove the mass is benign.

items.objective: Use macroscopic fat on CT to identify a renal angiomyolipoma.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man has a 5-cm left renal mass found incidentally on CT. Partial nephrectomy is performed. The tumour is well circumscribed, mahogany brown and has a central stellate scar. Microscopy shows nests of large cells with abundant, finely granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and round, uniform nuclei. Electron microscopy of these cells would most likely show an abundance of which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
A brown, well-circumscribed renal tumour with a central scar and large eosinophilic granular cells is an oncocytoma, a benign tumour of collecting duct intercalated cells. The granular pink cytoplasm is due to cells packed with mitochondria. Surgical removal is curative.

Takeaway: oncocytes are pink because they are full of mitochondria.

whyNot.A: Glycogen and lipid give clear cell renal carcinoma its clear cytoplasm, not granular eosinophilic cytoplasm.
whyNot.B: Lipid droplets also characterise clear cell carcinoma (and foamy macrophages), not oncocytes.
whyNot.D: Abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum marks protein-secreting cells such as plasma cells.
whyNot.E: Dense-core neurosecretory granules mark neuroendocrine tumours such as carcinoid or pheochromocytoma.

items.objective: Identify renal oncocytoma and its mitochondria-rich cells.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman has had three episodes of calcium oxalate kidney stones in 4 years and one episode of pyelonephritis. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. Excretory urography shows normal-sized kidneys with linear and rounded collections of contrast in the renal papillae of both kidneys, giving a brush-like appearance, and scattered medullary calcifications. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Contrast pooling in dilated medullary collecting ducts (a brush-like pattern in the papillae) with nephrocalcinosis, recurrent calcium stones and UTIs in a young adult with normal kidney function is medullary sponge kidney. Stasis in the ectatic ducts promotes stones and infection. The prognosis for kidney function is usually good.

Takeaway: normal-sized kidneys, medullary contrast streaks and recurrent stones point to medullary sponge kidney.

whyNot.A: Acquired cystic disease occurs in small, scarred kidneys of patients with long-standing kidney failure.
whyNot.B: ADPKD produces large kidneys with cortical and medullary cysts and declining function, not papillary streaks with normal size.
whyNot.C: Chronic pyelonephritis gives coarse cortical scars over blunted calyces, not dilated papillary ducts.
whyNot.E: Nephronophthisis causes salt wasting, polyuria and kidney failure in childhood or adolescence.

items.objective: Recognise medullary sponge kidney as a cause of recurrent stones with preserved kidney function.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man has received hemodialysis for 11 years for kidney failure due to hypertensive nephrosclerosis. Ultrasonography done for an episode of gross hematuria shows two small kidneys, each containing many cysts up to 2 cm. This condition most increases his risk of which of the following?

options.label: E
options.html: Squamous cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis

items.explanationHtml:
Many cysts in small, scarred kidneys after years of dialysis is acquired cystic kidney disease. The cyst lining can become hyperplastic, and the risk of renal cell carcinoma is several times that of the general population. Cyst bleeding explains his hematuria, but a new solid component would need evaluation for cancer.

Takeaway: acquired cystic disease of dialysis raises the risk of renal cell carcinoma.

whyNot.A: Angiomyolipoma is linked to tuberous sclerosis, not to dialysis.
whyNot.B: Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumour) is a childhood tumour of metanephric blastema.
whyNot.C: Oncocytoma is a sporadic benign tumour without a recognised link to dialysis.
whyNot.E: Squamous carcinoma of the renal pelvis follows chronic irritation such as staghorn calculi, not acquired cysts.

items.objective: Associate acquired cystic kidney disease on dialysis with renal cell carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease has a blood pressure of 152/96 mm Hg on three visits. His serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL and eGFR 108 mL/min/1.73 m². MRI shows both kidneys enlarged by innumerable cysts. Which of the following best explains his hypertension at this stage?

options.label: A
options.html: Autonomous aldosterone secretion from adrenal hyperplasia

options.label: B
options.html: Cyst expansion compressing intrarenal vessels and activating the renin-angiotensin system

options.label: C
options.html: Primary sympathetic overactivity from a pheochromocytoma

options.label: D
options.html: Sodium retention caused by a reduced glomerular filtration rate

options.label: E
options.html: Volume expansion from excess vasopressin release

items.explanationHtml:
Hypertension in ADPKD often appears before the GFR falls. Enlarging cysts stretch and compress intrarenal arteries, producing patchy ischemia that stimulates renin release; angiotensin II then raises blood pressure and promotes further kidney injury. This is why ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers are first-line antihypertensives in ADPKD.

Takeaway: early ADPKD hypertension is renin driven, from cyst compression of intrarenal vessels.

whyNot.A: Primary aldosteronism is not part of ADPKD and would cause hypokalemia with suppressed renin.
whyNot.C: Pheochromocytoma is linked to von Hippel-Lindau disease and MEN2, not ADPKD.
whyNot.D: His GFR is normal, so reduced filtration with sodium retention cannot explain the hypertension now.
whyNot.E: Vasopressin promotes cyst growth through cAMP but does not cause hypertension by volume expansion.

items.objective: Explain renin-angiotensin-driven hypertension early in ADPKD.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has CT of the abdomen with contrast for right lower quadrant pain, which shows acute appendicitis. The scan also shows a 3.5-cm round lesion in the upper pole of the left kidney with a thin, smooth wall, no septa or calcification, homogeneous water attenuation and no enhancement. He has no urinary symptoms, and his serum creatinine is normal. After appendectomy, which of the following is the most appropriate management of the renal lesion?

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the kidneys in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
A thin, smooth-walled, nonenhancing cyst of water density with no septa, calcification or solid component is a Bosniak I simple cyst. Its risk of malignancy is essentially nil, so no follow-up imaging or treatment is needed.

Takeaway: Bosniak I and II cysts are benign and need no follow-up.

whyNot.A: Biopsy is not needed for a simple cyst and adds risk without benefit.
whyNot.B: Repeat imaging is for Bosniak IIF or indeterminate lesions, not a clearly simple cyst.
whyNot.D: Surgery is reserved for Bosniak III or IV lesions (enhancing walls, septa or nodules).
whyNot.E: Surveillance imaging is used for Bosniak IIF cysts; a simple cyst does not need it.

items.objective: Manage an incidental Bosniak I simple renal cyst with no follow-up.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman was diagnosed with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease at age 24. Her mother, who also had the disease, died of a subarachnoid hemorrhage at age 49. She has no headaches or neurologic symptoms. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg on lisinopril. Neurologic examination is normal. eGFR is 92 mL/min/1.73 m². She asks whether anything else should be done. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Magnetic resonance angiography of the brain

options.label: E
options.html: No screening unless she develops headaches

items.explanationHtml:
Intracranial aneurysms cluster in families with ADPKD. Screening is recommended for patients with a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage, a previous rupture, a high-risk occupation or upcoming major surgery. MR angiography (without gadolinium if needed) is the screening test of choice because it is noninvasive and needs no radiation or iodinated contrast.

Takeaway: screen ADPKD patients with a family history of aneurysm or SAH using MR angiography.

whyNot.A: Catheter angiography is invasive and reserved for treatment planning or when noninvasive imaging is unclear.
whyNot.B: Lumbar puncture looks for blood after a suspected bleed; it does not detect unruptured aneurysms.
whyNot.D: Noncontrast CT detects acute hemorrhage but cannot reliably show unruptured aneurysms.
