Mild unilateral prenatal pelvic dilation with a normal bladder and normal amniotic fluid is followed up with postnatal ultrasonography after about 48 hours (usually within the first weeks). In the first 1–2 days newborns are relatively dehydrated and oliguric, so an early scan can underestimate dilation.

Takeaway: for mild unilateral prenatal hydronephrosis, scan after 48 hours of life; scan early only for bilateral disease or suspected valves.

whyNot.A: CT exposes a newborn to radiation and contrast and adds nothing here.
whyNot.B: Prenatal dilation needs at least one postnatal ultrasound to see whether it persists.
whyNot.C: A first-day scan can miss dilation because of physiologic neonatal oliguria.
whyNot.E: Voiding cystourethrography is invasive and is reserved for persistent dilation, ureteral dilation or suspected valves.

items.objective: Time the postnatal ultrasound after mild unilateral prenatal hydronephrosis.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, has a mid-trimester anatomy ultrasound at 20 weeks. There is no measurable amniotic fluid. Neither kidney nor the fetal bladder is visible on repeated scanning, including with colour Doppler of the renal arteries. Membranes are intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Serial amnioinfusion every week until delivery

options.label: B
options.html: Counselling about the lethal prognosis and her options

options.label: C
options.html: Fetal vesicoamniotic shunt placement this week

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat ultrasonography at 32 weeks before counselling

options.label: E
options.html: Planned cesarean delivery at 34 weeks with neonatal dialysis

items.explanationHtml:
Absent kidneys, absent bladder and anhydramnios at 20 weeks indicate bilateral renal agenesis. Lung development cannot proceed without amniotic fluid, so the outcome is lethal pulmonary hypoplasia. The appropriate step is clear, compassionate counselling about the prognosis and her options (continuing with perinatal palliative care, or ending the pregnancy), with genetic evaluation and support.

Takeaway: bilateral renal agenesis is lethal; counsel about prognosis and options rather than offering interventions that cannot change it.

whyNot.A: Serial amnioinfusion remains experimental in bilateral renal agenesis and is not a standard option to offer as routine treatment.
whyNot.C: Shunting treats lower urinary tract obstruction in a fetus with kidneys and a full bladder; there is no bladder to drain.
whyNot.D: The diagnosis is already clear, and delaying counselling removes choices from the patient.
whyNot.E: Early delivery cannot overcome pulmonary hypoplasia, and dialysis does not address the cause of death.

items.objective: Counsel about the lethal prognosis of bilateral renal agenesis found prenatally.

items.stemHtml: A 3-week-old girl has a nontender left flank mass found at a routine visit. She is feeding and growing well. Blood pressure is normal. Ultrasonography shows a left kidney replaced by many noncommunicating cysts of different sizes with no normal parenchyma, and a normal right kidney without dilation. A nuclear renal scan shows no function on the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Percutaneous aspiration of the largest cysts

items.explanationHtml:
This is a multicystic dysplastic kidney, a nonfunctioning dysplastic kidney that usually shrinks over time. Management is conservative with serial ultrasonography to confirm involution and compensatory growth of the other kidney, plus blood pressure checks. Nephrectomy is reserved for complications such as a growing mass, hypertension or a solid component.

Takeaway: multicystic dysplastic kidney is managed with serial ultrasound; surgery is for complications only.

whyNot.A: Routine nephrectomy carries surgical risk without benefit in an uncomplicated case.
whyNot.B: Aspirating cysts does not change the course and the cysts reaccumulate.
whyNot.C: Pyeloplasty relieves ureteropelvic junction obstruction in a kidney that works; this kidney has no function.
whyNot.E: Nothing suggests a malignant tumour; the appearance is diagnostic of dysplasia.

items.objective: Manage an uncomplicated multicystic dysplastic kidney with serial ultrasonography.

items.stemHtml: A 5-year-old girl has been wet day and night for as long as her parents remember, although she also voids normally every 3–4 hours. She has had no UTIs. Examination of the abdomen, back and lower limb neurologic function is normal, and her underwear is damp. Urinalysis is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Continuous wetness with a normal voiding pattern in a girl suggests an ectopic ureter opening below the sphincter, usually from the upper pole of a duplex kidney. The first test is renal and bladder ultrasonography, which typically shows the duplex kidney with a dilated upper pole; MRI urography or cystoscopy then locates the opening.

Takeaway: a girl who is always damp but voids normally needs renal and bladder ultrasonography to look for a duplex kidney with an ectopic ureter.

whyNot.A: An alarm treats nocturnal enuresis; it cannot stop leakage that bypasses the bladder.
whyNot.C: A normal back and neurologic examination make an occult spinal lesion unlikely; anatomy should be imaged first.
whyNot.D: Urodynamics evaluate bladder function, which is normal; they do not show an ectopic ureter.
whyNot.E: Continuous day-and-night wetness is not normal and must be investigated.

items.objective: Investigate continuous incontinence in a girl with renal and bladder ultrasonography.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl was recently diagnosed with Turner syndrome (45,X) after evaluation for short stature. Echocardiography shows a bicuspid aortic valve without coarctation. She has no urinary symptoms, and urinalysis and serum creatinine are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional evaluation at this time?

options.label: A
options.html: CT angiography of the renal arteries

options.label: C
options.html: No renal evaluation unless symptoms develop

items.explanationHtml:
About a third of girls with Turner syndrome have a structural kidney anomaly, most often a horseshoe kidney or a duplicated or malrotated collecting system. Renal ultrasonography at diagnosis is recommended for every patient, even without symptoms, because these anomalies predispose to obstruction, infection and hypertension.

Takeaway: screen every girl with Turner syndrome with renal ultrasonography at diagnosis.

whyNot.A: CT angiography uses radiation and contrast and is not a screening test for structural anomalies.
whyNot.B: A DMSA scan looks for cortical scarring after infection; ultrasound is the screening test.
whyNot.C: Renal anomalies are common and often silent, so screening is advised at diagnosis.
whyNot.E: Voiding cystourethrography is for suspected reflux after a febrile UTI or abnormal ultrasound.

items.objective: Screen for renal anomalies in Turner syndrome with ultrasonography.

items.stemHtml: A 2-month-old boy has moist umbilical drainage since his cord fell off at 10 days. The drainage is clear, more noticeable with crying, and its creatinine level is far above his serum creatinine. He is afebrile and the umbilicus is not red. He voids with a strong stream. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.label: A
options.html: Application of silver nitrate to the umbilicus

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the abdomen with oral contrast

options.label: C
options.html: Fistulogram through the umbilicus with barium

options.label: E
options.html: Ultrasonography of the umbilical region and bladder

items.explanationHtml:
Umbilical drainage with a high creatinine indicates a patent urachus. Ultrasonography is the first test to show the tract between the bladder dome and the umbilicus. Voiding cystourethrography is often added to exclude bladder outlet obstruction, which can keep the urachus open. Symptomatic remnants are excised.

Takeaway: suspected patent urachus: ultrasonography first, then surgical excision of the remnant.

whyNot.A: Silver nitrate treats an umbilical granuloma, which drains small amounts of serous fluid, not urine.
whyNot.B: CT exposes an infant to radiation and is not the first test for a superficial tract.
whyNot.C: A barium study would be used to look for a vitelline duct remnant draining bowel content, not urine.
whyNot.D: A patent urachus does not close on its own and risks infection, so it should be evaluated now.

items.objective: Evaluate a suspected patent urachus with ultrasonography.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy has had three episodes of left flank pain with vomiting over 6 months, each lasting several hours. Between episodes he is well. Ultrasonography shows marked dilation of the left renal pelvis and calyces with a normal-calibre left ureter and normal bladder; the right kidney is normal. Serum creatinine is 0.5 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to assess obstruction and the function of each kidney?

options.label: B
options.html: Diuretic renal scintigraphy with MAG3 and furosemide

items.explanationHtml:
Symptomatic hydronephrosis with a normal ureter suggests ureteropelvic junction obstruction. Diuretic renography (technetium-99m MAG3 with furosemide) shows whether tracer drains promptly after the diuretic, which separates true obstruction from a baggy but unobstructed pelvis, and it measures the split function of each kidney.

Takeaway: for suspected ureteropelvic junction obstruction, diuretic renography shows drainage and split function.

whyNot.A: CT urography gives anatomy but not reliable split function or drainage curves, and it uses more radiation.
whyNot.C: Intravenous pyelography is outdated and gives neither split function nor quantified drainage.
whyNot.D: Retrograde pyelography is invasive and is used during surgery, not as the first functional test.
whyNot.E: Voiding cystourethrography looks for reflux; the normal ureter makes reflux unlikely.

items.objective: Assess suspected ureteropelvic junction obstruction with diuretic renography.

items.stemHtml: Diuretic renography in the boy shows that the left kidney contributes 32% of total function, and tracer stays in the left renal pelvis with little drainage 30 minutes after furosemide. The right kidney drains promptly. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continuous antibiotic prophylaxis and repeat scan in 1 year

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent pain, reduced split function (below about 40%) and obstructed drainage all favour surgery. Dismembered pyeloplasty (open, laparoscopic or robotic) removes the narrowed segment, reattaches the ureter to the pelvis and repositions it in front of any crossing vessel, with high success.

Takeaway: symptomatic ureteropelvic junction obstruction with reduced split function needs pyeloplasty.

whyNot.A: Watching is reasonable for an asymptomatic child with preserved function, not for recurrent pain and reduced function.
whyNot.B: Lithotripsy breaks stones; there is no stone.
whyNot.D: A kidney with 32% function is well worth saving; nephrectomy is for a kidney with negligible function.
whyNot.E: Long-term stents are a temporary bridge with infection and encrustation risks, not definitive treatment.

items.objective: Choose pyeloplasty for symptomatic ureteropelvic junction obstruction with reduced split function.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man with hypertension and peripheral artery disease starts lisinopril. Two weeks later his serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL and potassium from 4.4 to 5.6 mEq/L. Urinalysis is bland. Doppler ultrasonography later shows high-grade stenosis of both renal arteries. Which of the following best explains the fall in glomerular filtration rate?

options.label: C
options.html: Immune complex deposition in the glomerular basement membrane

options.label: D
options.html: Injury to proximal tubule epithelial cells

options.label: E
options.html: Obstruction of tubules by drug crystals

items.explanationHtml:
With bilateral renal artery stenosis, glomerular pressure depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole. An ACE inhibitor removes that tone, the efferent arteriole dilates, glomerular capillary pressure falls and GFR drops sharply. Lower aldosterone explains the rising potassium.

Takeaway: ACE inhibitors and ARBs lower GFR by dilating the efferent arteriole; a large creatinine rise suggests renal artery stenosis.

whyNot.A: Afferent constriction is how NSAIDs and calcineurin inhibitors lower GFR, not ACE inhibitors.
whyNot.C: Immune complex glomerulonephritis gives an active sediment with hematuria and casts; this urine is bland.
whyNot.D: Direct proximal tubule injury is the mechanism of aminoglycosides and cisplatin and would give granular casts.
whyNot.E: Crystal nephropathy occurs with drugs such as acyclovir or methotrexate, not ACE inhibitors.

items.objective: Explain how ACE inhibitors reduce GFR by removing angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old woman with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction takes furosemide and carvedilol. She takes ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for 1 week for knee pain. Her serum creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.1 mg/dL. BUN is 48 mg/dL, urine sodium 12 mEq/L, and urine sediment is bland. Loss of which of the following normal effects most directly explains her acute kidney injury?

options.label: A
options.html: Aldosterone-driven sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct

options.label: B
options.html: Angiotensin II constriction of the efferent arteriole

options.label: D
options.html: Nitric oxide release from the macula densa

options.label: E
options.html: Prostaglandin dilation of the afferent arteriole

items.explanationHtml:
In heart failure, renal perfusion is low and GFR depends on prostaglandin E2 and prostacyclin dilating the afferent arteriole. NSAIDs block cyclooxygenase, so the afferent arteriole constricts and GFR falls. The prerenal picture (BUN:creatinine above 20, low urine sodium, bland urine) fits.

Takeaway: NSAIDs cause hemodynamic AKI in prostaglandin-dependent states such as heart failure, cirrhosis and volume depletion.

whyNot.A: NSAIDs reduce aldosterone and renin slightly, which raises potassium, but loss of sodium reabsorption would not lower GFR.
whyNot.B: Efferent constriction is lost with ACE inhibitors and ARBs, which she does not take.
whyNot.C: Antidiuretic hormone controls water reabsorption, not GFR.
whyNot.D: Macula densa signalling adjusts afferent tone through tubuloglomerular feedback, but the key NSAID effect is loss of prostaglandins.

items.objective: Explain NSAID-induced acute kidney injury through loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilation.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man is treated with intravenous gentamicin and piperacillin-tazobactam for Pseudomonas pneumonia. On day 8, his serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.3 mg/dL. Urine output is 1.8 L/day. Serum magnesium is 1.2 mEq/L. Urine microscopy shows many muddy brown granular casts. Which of the following steps in gentamicin handling most directly leads to this injury?

options.label: A
options.html: Binding to megalin and endocytosis into proximal tubule cells

options.label: B
options.html: Deposition of drug-antibody complexes in the glomerulus

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of cyclooxygenase in the renal medulla

options.label: D
options.html: Precipitation of the drug in acidic urine of the collecting duct

options.label: E
options.html: T-cell recognition of the drug bound to interstitial proteins

items.explanationHtml:
Aminoglycosides are filtered freely, then the positively charged molecules bind megalin on the proximal tubule brush border and are taken in by endocytosis. They accumulate in lysosomes, which eventually rupture and kill the cell, giving nonoliguric acute tubular necrosis after about a week, with granular casts and magnesium and potassium wasting.

Takeaway: aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity is proximal tubule necrosis from megalin-mediated uptake; it is usually nonoliguric and delayed.

whyNot.B: Immune complex disease would produce glomerulonephritis with hematuria, not granular casts and tubular magnesium loss.
whyNot.C: Cyclooxygenase inhibition is the NSAID mechanism of hemodynamic AKI.
whyNot.D: Intratubular crystal precipitation is typical of acyclovir, methotrexate and sulfonamides.
whyNot.E: T-cell hypersensitivity causes interstitial nephritis with white cell casts, the pattern of beta-lactams and PPIs.

items.objective: Describe the proximal tubular uptake mechanism of aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity.

items.stemHtml:
A 40-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukemia receives intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate for invasive aspergillosis. After 10 days her laboratory results are:

TestResult
Sodium139 mEq/L
Potassium2.8 mEq/L
Chloride114 mEq/L
Bicarbonate15 mEq/L
Magnesium1.1 mEq/L
Arterial pH7.30
Urine pH6.4

Which of the following best explains her acid-base disorder?

options.label: A
options.html: Back-leak of secreted hydrogen ions across the collecting duct epithelium

options.label: B
options.html: Excess production of ketoacids from fatty acid oxidation

options.label: C
options.html: Failure of proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption

options.label: E
options.html: Low aldosterone effect on the collecting duct

items.explanationHtml:
She has a normal anion gap (139 − 114 − 15 = 10) metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately high urine pH, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia: distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis. Amphotericin B binds membrane cholesterol and forms pores in collecting duct cells, so secreted H+ leaks back and K+ leaks out.

Takeaway: amphotericin B causes distal RTA with hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia by making collecting duct membranes leaky.

whyNot.B: Ketoacidosis gives a high anion gap; her gap is normal.
whyNot.C: Proximal (type 2) RTA lets urine acidify below 5.5 once bicarbonate falls; her urine pH stays high. Tenofovir and ifosfamide cause proximal RTA.
whyNot.D: Diarrhea also gives normal-gap acidosis, but the kidney responds by acidifying urine well below 5.5.
whyNot.E: Hypoaldosteronism (type 4 RTA) causes hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia.

items.objective: Recognise amphotericin B-induced distal renal tubular acidosis from laboratory values.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium for 12 years with levels in the therapeutic range. She now passes about 6 L of dilute urine a day and drinks large amounts of water. Serum sodium is 145 mEq/L. After water deprivation, urine osmolality is 170 mOsm/kg, and it rises to only 185 mOsm/kg after desmopressin. Which of the following best explains her polyuria?

options.label: C
options.html: Increased thirst from a hypothalamic effect of lithium

options.label: D
options.html: Reduced expression of aquaporin-2 in collecting duct principal cells

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced sodium chloride reabsorption in the thick ascending limb

items.explanationHtml:
Failure to concentrate urine despite desmopressin is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Lithium enters principal cells through the epithelial sodium channel, accumulates and inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3 signalling, which lowers aquaporin-2 production and insertion, so the collecting duct cannot respond to antidiuretic hormone.

Takeaway: lithium causes nephrogenic DI by reducing aquaporin-2 in principal cells; it enters them through ENaC.

whyNot.A: Central DI would respond to desmopressin with a large rise in urine osmolality.
whyNot.B: Glycosuria causes osmotic diuresis with urine that is not maximally dilute; she has no hyperglycemia.
whyNot.C: Primary polydipsia gives low or low-normal serum sodium and concentrates urine after water deprivation.
whyNot.E: Loop diuretics impair concentration by blocking the thick ascending limb; lithium acts mainly on principal cells.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has taken a regimen containing tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for HIV for 6 years. He has new bone pain. Serum glucose is 92 mg/dL, phosphorus 1.8 mg/dL, bicarbonate 18 mEq/L with a normal anion gap, and uric acid 1.9 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows 2+ glucose and low-grade proteinuria. Which part of the nephron is primarily affected?

options.label: E
options.html: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

items.explanationHtml:
Glycosuria with normal blood glucose, phosphate wasting (with osteomalacia causing bone pain), low uric acid and a normal-gap acidosis is Fanconi syndrome, a generalised failure of the proximal convoluted tubule, which reabsorbs glucose, phosphate, amino acids, urate and most bicarbonate. Tenofovir enters these cells through basolateral organic anion transporters and injures their mitochondria.

Takeaway: tenofovir disoproxil causes proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi syndrome); tenofovir alafenamide is much less toxic to the kidney.

whyNot.A: Collecting duct disease causes distal RTA or nephrogenic DI, not glycosuria and phosphate wasting.
whyNot.B: The distal convoluted tubule handles sodium chloride and calcium; it does not reabsorb glucose.
whyNot.C: Glomerular disease causes proteinuria and hematuria but not this pattern of tubular solute wasting.
whyNot.E: Thick ascending limb defects (as in Bartter syndrome) cause hypokalemic alkalosis, not acidosis with glycosuria.

items.objective: Localise tenofovir-induced Fanconi syndrome to the proximal tubule.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman with herpes simplex encephalitis receives high-dose intravenous acyclovir given as rapid infusions. She has been drinking little. On day 3, her serum creatinine rises from 0.7 to 2.0 mg/dL. Polarised microscopy of the urine shows many needle-shaped birefringent crystals within white blood cells and free in the urine. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of her kidney injury?

options.label: A
options.html: Immune-mediated injury to tubular basement membrane

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of prostaglandin-dependent renal blood flow

items.explanationHtml:
Acyclovir is poorly soluble in urine. With a high dose, rapid infusion and low urine flow it precipitates as needle-shaped crystals in the distal tubules and collecting ducts, obstructing them and causing inflammation. Prevention is adequate hydration and slower infusion; treatment is fluids and dose adjustment.

Takeaway: IV acyclovir, methotrexate, sulfonamides and indinavir cause crystal nephropathy; hydration prevents it.

whyNot.A: Anti-tubular basement membrane disease is rare and not linked to crystals.
whyNot.B: Blocked creatinine secretion (trimethoprim, cimetidine) raises creatinine slightly without crystals or true injury.
whyNot.D: Hemodynamic AKI from lost prostaglandins is the NSAID mechanism and gives a bland sediment.
whyNot.E: Thrombotic microangiopathy occurs with calcineurin inhibitors, gemcitabine or VEGF inhibitors, with hemolysis and low platelets.

items.objective: Recognise acyclovir crystal nephropathy and its mechanism.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman with lupus nephritis is about to start intravenous cyclophosphamide. To prevent a urinary bladder complication, she is given vigorous hydration and a second drug that contains a free sulfhydryl group and is concentrated in the urine. Which of the following is the action of this second drug?

options.label: A
options.html: It alkalinises urine to keep the parent drug in solution

options.label: B
options.html: It binds and inactivates acrolein in the bladder

options.label: C
options.html: It blocks muscarinic receptors on the detrusor

options.label: D
options.html: It inhibits hepatic conversion of cyclophosphamide to active metabolites

options.label: E
options.html: It supplies reduced folate to urothelial cells

items.explanationHtml:
Cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide are metabolised to acrolein, which is excreted in urine and damages the urothelium, causing hemorrhagic cystitis. Mesna is a thiol that is concentrated in urine, where it binds acrolein and makes it harmless, without affecting the drug's anticancer or immunosuppressive effect.

Takeaway: mesna (with hydration) prevents acrolein-induced hemorrhagic cystitis from cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide.

whyNot.A: Urine alkalinisation is used with methotrexate to prevent crystal nephropathy, not with cyclophosphamide.
whyNot.C: Antimuscarinics treat overactive bladder; they do not protect the urothelium.
whyNot.D: Blocking activation would remove the drug's therapeutic effect; mesna acts only on the toxic metabolite in urine.
whyNot.E: Reduced folate (leucovorin) rescues normal cells from methotrexate, not from cyclophosphamide.

items.objective: Explain how mesna prevents cyclophosphamide-induced hemorrhagic cystitis.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man who has received hemodialysis for 4 years has progressive tightening and woody induration of the skin of both legs and forearms over 3 months, with new flexion contractures of the knees. His face is spared. He had several contrast-enhanced imaging studies over the past year. Skin biopsy shows thickened collagen bundles in the dermis and subcutaneous septa with many CD34-positive spindle cells and no inflammation. Which agent is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Symmetric hardening of the skin of the limbs with contractures, sparing the face, in a patient on dialysis is nephrogenic systemic fibrosis. It follows exposure to gadolinium-based contrast when kidney clearance is severely reduced; free gadolinium deposits in tissue and recruits circulating fibrocytes (CD34-positive), which lay down collagen. Risk is highest with older linear agents.

Takeaway: gadolinium in advanced CKD or dialysis can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

whyNot.A: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents cause hypertension and thrombosis, not dermal fibrosis.
whyNot.C: Heparin can cause skin necrosis or thrombocytopenia but not this fibrosing disease.
whyNot.D: Iodinated contrast can cause acute kidney injury in patients not yet on dialysis, but not nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.
whyNot.E: Sevelamer is a phosphate binder with mainly gastrointestinal side effects.

items.objective: Link nephrogenic systemic fibrosis to gadolinium exposure in advanced kidney disease.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman has taken omeprazole for 4 months for reflux. Her serum creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 2.6 mg/dL. She has no fever or rash. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein, 15–20 white blood cells/hpf, white blood cell casts and a negative culture. Ultrasonography shows normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on kidney biopsy?

options.label: B
options.html: Interstitial edema with lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils

options.label: C
options.html: Necrotic proximal tubular cells sloughed into the lumen with no inflammation

options.label: E
options.html: Subepithelial immune deposits along the basement membrane

items.explanationHtml:
Sterile pyuria with white cell casts and a rising creatinine in someone taking a proton pump inhibitor is drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis, a T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction. The biopsy shows interstitial edema and an infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils, with tubulitis and normal glomeruli. PPI-associated AIN often lacks fever, rash and eosinophilia and begins months after the drug is started.

Takeaway: PPIs, beta-lactams and NSAIDs cause AIN: sterile pyuria, white cell casts, and an eosinophil-rich interstitial infiltrate.

whyNot.A: Crescents mark rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, with red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells.
whyNot.C: Acute tubular necrosis without inflammation fits aminoglycosides or ischemia, with granular rather than white cell casts.
whyNot.D: Nodular mesangial sclerosis is diabetic nephropathy, which develops over years.
whyNot.E: Subepithelial deposits are membranous nephropathy, which presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria.

items.objective: Recognise the histology of PPI-induced acute interstitial nephritis.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and stage G4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 26 mL/min/1.73 m²) has a new 3-cm colon mass on colonoscopy. A contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is planned for staging. He takes insulin glargine, amlodipine and naproxen as needed. He is euvolemic, with blood pressure 138/80 mm Hg and no edema. Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to reduce his risk of contrast-associated kidney injury?

options.label: A
options.html: Cancel the CT and stage the cancer with ultrasonography

options.label: B
options.html: Give high-dose oral N-acetylcysteine the day before and the day of the scan

options.label: C
options.html: Give intravenous isotonic saline before and after the scan and stop naproxen

options.label: D
options.html: Perform hemodialysis immediately after the scan

options.label: E
options.html: Substitute an MRI with a linear gadolinium agent

items.explanationHtml:
His eGFR below 30 puts him at higher risk of contrast-associated kidney injury, but the study is needed. In a euvolemic patient, intravenous isotonic crystalloid before and after contrast, the lowest needed dose of a low- or iso-osmolar agent, and pausing nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs are the evidence-based measures.

Takeaway: prevent contrast-associated AKI with isotonic IV fluids and by stopping nephrotoxins; N-acetylcysteine and prophylactic dialysis do not help.

whyNot.A: Withholding a needed staging study harms cancer care; ultrasonography cannot stage the chest and nodes adequately.
whyNot.B: Trials have shown no benefit of N-acetylcysteine for preventing contrast-associated kidney injury.
whyNot.D: Prophylactic dialysis does not prevent kidney injury in patients not already on dialysis.
whyNot.E: Linear gadolinium agents carry the highest risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis when eGFR is below 30.

items.objective: Use isotonic IV fluids and stop nephrotoxins to reduce contrast-associated AKI in a high-risk patient.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 420 mg/g) was started on lisinopril 10 mg daily 2 weeks ago. She feels well. Blood pressure has fallen from 148/90 to 132/80 mm Hg. Serum creatinine has risen from 1.30 to 1.55 mg/dL, and potassium from 4.6 to 4.9 mEq/L. She takes no NSAIDs and is not volume depleted. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue lisinopril and recheck laboratory values in a few weeks

options.label: B
options.html: Order renal artery duplex ultrasonography this week

options.label: C
options.html: Start sodium polystyrene sulfonate for the potassium

options.label: D
options.html: Stop lisinopril and start amlodipine instead

options.label: E
options.html: Switch lisinopril to losartan at an equivalent dose

items.explanationHtml:
The creatinine has risen by about 19% and potassium remains acceptable. A rise of up to about 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor reflects the intended fall in intraglomerular pressure, which slows CKD progression in albuminuric diabetes. The drug should be continued with repeat monitoring.

Takeaway: after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB, accept a creatinine rise of up to about 30% and keep the drug.

whyNot.B: Renovascular evaluation is for a larger rise (above about 30%) or other clues to renal artery stenosis.
whyNot.C: Potassium 4.9 mEq/L needs no binder.
whyNot.D: Stopping would lose the kidney-protective benefit; amlodipine does not lower albuminuria.
whyNot.E: An ARB acts on the same efferent arteriole and would give the same expected creatinine rise.

items.objective: Continue an ACE inhibitor when creatinine rises by less than about 30% after starting it.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man with HIV (CD4 count 140/mm³) starts trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis. Six days later, routine laboratory studies show serum creatinine 1.25 mg/dL (baseline 0.95 mg/dL), BUN 13 mg/dL (baseline 12 mg/dL) and potassium 5.1 mEq/L. He feels well and urine output is normal. Urinalysis shows no blood, protein, white cells, casts or crystals. Serum cystatin C is unchanged from baseline. Which of the following best explains the creatinine rise?
items.explanationHtml:
Trimethoprim competes with creatinine for tubular secretion through organic cation transporters, so serum creatinine rises by about 10–30% without a true fall in GFR. The clues are an unchanged BUN, unchanged cystatin C and a bland urine. Trimethoprim also blocks ENaC in the collecting duct, which explains the slight rise in potassium.

Takeaway: trimethoprim (and cimetidine) can raise creatinine by blocking its secretion; check BUN, urine and cystatin C before calling it AKI.

whyNot.A: Interstitial nephritis would produce pyuria, white cell casts and a falling true GFR (rising cystatin C).
whyNot.B: Tubular necrosis would show granular casts and a falling GFR with rising BUN.
whyNot.D: Prerenal azotemia raises BUN more than creatinine; his BUN is unchanged and he is not volume depleted.
whyNot.E: Sulfonamide crystals would be seen in the urine, and injury would raise cystatin C.

items.objective: Distinguish trimethoprim's inhibition of creatinine secretion from true acute kidney injury.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with metastatic melanoma has received pembrolizumab every 3 weeks for 5 months. His serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.4 mg/dL over 3 weeks. He takes no NSAIDs or proton pump inhibitors and has not received contrast. He is euvolemic. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein, white blood cells and white blood cell casts, with a negative culture. Ultrasonography shows normal kidneys without hydronephrosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue pembrolizumab and give intravenous fluids

options.label: B
options.html: Hold pembrolizumab and start oral prednisone

items.explanationHtml:
Sterile pyuria with white cell casts and a creatinine 2–3 times baseline in a patient on an immune checkpoint inhibitor, with other causes excluded, is immune-related acute interstitial nephritis. For this moderate injury, guidelines advise holding the checkpoint inhibitor and giving corticosteroids (prednisone about 0.5–1 mg/kg/day, then a slow taper). Kidney biopsy is considered when the diagnosis is uncertain.

Takeaway: checkpoint inhibitor AIN: hold the drug and give prednisone.

whyNot.A: Continuing the drug lets the immune injury progress; he is not volume depleted.
whyNot.C: He has no indication for dialysis (no refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, overload or uremia).
whyNot.D: Plasma exchange is for antibody-mediated disease such as anti-GBM disease, not T-cell AIN.
whyNot.E: Ipilimumab is another checkpoint inhibitor with a higher rate of immune-related adverse effects.

items.objective: Manage immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated interstitial nephritis by holding the drug and giving corticosteroids.

items.stemHtml:
A 57-year-old woman is receiving cisplatin-based chemotherapy for cervical cancer. She reports muscle cramps and fatigue. She has had no vomiting or diarrhea. Over the past week she has received oral potassium supplements, 80 mEq a day in two doses, but her potassium has not improved. Laboratory results:

TestResult
Sodium138 mEq/L
Potassium2.9 mEq/L
Bicarbonate27 mEq/L
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL
Calcium, total8.0 mg/dL
Magnesium0.9 mEq/L

ECG shows prominent U waves. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate along with potassium

options.label: E
options.html: Stop potassium and recheck in 1 week

items.explanationHtml:
Cisplatin injures the tubule and causes persistent renal magnesium wasting. Low intracellular magnesium removes its normal block on ROMK potassium channels, so the kidney keeps losing potassium and hypokalemia does not correct until magnesium is replaced. Low magnesium also impairs PTH release, contributing to her low calcium.

Takeaway: refractory hypokalemia (often with hypocalcemia) on cisplatin, aminoglycosides or amphotericin: replace magnesium.

whyNot.A: Spironolactone reduces potassium loss somewhat but does not fix the underlying magnesium deficit and adds hyperkalemia risk once corrected.
whyNot.B: More potassium alone will keep being lost in the urine while magnesium stays low.
whyNot.C: Calcium does not treat hypokalemia; her calcium will improve once magnesium is replaced.
whyNot.E: Stopping replacement with potassium 2.9 mEq/L and U waves is unsafe.

items.objective: Replace magnesium to correct refractory hypokalemia in cisplatin-induced magnesium wasting.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia began taking diphenhydramine nightly for insomnia 4 days ago. He now has lower abdominal pain and has passed only small dribbles of urine for 12 hours. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). The lower abdomen is distended and tender to the umbilicus. Bladder ultrasonography shows 950 mL of urine. Serum creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the abdomen and pelvis

options.label: B
options.html: Oral bethanechol and a repeat bladder scan in 6 hours

options.label: E
options.html: Suprapubic cystostomy in the operating room

items.explanationHtml:
He has acute urinary retention triggered by an anticholinergic antihistamine on a background of prostatic enlargement. The first step is bladder decompression with a urethral catheter. Then stop the diphenhydramine, start an alpha-1 blocker such as tamsulosin, and plan a trial without catheter after a few days.

Takeaway: drug-induced acute urinary retention: catheterise first, then stop the drug and add an alpha blocker.

whyNot.A: Imaging is not needed before relieving an obvious distended bladder.
whyNot.B: Bethanechol is not effective for acute retention and delaying drainage prolongs pain and kidney injury.
whyNot.D: Tamsulosin helps a later trial without catheter, but the full bladder must be drained now.
whyNot.E: Suprapubic drainage is reserved for failed or contraindicated urethral catheterisation.

items.objective: Decompress the bladder first in drug-induced acute urinary retention.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man with bipolar I disorder, stable on lithium for 9 years, has had increasing thirst and nocturia for 6 months. He drinks about 7 L of water a day. Lithium level is 0.8 mEq/L (therapeutic). Serum sodium is 146 mEq/L, glucose 94 mg/dL and calcium 9.6 mg/dL. Urine osmolality is 110 mOsm/kg. During a supervised water deprivation test, urine osmolality reaches 160 mOsm/kg; 1 hour after desmopressin it is 170 mOsm/kg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: E
options.html: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

items.explanationHtml:
Dilute urine that stays dilute after water deprivation and rises by less than 10% after desmopressin, with high-normal sodium, means the kidney cannot respond to antidiuretic hormone: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, here from long-term lithium.

Takeaway: no concentration after desmopressin means nephrogenic DI; lithium is the commonest drug cause.

whyNot.A: Central DI concentrates urine substantially (often by more than 50%) after desmopressin.
whyNot.C: Osmotic diuresis (for example glycosuria) gives urine osmolality near or above plasma; his glucose is normal.
whyNot.D: Primary polydipsia gives low-normal sodium and concentrates urine during water deprivation.
whyNot.E: SIADH causes hyponatremia with concentrated urine, the opposite pattern.

items.objective: Diagnose lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from a water deprivation test.

items.stemHtml: His psychiatrist advises that lithium has kept him well after several failed alternatives, and he wishes to continue it. His lithium level remains 0.8 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to reduce his polyuria?
items.explanationHtml:
Lithium reaches principal cells through the epithelial sodium channel. Amiloride blocks this channel, lowering intracellular lithium and partly restoring the response to antidiuretic hormone, with little effect on lithium levels. Thiazides also lessen polyuria but raise lithium levels, so they need close monitoring. Lithium levels, kidney function, calcium and TSH should still be checked regularly.

Takeaway: amiloride treats lithium-induced nephrogenic DI when lithium must continue.

whyNot.B: Demeclocycline itself causes nephrogenic DI and is used to treat SIADH.
whyNot.C: Desmopressin does not work because the collecting duct cannot respond to it.
whyNot.D: Furosemide increases urine output and can deplete volume, raising lithium levels.
whyNot.E: Tolvaptan blocks vasopressin V2 receptors and would worsen water loss.

items.objective: Treat lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with amiloride.

items.stemHtml: An 11-year-old girl has had increased thirst, bedwetting and a 4-kg weight loss over 5 weeks. Random plasma glucose is 412 mg/dL, and serum C-peptide is low. Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase are present. If pancreatic tissue had been examined at this stage, which of the following findings would most likely be seen in the islets?

options.label: A
options.html: Amyloid deposits between islet cells and capillaries

options.label: D
options.html: Lymphocytic infiltration with loss of beta cells

options.label: E
options.html: Replacement of acini and islets by dense fibrosis

items.explanationHtml:
Weight loss, polyuria, low C-peptide and anti-GAD antibodies in a child are type 1 diabetes. It is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disease: CD8 and CD4 lymphocytes infiltrate the islets (insulitis) and selectively destroy beta cells, while alpha and delta cells remain.

Takeaway: insulitis with beta-cell loss is the lesion of type 1 diabetes; islet amyloid belongs to type 2.

whyNot.A: Amyloid derived from amylin is the islet lesion of long-standing type 2 diabetes.
whyNot.B: Islet hyperplasia is seen in infants of mothers with diabetes, a response to fetal hyperglycemia.
whyNot.C: Iron in islets with diabetes is hereditary hemochromatosis, an adult disease with liver and skin findings.
whyNot.E: Fibrosis of both acini and islets is chronic pancreatitis, which causes diabetes late and with malabsorption.

items.objective: Identify insulitis as the islet lesion of type 1 diabetes.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman has a fasting plasma glucose of 121 mg/dL on a pre-employment check; A1c is 6.2%. Repeat values a year later are almost identical. She is not overweight, and islet autoantibodies are negative. Her mother and maternal grandfather have had similarly "slightly high sugars" for decades without treatment, and none has eye, kidney or nerve complications. Loss of function of which of the following best explains her hyperglycemia?
items.explanationHtml:
Lifelong, mild, stable fasting hyperglycemia without complications, autosomal dominant inheritance, normal weight and negative antibodies fit GCK-MODY. Glucokinase is the beta cell's glucose sensor; heterozygous loss of function shifts the threshold for insulin release upward, so glucose is regulated normally but at a higher set point. Treatment is usually unnecessary outside pregnancy.

Takeaway: glucokinase variants reset the beta-cell glucose set point and cause mild, stable, familial fasting hyperglycemia.

whyNot.B: Loss of SUR1 function keeps K-ATP channels closed and causes excess insulin release with hypoglycemia (congenital hyperinsulinism).
whyNot.C: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke disease) causes fasting hypoglycemia, not hyperglycemia.
whyNot.D: Severe insulin receptor defects cause marked hyperinsulinemia, acanthosis nigricans and often severe diabetes, not a mild stable rise.
whyNot.E: Impaired GLUT4 translocation is part of acquired insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes and obesity, which does not fit a lean woman with a dominant mild pattern.

items.objective: Recognise glucokinase MODY from its mild, stable, familial phenotype.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes was started on glipizide 3 weeks ago in addition to metformin. Since then he has had two episodes of sweating, tremor and confusion in the late afternoon, relieved by orange juice. During one episode capillary glucose was 48 mg/dL. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which the new drug causes these episodes?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of a nuclear receptor that increases insulin sensitivity

options.label: B
options.html: Binding to a beta-cell receptor subunit that closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of an enzyme that degrades endogenous incretins

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule

options.label: E
options.html: Slowing of carbohydrate digestion at the intestinal brush border

items.explanationHtml:
Glipizide is a sulfonylurea. It binds the SUR1 subunit of the beta-cell K-ATP channel and closes it, depolarising the cell and releasing insulin whatever the glucose level. Insulin release continues when glucose is already low, so hypoglycemia is the main adverse effect, especially with missed meals, older age or kidney impairment.

Takeaway: sulfonylureas close K-ATP channels and cause glucose-independent insulin release, so they cause hypoglycemia; metformin alone does not.

whyNot.A: PPAR-gamma agonists (pioglitazone) sensitise tissues to insulin and do not cause hypoglycemia alone.
whyNot.C: DPP-4 inhibitors raise incretin levels, whose effect on insulin depends on high glucose, so hypoglycemia is rare.
whyNot.D: SGLT2 inhibitors cause glycosuria but rarely hypoglycemia because they do not raise insulin.
whyNot.E: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors blunt postprandial glucose and do not cause hypoglycemia on their own.

items.objective: Explain how sulfonylureas close beta-cell K-ATP channels and cause hypoglycemia.

items.stemHtml:
A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain after a dental infection that kept her from eating. She takes metformin and a second drug added 2 months ago, which also caused an episode of vulvovaginal candidiasis. Respirations are deep and rapid.

Serum studyValue
Glucose196 mg/dL
Sodium136 mEq/L
Chloride100 mEq/L
Bicarbonate11 mEq/L
Arterial pH7.18
Beta-hydroxybutyrate5.8 mmol/L (N < 0.6)
Lactate, venous1.4 mmol/L

Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the second drug?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of AMP-activated protein kinase in hepatocytes

options.label: B
options.html: Agonism at the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor

options.label: C
options.html: Blockade of the sodium-glucose cotransporter in the proximal tubule

options.label: D
options.html: Closure of ATP-sensitive potassium channels in beta cells

items.explanationHtml:
She has a ketoacidosis (anion gap 25, high beta-hydroxybutyrate) with glucose below 200 mg/dL: euglycemic DKA. SGLT2 inhibitors lower glucose by glycosuria, so insulin secretion falls and glucagon rises; with poor intake, ketogenesis takes off while glucose stays modest. Genital candidiasis from glycosuria is another clue to the drug.

Takeaway: an anion gap ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose in someone on an SGLT2 inhibitor is euglycemic DKA.

whyNot.A: Metformin acts partly through AMPK; its feared acid-base effect is lactic acidosis, but lactate here is normal and ketones are high.
whyNot.B: GLP-1 receptor agonists cause nausea but not glycosuria, candidiasis or ketoacidosis.
whyNot.D: Sulfonylureas raise insulin, which suppresses ketogenesis; they cause hypoglycemia, not ketoacidosis.
whyNot.E: DPP-4 inhibitors are weight neutral and well tolerated; they are not linked to euglycemic DKA or genital infections.

items.objective: Recognise euglycemic DKA as an adverse effect of SGLT2 inhibitors.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man has had type 1 diabetes for 30 years with A1c values usually above 9%. He has burning pain and numbness in both feet and early bilateral lens opacities. Researchers studying his Schwann cells find accumulation of an osmotically active sugar alcohol that the cells can only slowly metabolise further. Which of the following enzymes produces this compound?
items.explanationHtml:
In tissues that take up glucose independently of insulin, high glucose is reduced to sorbitol by aldose reductase (using NADPH). Schwann cells, lens and retina have little sorbitol dehydrogenase, so sorbitol accumulates, draws in water and depletes NADPH, contributing to neuropathy and cataracts.

Takeaway: aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, which accumulates in lens, nerve and retina in poorly controlled diabetes.

whyNot.B: Galactokinase phosphorylates galactose; its deficiency causes galactitol cataracts in infants, not diabetic neuropathy.
whyNot.C: G6PD makes NADPH in the pentose phosphate pathway; it does not produce sorbitol.
whyNot.D: Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, which is not osmotically trapped as a sugar alcohol.
whyNot.E: Sorbitol dehydrogenase converts sorbitol onward to fructose; its low activity is why sorbitol builds up, not the source of it.

items.objective: Link aldose reductase and sorbitol accumulation to diabetic neuropathy and cataracts.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman has had type 2 diabetes for 20 years and hypertension. Her urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 1,400 mg/g, and eGFR is 38 mL/min/1.73 m². Kidney biopsy shows diffusely thickened glomerular basement membranes, mesangial expansion with round, acellular, PAS-positive nodules, and hyaline thickening of both afferent and efferent arterioles. Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and albumin along the basement membranes without granular deposits. Which of the following processes contributes most to these changes?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of the alternative complement pathway

options.label: C
options.html: Immune complex deposition in the mesangium

options.label: D
options.html: Nonenzymatic glycation of matrix and basement membrane proteins

options.label: E
options.html: Osmotic injury from sorbitol accumulation in podocytes

items.explanationHtml:
Nodular (Kimmelstiel-Wilson) glomerulosclerosis with GBM thickening and hyaline arteriolosclerosis of both arterioles is diabetic kidney disease. Chronic hyperglycemia glycates matrix proteins nonenzymatically; advanced glycation end-products cross-link collagen, stimulate mesangial matrix production and trap plasma proteins (hence the nonspecific linear IgG and albumin, which is not anti-GBM disease).

Takeaway: nonenzymatic glycation drives the basement membrane thickening, mesangial nodules and hyaline arteriolosclerosis of diabetic nephropathy.

whyNot.A: Alternative pathway overactivity causes C3 glomerulopathy with C3-dominant staining and a proliferative pattern.
whyNot.B: AL amyloid forms Congo red-positive, apple-green birefringent mesangial deposits, not PAS-positive nodules with arteriolar hyalinosis.
whyNot.C: Granular mesangial immune complexes (for example IgA) are absent here; the linear staining is nonspecific trapping.
whyNot.E: The polyol pathway contributes to neuropathy and cataracts; it is not the main mechanism of the glomerular nodules.

items.objective: Attribute the lesions of diabetic nephropathy to nonenzymatic glycation.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is brought from home after 5 days of increasing confusion and poor oral intake during a urinary infection. Plasma glucose is 1,060 mg/dL, sodium 142 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L and BUN 74 mg/dL. Arterial pH is 7.36. Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate is only slightly raised. Which of the following best explains why she has little ketoacidosis despite extreme hyperglycemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Her glucagon secretion is suppressed by the hyperglycemia

options.label: B
options.html: Her liver lacks the enzymes needed for ketogenesis

options.label: C
options.html: Ketones are being excreted rapidly in the urine

options.label: D
options.html: Residual insulin secretion is enough to restrain lipolysis but not hepatic glucose output

options.label: E
options.html: Severe dehydration prevents fatty acids from reaching the liver

items.explanationHtml:
This is the hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. In type 2 diabetes some insulin is still secreted. Inhibiting hormone-sensitive lipase (and hence the fatty-acid supply for ketogenesis) needs far less insulin than suppressing hepatic glucose output and driving peripheral glucose uptake. So glucose climbs for days with osmotic diuresis and dehydration, while ketoacid production stays modest.

Takeaway: in HHS, residual insulin prevents ketosis but not extreme hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality.

whyNot.A: Glucagon is typically raised in both DKA and HHS, not suppressed.
whyNot.B: Hepatic ketogenic enzymes are intact; ketogenesis is limited by substrate and hormonal signals.
whyNot.C: Ketonuria cannot explain low serum ketones; in DKA large urinary losses coexist with high serum levels.
whyNot.E: Dehydration does not block fatty acid delivery; DKA occurs with severe dehydration too.

items.objective: Explain the absence of significant ketosis in the hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and stable coronary disease started a new oral drug 4 months ago. His A1c has fallen from 8.3% to 7.2%, but he has gained 4 kg and has new bilateral ankle edema and exertional dyspnea. The drug binds an intracellular receptor that forms a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor and changes transcription of genes in adipose tissue. Which of the following drugs was most likely started?
items.explanationHtml:
Pioglitazone is a thiazolidinedione, an agonist of PPAR-gamma, a nuclear receptor that pairs with RXR to change gene transcription, mainly in fat. It improves insulin sensitivity but causes weight gain and renal sodium and fluid retention, which can unmask or worsen heart failure; it is avoided in symptomatic heart failure. Fracture risk is also raised.

Takeaway: thiazolidinediones are PPAR-gamma agonists that cause fluid retention, weight gain and heart failure exacerbation.

whyNot.A: Acarbose acts in the gut lumen on alpha-glucosidases and causes flatulence, not edema.
whyNot.B: Glimepiride closes K-ATP channels at the membrane; it causes weight gain and hypoglycemia but not a nuclear-receptor effect or fluid retention.
whyNot.C: Linagliptin inhibits DPP-4, an extracellular enzyme, and is weight neutral.
whyNot.E: Repaglinide is a meglitinide that closes K-ATP channels, like a short-acting sulfonylurea.

items.objective: Recognise PPAR-gamma agonism and fluid retention with thiazolidinediones.

items.stemHtml:
A 46-year-old man has a screening visit. He has no symptoms. BMI is 31 kg/m² and blood pressure is 134/84 mm Hg. Laboratory studies on a single fasting sample:

TestResult
Hemoglobin A1c6.8%
Fasting plasma glucose114 mg/dL
Hemoglobin14.6 g/dL
MCV88 fL
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Diagnose prediabetes and recheck in 1 year

options.label: B
options.html: Diagnose type 2 diabetes and start metformin

items.explanationHtml:
A1c is in the diabetes range but fasting glucose is in the prediabetes range. Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, diabetes needs two abnormal results; when two tests disagree, repeat the test that was abnormal. If the repeat A1c is 6.5% or higher, he has diabetes. There is nothing (anemia, kidney failure) to make A1c unreliable here.

Takeaway: discordant screening tests: repeat the abnormal one before labelling diabetes.

whyNot.A: A1c of 6.8% is above the prediabetes range; it cannot simply be called prediabetes without confirmation.
whyNot.B: Only one test is diagnostic, so the diagnosis is not yet confirmed.
whyNot.C: Nothing suggests autoimmune diabetes in an asymptomatic adult with obesity; antibodies are not first steps.
whyNot.E: Insulin is not indicated for a mildly raised A1c, even if diabetes is confirmed.

items.objective: Confirm a diagnosis of diabetes by repeating the abnormal test when results are discordant.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman was found to have type 2 diabetes 2 weeks ago (A1c 7.6% on two occasions) and started metformin. She has no visual symptoms, numbness or other complaints. Blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Which of the following should be arranged now as part of her baseline evaluation?
items.explanationHtml:
Type 2 diabetes is often present for years before diagnosis, so complications may already exist. A dilated eye examination (or retinal photography) at diagnosis is recommended, then every 1–2 years if normal. Baseline urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, eGFR, lipids and a foot examination are also done now.

Takeaway: in type 2 diabetes, screen for retinopathy at diagnosis; in type 1, start within 5 years of onset.

whyNot.A: Routine coronary imaging in asymptomatic patients with diabetes is not recommended.
whyNot.C: Neuropathy screening is clinical (monofilament, vibration, reflexes); nerve conduction studies are for atypical cases.
whyNot.D: Waiting 5 years applies to type 1 diabetes, whose onset is abrupt and well dated.
whyNot.E: Screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria is not recommended in diabetes.

items.objective: Arrange a retinal examination at the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 3 years takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. He wants help losing weight. He has no cardiovascular disease, heart failure or kidney disease, and no personal or family history of thyroid cancer or pancreatitis. BMI is 37 kg/m². A1c is 8.4%, eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73 m² and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 12 mg/g. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Neutral protamine Hagedorn insulin at bedtime

items.explanationHtml:
When weight is a priority, a GLP-1 receptor agonist (or the dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist tirzepatide) gives the greatest weight loss along with substantial A1c lowering and a low risk of hypoglycemia. Adverse effects are mainly gastrointestinal; it is avoided with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2.

Takeaway: for type 2 diabetes with obesity, add a GLP-1 receptor agonist or tirzepatide.

whyNot.A: Sulfonylureas cause weight gain and hypoglycemia, working against his main goal.
whyNot.B: Insulin causes weight gain and is not needed at an A1c of 8.4% without catabolic symptoms.
whyNot.C: Pioglitazone lowers glucose but causes weight gain and fluid retention.
whyNot.D: Sitagliptin is weight neutral and lowers A1c less than a GLP-1 receptor agonist.

items.objective: Choose a GLP-1 receptor agonist for type 2 diabetes when weight loss is a priority.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, moderate dementia, CKD (eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73 m²) and two falls in 3 months is seen with her daughter. She takes glyburide 5 mg twice daily and linagliptin. Her daughter has found her sweaty and confused twice before lunch, with fingerstick glucose readings of 52 and 58 mg/dL. A1c is 6.1%. Which of the following is the most appropriate change?

options.label: A
options.html: Add a bedtime snack and continue current drugs

options.label: B
options.html: Change glyburide to glipizide at the same dose

options.label: D
options.html: Start basal insulin and stop both drugs

items.explanationHtml:
She is overtreated. For an older adult with dementia, falls and CKD, a less strict A1c target (around 8.0%) is appropriate, and avoiding hypoglycemia matters most. Glyburide has active metabolites cleared by the kidney and causes prolonged hypoglycemia; it should be stopped. Linagliptin alone carries little hypoglycemia risk and needs no renal dose change.

Takeaway: in frail older adults with hypoglycemia, deintensify and stop sulfonylureas, especially glyburide.

whyNot.A: Snacks paper over overtreatment and leave a drug that causes dangerous hypoglycemia.
whyNot.B: Glipizide is safer than glyburide, but her A1c of 6.1% means she needs less treatment, not a substitute sulfonylurea at the same dose.
whyNot.C: Escalating therapy is wrong when A1c is already below her target and she is hypoglycemic.
whyNot.D: Insulin would add hypoglycemia risk and complexity for a patient with dementia.

items.objective: Deintensify glucose-lowering therapy and stop glyburide in a frail older adult with hypoglycemia.

items.stemHtml:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes takes metformin, empagliflozin and insulin glargine 18 units at bedtime, started 6 weeks ago. He has had no hypoglycemia. His 2-week glucose log (mg/dL):

TimeRange
Fasting (before breakfast)168–196
Before lunch132–150
Before dinner124–146
Bedtime138–160
Hemoglobin A1c8.6%

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Add prandial insulin before each meal

options.label: B
options.html: Increase glargine by 2 units every 3 days until fasting glucose is at target

options.label: C
options.html: Move the glargine dose to the morning

options.label: D
options.html: Reduce glargine to avoid nocturnal hypoglycemia

items.explanationHtml:
Basal insulin is titrated against the fasting glucose. His fasting values are well above a usual target of about 80–130 mg/dL, with no hypoglycemia, so the glargine dose is too low. A simple patient-led titration (for example 2 units every 3 days) is used until fasting glucose is at target. Prandial insulin or a GLP-1 receptor agonist is added only if A1c stays high once fasting glucose is controlled.

Takeaway: high fasting glucose on basal insulin without hypoglycemia: titrate the basal dose up.

whyNot.A: His daytime readings are near target; mealtime insulin is premature until the fasting glucose is fixed.
whyNot.C: Changing the timing of a flat basal insulin does not correct an inadequate dose.
whyNot.D: There is no hypoglycemia and fasting glucose is high, so reducing the dose would worsen control.
whyNot.E: The SGLT2 inhibitor is useful, and a sulfonylurea would add hypoglycemia risk without addressing basal insulin need.

items.objective: Titrate basal insulin to the fasting glucose.

items.stemHtml:
A 76-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who lives alone is brought in after 4 days of increasing confusion and poor intake. He has dry mucous membranes, temperature 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse 116/min and blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg.

Serum studyValue
Glucose944 mg/dL
Sodium139 mEq/L
Potassium4.6 mEq/L
Chloride104 mEq/L
Bicarbonate22 mEq/L
BUN68 mg/dL
Creatinine2.2 mg/dL
Osmolality, serum356 mOsm/kg
Arterial pH7.36
Beta-hydroxybutyrate0.8 mmol/L (N < 0.6)

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step?

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous 0.9% saline, about 1 L over the first hour

options.label: C
options.html: Intravenous regular insulin bolus before any fluids

items.explanationHtml:
Extreme hyperglycemia, osmolality 356 mOsm/kg, altered mental status and minimal ketosis without acidosis define the hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. Fluid deficits are very large, so the first step is rapid isotonic crystalloid to restore circulating volume; fluids alone also lower glucose. Insulin follows, and the precipitant (probably infection) is sought.

Takeaway: HHS: isotonic fluids first, then insulin, with close electrolyte monitoring.

whyNot.A: Hypotonic fluid at a slow rate does not restore volume in a hypotensive patient; it may be used later once volume is restored.
whyNot.C: Insulin before fluids drives glucose and water into cells and can worsen hypotension; boluses are not needed.
whyNot.D: There is no significant acidosis, so bicarbonate has no role.
whyNot.E: A confused, hypotensive patient cannot safely drink enough to correct a deficit of several litres.

items.objective: Start isotonic fluid resuscitation first in the hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.

items.stemHtml: The patient receives 2 L of 0.9% saline over 2 hours. His blood pressure rises to 118/70 mm Hg, and urine output is 60 mL/hour. Repeat studies show glucose 690 mg/dL and potassium 3.0 mEq/L. ECG shows prominent U waves. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Give IV potassium and start insulin once potassium is at least 3.3 mEq/L

options.label: B
options.html: Start an insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour now

options.label: C
options.html: Start an insulin infusion and recheck potassium in 6 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Switch fluids to 5% dextrose in water

options.label: E
options.html: Give subcutaneous insulin glargine and oral potassium

items.explanationHtml:
Insulin shifts potassium into cells. Starting it with a serum potassium of 3.0 mEq/L (with U waves) risks dangerous hypokalemia and arrhythmia. The rule: if potassium is below 3.3 mEq/L, hold insulin and replace potassium IV until it is 3.3 or higher, then start the insulin infusion with potassium in the fluids.

Takeaway: in DKA and HHS, potassium below 3.3 mEq/L means potassium first, insulin second.

whyNot.B: Insulin now would drop his potassium further and risk ventricular arrhythmia.
whyNot.C: Six hours is far too long between potassium checks during insulin treatment.
whyNot.D: Dextrose-only fluid is added when glucose falls to about 300 mg/dL in HHS; glucose is still 690 mg/dL.
whyNot.E: Subcutaneous basal insulin and oral potassium are too slow and unreliable in this setting.

items.objective: Replace potassium before starting insulin when it is below 3.3 mEq/L.

items.stemHtml: Potassium is corrected and an insulin infusion is started. Eight hours later he is more alert. Glucose is 286 mg/dL, sodium 146 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L and calculated serum osmolality 318 mOsm/kg. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Add dextrose to the intravenous fluids and reduce the insulin infusion rate

options.label: C
options.html: Increase the insulin infusion to lower glucose below 150 mg/dL quickly

options.label: D
options.html: Stop the insulin infusion and observe

options.label: E
options.html: Stop intravenous fluids and encourage oral intake

items.explanationHtml:
In HHS, once glucose falls to about 300 mg/dL, dextrose is added to the fluids and the insulin rate is reduced, keeping glucose roughly in the 200–300 mg/dL range until osmolality and mental status normalise. This avoids hypoglycemia and too-rapid falls in osmolality, which can shift water into brain cells.

Takeaway: add dextrose when glucose reaches about 300 mg/dL in HHS (about 250 mg/dL in DKA) and keep insulin going at a lower rate.

whyNot.B: Hypertonic saline is for severe symptomatic hyponatremia; his sodium is already high.
whyNot.C: Lowering glucose quickly drops osmolality too fast and risks hypoglycemia and cerebral edema.
whyNot.D: Stopping insulin abruptly lets glucose climb again before he is ready for subcutaneous insulin.
whyNot.E: Osmolality is still high and he is not yet fully alert; IV fluids should continue.

items.objective: Add dextrose and lower the insulin rate when glucose reaches about 300 mg/dL in HHS.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy has a painless ulcer under the head of the right first metatarsal for 6 weeks. He walks on it daily in ordinary shoes. The ulcer is 1.5 cm across, clean, with a callused rim and no surrounding erythema, warmth, drainage or odour; bone cannot be probed. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable, and ankle-brachial index is 1.05. Foot radiographs are normal. Which of the following is the most important next step to promote healing?

options.label: C
options.html: Pressure offloading with a total contact cast

items.explanationHtml:
This is a neuropathic (pressure) ulcer with adequate perfusion and no infection. Repeated pressure while walking is what keeps it open, so offloading (a total contact cast or a removable knee-high walker), plus debridement of the callus, is the key to healing. Glucose control and foot care education follow.

Takeaway: a noninfected neuropathic plantar ulcer with good perfusion heals with offloading and debridement.

whyNot.A: Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct for selected nonhealing ulcers, not first-line care before offloading.
whyNot.B: Antibiotics are for clinically infected ulcers; this ulcer has no signs of infection.
whyNot.D: Topical antibiotics do not address pressure and are not recommended for uninfected ulcers.
whyNot.E: Pulses and the ankle-brachial index are normal, so revascularisation is not needed.

items.objective: Treat a neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer with offloading and debridement.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes calls because she has had vomiting and diarrhea for 12 hours after a family member had the same illness. She cannot eat but can sip fluids. She uses insulin glargine at night and insulin lispro with meals. Her fingerstick glucose is 238 mg/dL, and a home urine ketone test shows trace ketones. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue glargine, sip sugary fluids and check glucose and ketones every 2–4 hours

options.label: B
options.html: Double tonight's glargine dose and stop all mealtime lispro until she eats

options.label: C
options.html: Skip tonight's glargine dose because she is not eating any meals

options.label: D
options.html: Stop all insulin until the vomiting has settled, then restart usual doses

options.label: E
options.html: Take an extra 20 units of lispro now and recheck her glucose tomorrow

items.explanationHtml:
In type 1 diabetes, insulin is needed even without food, because counter-regulatory hormones rise during illness and the liver keeps producing glucose and ketones. Basal insulin is never stopped. She should keep sipping fluids that contain carbohydrate, monitor glucose and ketones every few hours, take correction doses of rapid-acting insulin as needed, and seek urgent care if vomiting persists, ketones rise to moderate or large, or she becomes drowsy.

Takeaway: on sick days in type 1 diabetes, continue basal insulin and monitor glucose and ketones closely.

whyNot.B: Doubling basal insulin without monitoring risks hypoglycemia, and stopping all lispro removes the correction doses she may need.
whyNot.C: Missing basal insulin is a leading trigger of DKA.
whyNot.D: Stopping all insulin causes ketoacidosis within hours in type 1 diabetes.
whyNot.E: A large fixed bolus without close monitoring risks hypoglycemia, and waiting until tomorrow misses developing DKA.

items.objective: Give sick-day advice for type 1 diabetes: continue basal insulin and monitor ketones.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 15 years wants to become pregnant in the next few months. She uses an insulin pump. Her A1c is 8.4%. She takes lisinopril for moderately increased albuminuria and atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia. Her last eye examination was 3 years ago. She uses condoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Conceive now, then stop lisinopril and atorvastatin once pregnancy is confirmed

options.label: B
options.html: Keep using contraception, stop lisinopril and atorvastatin, start folic acid, lower A1c

options.label: C
options.html: Continue lisinopril for kidney protection in pregnancy and stop atorvastatin only

options.label: D
options.html: Replace her insulin pump with metformin and conceive once A1c is below 7%

options.label: E
options.html: Change from the insulin pump to twice-daily NPH insulin before conceiving

items.explanationHtml:
Poor glucose control at conception raises the risk of miscarriage and major malformations. Before pregnancy she should keep using contraception while working toward an A1c below about 6.5% if safely achievable, start folic acid, have a dilated eye examination (retinopathy can progress in pregnancy), and stop teratogenic drugs: ACE inhibitors (fetal renal dysgenesis) and statins.

Takeaway: type 1 diabetes and planned pregnancy: optimise A1c first, stop ACE inhibitors and statins, add folic acid, check the eyes.

whyNot.A: Conceiving with an A1c of 8.4% exposes the embryo to hyperglycemia during organogenesis, which happens before many pregnancies are confirmed.
whyNot.C: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal kidney toxicity.
whyNot.D: Metformin cannot replace insulin in type 1 diabetes, and 7% is above the preconception target.
whyNot.E: Insulin pumps are effective and commonly used in pregnancy; there is no need to switch to NPH, and this alone does not address her A1c or teratogenic drugs.

items.objective: Plan pregnancy in type 1 diabetes: optimise glucose and stop teratogenic drugs before conception.

items.stemHtml:
A 46-year-old woman has had episodes of confusion and sweating before breakfast and after missing meals for 6 months, relieved by eating. She has gained 7 kg. She takes no medications and has no diabetes in her household. During a supervised fast she becomes confused at 18 hours. Blood drawn at that moment shows:

TestResult
Glucose41 mg/dL (2.3 mmol/L)
Insulin14 µU/mL (N below 3 during hypoglycemia)
C-peptide1.9 ng/mL (N below 0.6 during hypoglycemia)
Proinsulin28 pmol/L (N below 5 during hypoglycemia)
Beta-hydroxybutyrate0.2 mmol/L (low)
Sulfonylurea and meglitinide screenNegative
Insulin antibodiesNegative

After 1 mg of intravenous glucagon, glucose rises by 40 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Fasting hypoglycemia with inappropriately high insulin, high C-peptide and high proinsulin, suppressed ketones, a brisk glucose response to glucagon and a negative secretagogue screen shows endogenous hyperinsulinism without a drug: an insulinoma. Weight gain from eating to avoid symptoms is typical.

Takeaway: endogenous insulin (high C-peptide and proinsulin) with a negative drug screen during fasting hypoglycemia means insulinoma.

whyNot.A: Cortisol deficiency causes hypoglycemia with suppressed insulin and C-peptide, and ketones would be high.
whyNot.B: Insulin antibodies are negative, and that disorder typically causes symptoms hours after meals with extremely high insulin levels.
whyNot.D: Injected insulin suppresses the patient's own secretion, so C-peptide and proinsulin would be low.
whyNot.E: IGF-2 suppresses insulin secretion, so insulin and C-peptide would both be low.

items.objective: Diagnose insulinoma from the insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin and drug-screen pattern during fasting hypoglycemia.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found confused on a Sunday morning. He drank heavily through Saturday and ate little for 2 days. Plasma glucose is 36 mg/dL, and blood lactate is mildly elevated. Insulin and C-peptide are appropriately suppressed. He improves with intravenous dextrose. Which of the following best explains his hypoglycemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Ethanol activates hepatic glucokinase and traps glucose in the liver

options.label: B
options.html: Ethanol directly stimulates insulin release from beta cells

options.label: C
options.html: Ethanol inhibits glucagon release from alpha cells

options.label: D
options.html: Ethanol metabolism raises the hepatic NADH/NAD<sup>+</sup> ratio and limits gluconeogenesis

options.label: E
options.html: Ethanol speeds intestinal transit and reduces glucose absorption

items.explanationHtml:
Alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase both reduce NAD+ to NADH. The high NADH/NAD+ ratio pushes pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, removing the substrates of gluconeogenesis. After 1–2 days of poor intake, liver glycogen is gone, gluconeogenesis is the only source of glucose, and glucose falls. The same redox shift explains the lactate rise.

Takeaway: alcohol causes fasting hypoglycemia by blocking gluconeogenesis through a high NADH/NAD+ ratio once glycogen is depleted.

whyNot.A: Glucokinase traps glucose after meals; ethanol does not lower glucose this way.
whyNot.B: Ethanol does not trigger insulin secretion; his insulin and C-peptide are suppressed.
whyNot.C: Glucagon release is intact; the problem is that there is little glycogen or gluconeogenic substrate for glucagon to act on.
whyNot.E: He has eaten little, so absorption is not the issue, and alcohol does not cause hypoglycemia by speeding transit.

items.objective: Explain alcohol-related fasting hypoglycemia through the NADH/NAD+ ratio and gluconeogenesis.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman has lost 9 kg over 6 months and has a painful, red, crusting rash that spreads outward with central healing over her groin, buttocks and thighs. She has a sore, smooth red tongue. Fasting glucose is 188 mg/dL; she has no previous diabetes. She was treated last month for a deep venous thrombosis. CT shows a 5-cm mass in the tail of the pancreas. The tumour most likely arises from which cell type, and what does that cell normally secrete?
items.explanationHtml:
Necrolytic migratory erythema, new diabetes, weight loss, glossitis and venous thrombosis with a pancreatic tail mass are the picture of a glucagonoma, an alpha-cell tumour. Excess glucagon drives gluconeogenesis and amino acid catabolism; low amino acids are thought to contribute to the rash.

Takeaway: necrolytic migratory erythema plus diabetes and thrombosis means an alpha-cell glucagonoma.

whyNot.B: An insulinoma causes hypoglycemia and weight gain, not diabetes, weight loss and a rash.
whyNot.C: Somatostatinoma causes diabetes with gallstones and steatorrhea, not necrolytic migratory erythema.
whyNot.D: Carcinoid tumours cause flushing, diarrhea and right heart valve disease when they reach the liver.
whyNot.E: Gastrinoma causes peptic ulcers and diarrhea, not a migratory rash or diabetes.

items.objective: Recognise glucagonoma as an alpha-cell tumour from its clinical features.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has had 3 months of watery diarrhea, about 4 L a day, that continues during a 48-hour fast. He is weak. Serum potassium is 2.6 mEq/L and bicarbonate 17 mEq/L. Stool osmotic gap is 20 mOsm/kg. Gastric acid output is very low. CT shows a 4-cm pancreatic mass. The hormone secreted by this tumour causes the diarrhea mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Damage to the brush border, which causes lactose malabsorption

options.label: B
options.html: Increased cAMP in intestinal epithelial cells, which drives chloride secretion

options.label: C
options.html: Inactivation of pancreatic lipase by excess gastric acid

options.label: D
options.html: Increased intestinal motility through serotonin receptors

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of bile acid reabsorption in the terminal ileum

items.explanationHtml:
Large-volume diarrhea that continues during fasting with a small osmotic gap is secretory. With hypokalemia and achlorhydria this is a VIPoma.
