Vasoactive intestinal peptide binds Gs-coupled receptors on enterocytes, raises cAMP and opens CFTR chloride channels; water and potassium follow into the lumen. VIP also inhibits gastric acid secretion.

Takeaway: VIPoma causes secretory diarrhea, hypokalemia and achlorhydria through cAMP-driven chloride secretion.

whyNot.A: Lactose malabsorption is an osmotic diarrhea with a large osmotic gap that stops with fasting.
whyNot.C: Acid inactivating lipase is the gastrinoma mechanism, and this patient has low acid output.
whyNot.D: Serotonin-driven motility fits carcinoid syndrome, which also causes flushing and wheezing.
whyNot.E: Bile acid diarrhea follows ileal disease or resection and usually improves with fasting.

items.objective: Explain the cAMP-mediated secretory diarrhea of VIPoma.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man has a 15-cm mass in the right hemithorax, which biopsy shows to be a solitary fibrous tumour of the pleura. He has had several early-morning episodes of confusion. During one, plasma glucose is 34 mg/dL, and insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin are all undetectable. Beta-hydroxybutyrate is low. A sulfonylurea screen is negative. Which of the following most likely causes his hypoglycemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibodies that activate the insulin receptor

options.label: B
options.html: Destruction of the adrenal glands by metastases

options.label: C
options.html: Glucose consumption by the tumour's large mass

options.label: D
options.html: Ectopic secretion of insulin by the tumour

options.label: E
options.html: Secretion of incompletely processed IGF-2 by the tumour

items.explanationHtml:
Hypoglycemia with suppressed insulin and C-peptide but also low ketones means something insulin-like is acting. Large mesenchymal tumours can secrete incompletely processed ("big") IGF-2, which binds insulin receptors, increases glucose uptake, suppresses hepatic glucose output and ketogenesis, and suppresses growth hormone and the patient's own insulin. This is non-islet cell tumour hypoglycemia; removing the tumour cures it.

Takeaway: low insulin, low C-peptide and low ketones with a large tumour points to IGF-2-mediated hypoglycemia.

whyNot.A: Insulin-receptor antibodies are rare, occur mainly with autoimmune disease, and do not explain a link to a large pleural tumour.
whyNot.B: Adrenal insufficiency would allow ketone production, so beta-hydroxybutyrate would be high.
whyNot.C: Glucose use by the tumour contributes little and would not suppress ketogenesis.
whyNot.D: Ectopic insulin secretion is extremely rare, and insulin is undetectable here.

items.objective: Recognise IGF-2-mediated non-islet cell tumour hypoglycemia from its laboratory pattern.

items.stemHtml: A boy is born at 38 weeks' gestation to a mother with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes. Birth weight is 4,600 g. At 2 hours of age he is jittery and feeds poorly, and plasma glucose is 28 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains his hypoglycemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Absent hepatic glycogen stores due to placental insufficiency

options.label: C
options.html: Fetal beta-cell hyperplasia that continues to secrete insulin after birth

options.label: D
options.html: Maternal insulin that crossed the placenta and persists in his blood

items.explanationHtml:
Maternal glucose crosses the placenta, but maternal insulin does not. Chronic fetal hyperglycemia stimulates fetal beta-cell hyperplasia and hyperinsulinemia, which also drives growth (macrosomia). When the cord is clamped, the glucose supply stops abruptly while insulin output stays high, so glucose falls within hours of birth.

Takeaway: infants of mothers with diabetes become hypoglycemic after birth because their own hyperplastic beta cells keep secreting insulin.

whyNot.A: A large-for-gestational-age infant of a mother with diabetes has ample glycogen; low stores fit growth-restricted infants.
whyNot.B: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke disease) causes hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly, usually after the first months when feeds space out.
whyNot.D: Insulin is a large peptide that does not cross the placenta in meaningful amounts.
whyNot.E: Neonatal adrenal insufficiency is rare and not linked to maternal diabetes.

items.objective: Explain neonatal hypoglycemia in the infant of a mother with diabetes.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes feels shaky, sweaty and hungry during an afternoon at work, 3 hours after taking his usual insulin and eating a smaller lunch than usual. His fingerstick glucose is 52 mg/dL. He is alert, answering questions normally and able to swallow. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Eat 15–20 g of glucose tablets and recheck glucose in 15 minutes

options.label: B
options.html: Eat a high-fat meal such as a cheese sandwich and recheck in 1 hour

options.label: D
options.html: Skip his next insulin dose and rest until symptoms pass

options.label: E
options.html: Take his rapid-acting insulin dose early to correct the timing

items.explanationHtml:
A conscious patient who can swallow is treated with 15–20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, preferably glucose, and glucose is rechecked after 15 minutes, repeating if still low; a snack or meal follows once glucose is normal.

Takeaway: conscious hypoglycemia: 15–20 g of glucose, recheck in 15 minutes.

whyNot.B: Fat slows gastric emptying and delays the glucose rise.
whyNot.C: Glucagon is for a person who cannot safely take sugar by mouth.
whyNot.D: Rest without carbohydrate lets glucose keep falling while insulin is still acting.
whyNot.E: More insulin would deepen the hypoglycemia.

items.objective: Treat mild symptomatic hypoglycemia with oral glucose and recheck after 15 minutes.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes is found by her mother at home, unresponsive and sweaty, 2 hours after an evening of intense soccer practice. Her meter reads 34 mg/dL. She is breathing normally and has a pulse. She does not respond to her name. Emergency services have been called and are 20 minutes away. Which of the following should her mother do now?

options.label: A
options.html: Give intranasal or intramuscular glucagon and turn her onto her side

options.label: B
options.html: Give a glass of orange juice slowly by mouth

options.label: C
options.html: Inject her rapid-acting insulin to cover the exercise

options.label: D
options.html: Rub honey between her cheek and gum and wait

options.label: E
options.html: Wait for emergency services, because glucagon is unsafe at home

items.explanationHtml:
She has severe (level 3) hypoglycemia and cannot swallow safely. Family members of insulin-treated patients should give glucagon, by intramuscular or subcutaneous injection or as intranasal powder. Placing her in the recovery position protects the airway, because vomiting is common after glucagon. Once awake and able to swallow, she should eat.

Takeaway: unconscious hypoglycemia outside hospital: glucagon, recovery position, nothing by mouth.

whyNot.B: Fluid by mouth in an unresponsive patient risks aspiration.
whyNot.C: Insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia.
whyNot.D: Food in the mouth of a person who cannot swallow risks choking and aspiration and is unreliable.
whyNot.E: Glucagon is designed for use by trained lay people; delay prolongs neuroglycopenia.

items.objective: Treat severe hypoglycemia in an unconscious patient outside hospital with glucagon.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m²) is brought in confused. She takes glyburide and lisinopril. Plasma glucose is 38 mg/dL. She wakes after 25 g of intravenous dextrose, but 2 hours later glucose is 49 mg/dL despite a 10% dextrose infusion, and she becomes drowsy again. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Switch glyburide to glipizide and discharge home

items.explanationHtml:
Glyburide is long-acting, and its active metabolites accumulate in kidney failure, so hypoglycemia recurs. Each dextrose load stimulates further insulin release from the drug-primed beta cells. Octreotide inhibits beta-cell insulin secretion and prevents recurrent hypoglycemia; she needs admission with glucose monitoring for at least a day and permanent withdrawal of the sulfonylurea.

Takeaway: recurrent hypoglycemia from a sulfonylurea: dextrose plus octreotide, and admit.

whyNot.A: Insulin is the wrong direction; she already has too much.
whyNot.B: Steroids are for adrenal insufficiency, which nothing here suggests.
whyNot.C: Glucagon gives only a brief rise and also stimulates insulin secretion; repeated doses are not the answer.
whyNot.E: Any sulfonylurea is risky in an 81-year-old with advanced CKD, and she is still hypoglycemic.

items.objective: Use octreotide for recurrent sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has had type 1 diabetes for 22 years and uses multiple daily insulin injections with fingerstick monitoring. Her hemoglobin A1c is 6.1%. In the past month she has had two episodes of confusion at work that colleagues treated with juice; she had no shaking or sweating beforehand. Her fingerstick log shows several readings between 45 and 60 mg/dL without symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Add a sulfonylurea at bedtime to smooth overnight glucose

options.label: B
options.html: Begin a beta-blocker to reduce work-related anxiety

options.label: C
options.html: Increase basal insulin to bring her A1c below 6%

options.label: D
options.html: Continuous glucose monitoring with alerts and looser targets

options.label: E
options.html: Referral for pancreas transplantation this month

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent hypoglycemia without warning symptoms is hypoglycemia unawareness, from blunted glucagon and adrenergic responses after repeated lows. A continuous glucose monitor with low alerts, adjustment of insulin and a period of strict hypoglycemia avoidance with temporarily higher targets can restore some awareness. Her A1c of 6.1% is lower than is safe for her.

Takeaway: hypoglycemia unawareness: CGM with alerts and relaxed targets for weeks.

whyNot.A: Sulfonylureas need working beta cells and would add hypoglycemia risk.
whyNot.B: Beta-blockers can mask the remaining adrenergic warning signs.
whyNot.C: Lowering glucose further would cause more hypoglycemia and worsen unawareness.
whyNot.E: Transplantation is a specialist option for refractory severe hypoglycemia after technology and education have failed.

items.objective: Manage hypoglycemia unawareness in type 1 diabetes with CGM and relaxed targets.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 2 years ago and has lost 48 kg. For 4 months she has had sweating, palpitations and confusion about 2 hours after meals, especially those with bread or sweets. Fingerstick glucose during an episode was 46 mg/dL. Fasting glucose is normal, and she has never had symptoms before breakfast. She takes no diabetes medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.html: Distal pancreatectomy to remove excess beta cells

options.label: B
options.html: Small, frequent meals low in refined carbohydrate

options.label: C
options.html: Surgical reversal of the gastric bypass

items.explanationHtml:
Symptoms 1–3 hours after meals years after gastric bypass, with normal fasting glucose, fit post-bariatric hypoglycemia: rapid delivery of carbohydrate to the small bowel causes an exaggerated insulin response. First-line treatment is dietary: small, frequent meals with protein and fat, avoiding rapidly absorbed carbohydrate. Acarbose is the usual next step.

Takeaway: post-meal hypoglycemia after gastric bypass is treated with diet first.

whyNot.A: Pancreatic resection is no longer used for this condition and does not address the cause.
whyNot.C: Reversal is reserved for rare refractory cases after diet and drugs fail.
whyNot.D: Imaging for an insulinoma is not indicated; the pattern is postprandial and the history explains it.
whyNot.E: A prolonged fast tests for fasting hypoglycemia; a mixed-meal test is the provocation that fits postprandial symptoms.

items.objective: Treat post-bariatric hypoglycemia with dietary changes first.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old man has had three episodes over 2 months of confusion and sweating late in the morning when he skipped breakfast; each resolved after paramedics gave glucose. One paramedic record documents a glucose of 39 mg/dL. He does not drink alcohol, takes no medications, and no one in his household has diabetes. Examination and basic chemistry, including cortisol, are normal. Glucose today is 82 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Multiphase contrast CT of the pancreas

options.label: C
options.html: Hemoglobin A1c and fasting lipid panel

options.label: D
options.html: Oral glucose tolerance test over 5 hours

options.label: E
options.html: Supervised fast with hormone and drug testing at hypoglycemia

items.explanationHtml:
He has documented Whipple's triad without an obvious cause, so endogenous hyperinsulinism must be tested for. The episodes are fasting-related, so the next step is a supervised fast of up to 72 hours, drawing glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, beta-hydroxybutyrate and a sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen when glucose falls below 55 mg/dL, then giving glucagon and measuring the glucose response.

Takeaway: prove insulin-mediated hypoglycemia biochemically before imaging the pancreas.

whyNot.A: Imaging comes only after biochemical proof; small insulinomas are often missed and incidental findings mislead.
whyNot.B: Endoscopic ultrasonography is a localisation test, used after the diagnosis is established.
whyNot.C: A1c says nothing about the cause of fasting hypoglycemia.
whyNot.D: Prolonged glucose tolerance tests produce low readings in healthy people and are not used to diagnose hypoglycemia.

items.objective: Investigate documented fasting hypoglycemia with a supervised fast and full biochemistry.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old woman has endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia confirmed during a supervised fast, with high insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin, a negative sulfonylurea and meglitinide screen, and negative insulin antibodies. Serum calcium and prolactin are normal, and she has no family history of endocrine tumours. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Multiphase contrast CT or MRI of the pancreas

options.label: E
options.html: Selective arterial calcium stimulation as the first test

items.explanationHtml:
With the biochemical diagnosis of insulinoma made, the tumour is localised, starting with multiphase contrast CT or MRI of the pancreas; endoscopic ultrasonography follows if these are negative, and invasive or specialised tests are reserved for tumours that stay hidden. Most insulinomas are solitary and benign, and surgical removal is curative.

Takeaway: after biochemical confirmation, localise an insulinoma with pancreatic CT or MRI, then EUS, and remove it.

whyNot.A: Blind resection is not done; most tumours can be localised and enucleated.
whyNot.B: Most insulinomas are well differentiated and FDG-avid only uncommonly.
whyNot.C: Diazoxide is for patients who cannot have surgery; a likely curable tumour should be found.
whyNot.E: Arterial calcium stimulation is invasive and reserved for tumours not found by noninvasive imaging and EUS.

items.objective: Localise a biochemically confirmed insulinoma with cross-sectional imaging first.

items.stemHtml:
A 33-year-old woman who works as a receptionist has had four episodes of confusion and sweating in 3 weeks; glucose was below 45 mg/dL each time. She has no diabetes and takes only an oral contraceptive. Her husband has type 2 diabetes. During an episode in hospital, blood shows:

TestResult
Glucose38 mg/dL
Insulin22 µU/mL (N below 3 during hypoglycemia)
C-peptide2.4 ng/mL (N below 0.6 during hypoglycemia)
Proinsulin18 pmol/L (N below 5 during hypoglycemia)
Beta-hydroxybutyrate0.1 mmol/L (low)

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Plasma screen for sulfonylureas and meglitinides

items.explanationHtml:
The pattern is endogenous hyperinsulinism (high insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin, low ketones). That pattern is shared by an insulinoma and an insulin secretagogue. With access to her husband's diabetes medicines, a sulfonylurea and meglitinide screen must be done before any imaging.

Takeaway: high insulin plus high C-peptide needs a secretagogue screen before pancreatic imaging.

whyNot.A: Imaging before excluding a drug risks chasing an incidental finding.
whyNot.B: EUS is for localising a tumour once a drug cause is excluded.
whyNot.D: IGF-2 tumours suppress insulin and C-peptide, which are high here.
whyNot.E: Treatment without a diagnosis would miss a drug cause.

items.objective: Screen for insulin secretagogues when insulin and C-peptide are both high.

items.stemHtml: The screen is positive for glipizide. The pharmacy confirms that her own prescriptions were dispensed correctly and that she has never been prescribed glipizide. She is alone in her hospital room and asks whether the tests have found anything. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Arrange pancreatic imaging to be thorough before discussing results

options.label: B
options.html: Discharge her without discussing the result to avoid conflict

options.label: C
options.html: Discuss the result with her privately and without blame, and offer psychiatric support

options.label: D
options.html: Inform her husband first so he can confront her at home

options.label: E
options.html: Search her belongings for tablets while she is out of the room

items.explanationHtml:
A positive glipizide screen with no prescription or dispensing error points to surreptitious secretagogue use (factitious disorder, or harm by another person, which must also be considered). The physician should share the finding honestly and privately, without accusation, explore what happened, assess her safety and offer psychiatric care. Withholding the result or involving others without consent breaches trust and confidentiality.

Takeaway: disclose a positive secretagogue screen to the patient privately and supportively, and offer psychiatric care.

whyNot.A: Imaging is unnecessary once the cause is identified and delays honest disclosure.
whyNot.B: Discharging her without discussion leaves a dangerous cause unaddressed and is dishonest.
whyNot.D: Telling her husband first breaches confidentiality; he could also be the source of the drug.
whyNot.E: Searching a patient's belongings without consent violates her autonomy and trust.

items.objective: Disclose evidence of factitious hypoglycemia honestly and supportively.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy has a painless, 2-cm, round, midline neck mass just below the hyoid bone that has been present for months and swelled during a recent cold. The mass moves upward when he sticks out his tongue. Thyroid function is normal, and ultrasonography shows a normal thyroid gland in its usual position. From which embryologic structure does this mass most likely arise?

options.label: A
options.html: Remnant of the second pharyngeal cleft

options.label: B
options.html: Remnant of the third pharyngeal pouch

options.label: C
options.html: Remnant of the tract between the foramen cecum and the thyroid

options.label: D
options.html: Ultimobranchial body of the fourth pharyngeal pouch

items.explanationHtml:
A midline mass near the hyoid that rises with tongue protrusion is a thyroglossal duct cyst, a persistent part of the duct along which the thyroid descended from the foramen cecum. It may enlarge or become infected with upper respiratory infections. Excision includes the central hyoid and the tract (Sistrunk procedure) to prevent recurrence; imaging first confirms normal thyroid tissue elsewhere.

Takeaway: a midline neck mass that moves with tongue protrusion is a thyroglossal duct cyst.

whyNot.A: Branchial cleft cysts lie laterally, along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, and do not move with the tongue.
whyNot.B: Third pouch derivatives are the thymus and inferior parathyroids; their cysts are lateral or mediastinal.
whyNot.D: The ultimobranchial body gives the parafollicular C cells; it does not form midline cysts.
whyNot.E: Lymphatic malformations (cystic hygroma) are soft, lateral or posterior, transilluminate and do not rise with the tongue.

items.objective: Recognise a thyroglossal duct cyst and its embryologic origin.

items.stemHtml:
A 31-year-old woman has thyroid tests drawn as part of a fatigue work-up. She has no goiter, and her pulse is 72/min. She has taken a combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive for 4 years.

TestResultReference range
TSH2.1 µU/mL0.5–5.0
Total T414.8 µg/dL5–12
Free T41.3 ng/dL0.8–1.8

Which of the following best explains these results?

options.label: A
options.html: Autonomous hormone production by a thyroid nodule

options.label: B
options.html: Increased hepatic synthesis of thyroxine-binding globulin

options.label: C
options.html: Reduced peripheral conversion of T4 to T3

options.label: D
options.html: Stimulation of the TSH receptor by an autoantibody

options.label: E
options.html: Thyroid hormone resistance from a receptor mutation

items.explanationHtml:
Estrogen raises hepatic production (and slows clearance) of thyroxine-binding globulin. More hormone is bound, so total T4 rises, but the gland adjusts until free T4 and TSH are normal: she is euthyroid. Pregnancy does the same.

Takeaway: high total T4 with normal free T4 and TSH means more binding protein, not thyroid disease.

whyNot.A: An autonomous nodule raises free T4 and suppresses TSH.
whyNot.C: Impaired conversion lowers T3 and is seen in illness; it does not raise total T4 with normal free T4.
whyNot.D: TSH-receptor antibodies (Graves) raise free T4 and suppress TSH.
whyNot.E: Hormone resistance raises free T4 with a normal or high TSH, and the free hormone would be elevated.

items.objective: Interpret thyroid tests when thyroxine-binding globulin is raised by estrogen.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman has had hypothyroidism from Hashimoto thyroiditis for 20 years, controlled with levothyroxine. Over 6 weeks her neck has enlarged rapidly, and she now has hoarseness and a sense of pressure on swallowing. The thyroid is diffusely enlarged and firm. Core biopsy shows sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells that express CD20 and efface the follicles. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the thyroid

items.explanationHtml:
Long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis supplies chronically stimulated intrathyroidal B cells, and it is the main risk factor for primary thyroid lymphoma, most often diffuse large B-cell or MALT lymphoma. It presents as a rapidly enlarging gland with compressive symptoms. Sheets of large CD20-positive cells confirm it. Treatment is chemoimmunotherapy with or without radiation, not thyroidectomy.

Takeaway: rapid thyroid enlargement in long-standing Hashimoto suggests primary thyroid B-cell lymphoma.

whyNot.A: Anaplastic carcinoma also grows fast in older adults, but its cells are pleomorphic epithelial and spindle cells, not CD20-positive lymphoid cells.
whyNot.C: Follicular carcinoma is a slowly growing epithelial tumour defined by capsular or vascular invasion.
whyNot.D: Medullary carcinoma is made of C cells in amyloid stroma and expresses calcitonin.
whyNot.E: Riedel thyroiditis is dense fibrosis with IgG4-positive plasma cells, not sheets of atypical B cells.

items.objective: Associate Hashimoto thyroiditis with primary thyroid B-cell lymphoma.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman with Graves disease, who smokes, has gritty eyes, double vision on upward gaze and bilateral proptosis. MRI of the orbits shows enlarged extraocular muscle bellies with sparing of the tendons and increased orbital fat. Which of the following best explains the orbital changes?

options.label: A
options.html: Amyloid deposition derived from immunoglobulin light chains

options.label: B
options.html: Antibodies blocking acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction

options.label: C
options.html: Increased sympathetic tone to the levator palpebrae superioris

options.label: D
options.html: Orbital fibroblast activation with glycosaminoglycan deposition and adipogenesis

options.label: E
options.html: Venous congestion from a carotid-cavernous fistula

items.explanationHtml:
Orbital fibroblasts and preadipocytes express the TSH receptor (with the IGF-1 receptor). TSH-receptor antibodies and infiltrating T cells activate them to secrete hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans (hyaluronan), which draw in water, and to differentiate into fat cells. Muscles swell (tendons spared) and orbital fat expands, pushing the globe forward. Smoking makes it worse.

Takeaway: Graves orbitopathy is autoimmune activation of orbital fibroblasts: glycosaminoglycans plus new fat.

whyNot.A: Light-chain amyloid can infiltrate orbital tissue, but it is unrelated to Graves disease and does not spare tendons in this pattern.
whyNot.B: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause myasthenia gravis: fatigable ptosis and diplopia without proptosis or enlarged muscles.
whyNot.C: Sympathetic overactivity causes lid retraction and lid lag in any thyrotoxicosis, but not proptosis or muscle enlargement.
whyNot.E: A carotid-cavernous fistula causes pulsatile proptosis, a bruit and dilated superior ophthalmic vein, usually after trauma.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of Graves orbitopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman has had fever, fatigue and a painful neck for 10 days, beginning 2 weeks after a sore throat and cough. The pain radiates to her jaw. The thyroid is exquisitely tender. Pulse is 108/min. TSH is suppressed, free T4 is high, and ESR is 88 mm/h. Radioactive iodine uptake at 24 hours is 2% (normal 10–30%). If a biopsy were done, which of the following would it most likely show?

options.label: A
options.html: Dense fibrosis with IgG4-positive plasma cells extending into neck muscles

options.label: B
options.html: Diffuse hyperplasia of tall follicular cells with scalloped colloid

options.label: C
options.html: Granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells around disrupted follicles

options.label: D
options.html: Lymphoid follicles with germinal centres and Hürthle cells

options.label: E
options.html: Papillae with psammoma bodies and grooved, clear nuclei

items.explanationHtml:
A tender thyroid after a viral illness, high ESR and thyrotoxicosis with very low uptake is subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis. Follicles rupture and leak stored hormone; colloid provokes granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells. Treatment is NSAIDs (glucocorticoids if severe) and a β-blocker; thionamides do not help.

Takeaway: painful thyroid, high ESR and low uptake: subacute granulomatous thyroiditis.

whyNot.A: This is Riedel thyroiditis, a painless, rock-hard gland that is not usually thyrotoxic.
whyNot.B: Hyperplasia with scalloped colloid is Graves disease, which has a painless gland and high uptake.
whyNot.D: Lymphoid follicles and Hürthle cells describe Hashimoto thyroiditis, which is painless.
whyNot.E: These are features of papillary carcinoma, which does not cause painful thyrotoxicosis.

items.objective: Recognise subacute granulomatous thyroiditis and its histology.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman, who received neck irradiation as a child for lymphoma, has a 2-cm firm thyroid nodule and an enlarged ipsilateral cervical lymph node. Fine-needle aspiration shows cells with enlarged, overlapping nuclei that have finely dispersed pale chromatin, longitudinal grooves and intranuclear cytoplasmic pseudoinclusions, along with laminated calcified bodies. Which of the following genetic alterations is most likely in this tumour?
items.explanationHtml:
Clear, grooved nuclei with pseudoinclusions and psammoma bodies are papillary thyroid carcinoma, the most common thyroid cancer and the one linked to childhood radiation. It spreads to cervical nodes and has an excellent prognosis. The most common driver is BRAF V600E; RET/PTC rearrangements are typical after radiation exposure.

Takeaway: papillary carcinoma nuclei plus psammoma bodies; BRAF V600E or RET/PTC.

whyNot.B: MEN1 causes parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumours, not thyroid carcinoma.
whyNot.C: Germline activating RET variants cause medullary carcinoma (MEN2), a C-cell tumour without these nuclear features. (RET rearrangements in papillary cancer are somatic fusions, not germline activating variants.)
whyNot.D: PAX8-PPARG fusion is typical of follicular carcinoma, which lacks papillary nuclear features.
whyNot.E: TP53 loss marks anaplastic carcinoma, a pleomorphic, rapidly growing tumour of older adults.

items.objective: Link papillary thyroid carcinoma histology to BRAF and RET/PTC alterations.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman with known Graves disease is admitted after a urinary tract infection with temperature 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse 154/min in atrial fibrillation, agitation and vomiting. The team chooses one thionamide over the other because it lowers circulating T3 faster. Which of the following additional actions explains this choice?

options.label: B
options.html: Inhibiting peripheral conversion of T4 to T3

options.label: D
options.html: Preventing thyroid hormone binding to nuclear receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Both methimazole and propylthiouracil block thyroid peroxidase, stopping new hormone synthesis. PTU also inhibits peripheral 5′-deiodinase, so less T4 becomes active T3; this is why it is preferred in thyroid storm. Glucocorticoids and high-dose propranolol add to this effect. Iodine is given at least an hour after the thionamide to block release.

Takeaway: PTU blocks both thyroid peroxidase and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion.

whyNot.A: Perchlorate and pertechnetate compete at the symporter; thionamides do not act there.
whyNot.C: Large iodide doses (and lithium) inhibit release of hormone from thyroglobulin; thionamides do not.
whyNot.D: No drug used in storm blocks nuclear thyroid hormone receptors.
whyNot.E: TSH is already suppressed in Graves; lowering it further would not help.

items.objective: Explain why propylthiouracil is preferred in thyroid storm (it blocks peripheral deiodination).

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man with Hashimoto thyroiditis that has never needed treatment (positive anti-TPO antibodies, normal TSH a year ago) is started on amiodarone for ventricular tachycardia. Four months later he has fatigue, weight gain and constipation. TSH is 24 µU/mL (N = 0.5–5.0) and free T4 is low. Which of the following best explains his hypothyroidism?

options.label: A
options.html: Amiodarone-induced destructive thyroiditis with release of stored hormone

options.label: B
options.html: Failure of his thyroid to escape the inhibition of organification caused by excess iodide

options.label: C
options.html: Increased thyroxine-binding globulin synthesis lowering free hormone

options.label: D
options.html: Pituitary suppression of TSH by amiodarone metabolites

options.label: E
options.html: Stimulation of hormone synthesis by excess iodide substrate

items.explanationHtml:
Amiodarone is about one third iodine by weight. A large iodide load acutely inhibits organification (the Wolff-Chaikoff effect); a normal gland escapes within days by down-regulating the symporter. A gland already damaged by Hashimoto thyroiditis cannot escape, so hypothyroidism develops. Treatment is levothyroxine; amiodarone can usually continue.

Takeaway: amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism is failure to escape Wolff-Chaikoff, most likely in underlying autoimmune thyroiditis.

whyNot.A: Destructive thyroiditis (type 2 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis) causes thyrotoxicosis, not primary hypothyroidism with a high TSH.
whyNot.C: TBG changes alter total, not free, hormone; free T4 here is truly low.
whyNot.D: A high TSH shows the pituitary is responding normally; the defect is in the thyroid.
whyNot.E: Extra iodide fuelling synthesis is the type 1 mechanism of thyrotoxicosis in nodular or Graves glands.

items.objective: Explain amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism as failure to escape the Wolff-Chaikoff effect.

items.stemHtml:
A 47-year-old man had transsphenoidal resection of a nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma 6 months ago. He takes hydrocortisone 15 mg daily and testosterone. Levothyroxine 75 µg daily was started for central hypothyroidism 8 weeks ago. He still feels tired and cold.

TestBefore levothyroxineTodayReference range
TSH1.1 µU/mL0.3 µU/mL0.5–5.0
Free T40.5 ng/dL0.8 ng/dL0.8–1.8

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Add liothyronine (T3) to the current dose

options.label: B
options.html: Continue the same dose, because TSH is now suppressed

options.label: C
options.html: Increase the levothyroxine dose and recheck free T4 in 6 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Reduce the levothyroxine dose because TSH is below normal

options.label: E
options.html: Stop levothyroxine and measure TSH-receptor antibodies

items.explanationHtml:
In central hypothyroidism the pituitary cannot produce a meaningful TSH, so TSH is useless for dosing and any value (low, normal or low on treatment) is uninterpretable. Titrate levothyroxine to bring free T4 into the upper half of the normal range. His free T4 is at the bottom of the range with persistent symptoms, so the dose should go up. Glucocorticoid replacement was correctly started first.

Takeaway: in pituitary disease, dose levothyroxine by free T4, not TSH.

whyNot.A: Combination T3 therapy is not standard and does not fix an inadequate T4 dose.
whyNot.B: The low TSH reflects pituitary disease plus treatment, not over-replacement; free T4 is still low.
whyNot.D: Reducing the dose would worsen his hypothyroidism.
whyNot.E: There is no sign of Graves disease; the low TSH is expected in central hypothyroidism.

items.objective: Titrate levothyroxine by free T4 in central hypothyroidism.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman has a routine checkup. She feels well and does not plan pregnancy. Her mother has hypothyroidism. Examination shows no goiter. TSH is 7.2 µU/mL (N = 0.5–5.0) and free T4 is 1.1 ng/dL (N = 0.8–1.8). She has no previous thyroid tests. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Order radioactive iodine uptake and scan

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat TSH and free T4 in 2–3 months

items.explanationHtml:
A single mildly raised TSH with normal free T4 is subclinical hypothyroidism, but many such values return to normal (recovering thyroiditis, assay variation, illness). The first step is to repeat TSH with free T4 in about 2–3 months; anti-TPO antibodies help predict progression. Treatment is clearly indicated if TSH stays at 10 µU/mL or more, and is individualised below that (symptoms, pregnancy plans).

Takeaway: confirm subclinical hypothyroidism with repeat testing before treating; treat persistent TSH of 10 or more.

whyNot.A: Full replacement is not indicated for an unconfirmed, mild TSH elevation without symptoms.
whyNot.B: Low-dose treatment may be reasonable later for persistent elevation with symptoms or pregnancy plans, but not on one value.
whyNot.C: Uptake scans evaluate thyrotoxicosis, not a high TSH.
whyNot.D: Ultrasonography is for palpable nodules or goiter, not for an isolated TSH rise.

items.objective: Confirm subclinical hypothyroidism with repeat TSH and free T4 before treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old nurse has 2 months of palpitations, heat intolerance and a 5-kg weight loss. Pulse is 112/min. The thyroid is not enlarged or tender, and there is no eye disease. TSH is below 0.01 µU/mL (N = 0.5–5.0), and free T4 is 3.1 ng/dL (N = 0.8–1.8). ESR is normal. Radioactive iodine uptake at 24 hours is 1% (normal 10–30%). Which of the following findings would most strongly support the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: E
options.html: Single hot nodule on the radionuclide scan

items.explanationHtml:
Thyrotoxicosis with a small, nontender gland and near-zero uptake means hormone is not being made by the thyroid: thyroiditis, iodine load or exogenous hormone. In a health worker with no goiter, surreptitious levothyroxine is likely. Exogenous hormone suppresses TSH and the gland, so thyroglobulin is low; in thyroiditis, follicle destruction releases thyroglobulin and it is high.

Takeaway: low uptake plus low thyroglobulin points to exogenous thyroid hormone.

whyNot.A: TSH-receptor antibodies mean Graves disease, which has high, diffuse uptake.
whyNot.B: High thyroglobulin points to thyroiditis, which leaks stored hormone; it argues against exogenous hormone.
whyNot.D: Anti-TPO antibodies are common and nonspecific; they would support painless thyroiditis, not the likely diagnosis here.
whyNot.E: A hot nodule would show high focal uptake, not 1% overall uptake.

items.objective: Distinguish factitious thyrotoxicosis from thyroiditis using thyroglobulin when uptake is low.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman is brought from home in January after her neighbour found her drowsy. She stopped taking her medications several months ago. Rectal temperature is 33.6°C (92.5°F), pulse 48/min, respirations 8/min and blood pressure 88/56 mm Hg. She has periorbital puffiness, coarse dry skin and delayed relaxation of ankle reflexes. Sodium is 122 mEq/L, glucose 61 mg/dL and arterial PaCO2 64 mm Hg. TSH is 86 µU/mL (N = 0.5–5.0) and free T4 is undetectable. A random cortisol has been drawn. She is intubated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

options.label: E
options.html: 3% saline to raise the sodium to normal over 6 hours

items.explanationHtml:
This is myxedema coma: hypothermia, depressed consciousness, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, hyponatremia and hypoglycemia with profound hypothyroidism. Give IV levothyroxine (a loading dose) because gut absorption is unreliable, together with IV hydrocortisone until adrenal insufficiency is excluded, since restoring metabolism raises cortisol clearance and could precipitate adrenal crisis. Add supportive care in an ICU.

Takeaway: myxedema coma: IV hydrocortisone with IV levothyroxine, plus ventilatory and circulatory support.

whyNot.B: Thyroid hormone without glucocorticoid cover risks adrenal crisis if coexisting adrenal insufficiency is present.
whyNot.C: Small oral doses are for stable older outpatients; absorption is poor and the response far too slow in myxedema coma.
whyNot.D: T3 alone carries cardiac risk, is still given with T4 when used, and oral absorption is unreliable here.
whyNot.E: Hyponatremia improves with treatment of hypothyroidism; correcting it fully within hours risks osmotic demyelination.

items.objective: Treat myxedema coma with IV levothyroxine plus stress-dose hydrocortisone.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman started methimazole 20 mg daily for Graves disease 5 weeks ago. Since yesterday she has had a sore throat, mouth ulcers and a temperature of 38.9°C (102°F). Pulse is 100/min and blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Continue methimazole and test for group A streptococcus

options.label: C
options.html: Stop methimazole and obtain a complete blood count with differential

options.label: E
options.html: Switch to radioactive iodine therapy this week

items.explanationHtml:
Fever and sore throat in a patient on a thionamide suggest agranulocytosis, which usually occurs in the first months. The drug must be stopped immediately and a CBC with differential obtained; if the neutrophil count is very low, she needs admission and broad-spectrum antibiotics for febrile neutropenia. The other thionamide must not be used because of cross-reactivity; definitive therapy is planned once she recovers.

Takeaway: fever or sore throat on a thionamide: stop the drug and check the neutrophil count.

whyNot.A: Continuing methimazole could allow agranulocytosis to progress to life-threatening sepsis.
whyNot.B: Testing for streptococci without stopping the drug misses the dangerous cause.
whyNot.D: PTU cross-reacts with methimazole and can cause the same agranulocytosis.
whyNot.E: Radioiodine may later be the right definitive therapy, but the immediate priority is the neutrophil count and stopping the drug.

items.objective: Recognise and manage suspected thionamide-induced agranulocytosis.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman had a 1.9-cm right thyroid nodule found on examination. TSH was 1.8 µU/mL (N = 0.5–5.0). Ultrasonography showed a solid, isoechoic nodule with smooth margins and no calcifications, which was classified as intermediate suspicion (not high suspicion); no abnormal lymph nodes were seen. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration is reported as benign (Bethesda category II). She is asymptomatic. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Levothyroxine to suppress TSH and shrink the nodule

items.explanationHtml:
A benign (Bethesda II) cytology result carries a low risk of malignancy. For a nodule with a low- or intermediate-suspicion sonographic pattern, follow-up is repeat ultrasonography in about 12–24 months; repeat FNA is reserved for significant growth or new suspicious features. (High-suspicion nodules with benign cytology are re-sampled sooner.)

Takeaway: benign FNA in a low- or intermediate-suspicion nodule: ultrasound surveillance.

whyNot.A: TSH suppression is not recommended for benign nodules; it risks atrial fibrillation and bone loss with little benefit.
whyNot.B: A scan is useful only when TSH is low, to look for a hot nodule.
whyNot.C: Early routine repeat FNA is not needed for benign cytology in a nodule without high-suspicion features.
whyNot.D: Surgery is for malignant, suspicious or symptomatic compressive nodules, not an asymptomatic benign one.

items.objective: Follow a cytologically benign thyroid nodule with ultrasonography.

items.stemHtml:
A 63-year-old man has been in the ICU for 9 days with septic shock from pneumonia. He has been off vasopressors for 2 days and is improving. Thyroid tests were sent by a consulting team. He has no history of thyroid disease, no goiter and takes no thyroid-affecting drugs.

TestResultReference range
TSH0.6 µU/mL0.5–5.0
Free T40.9 ng/dL0.8–1.8
Total T348 ng/dL80–180
Reverse T3High—

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: No thyroid treatment; repeat tests some weeks after recovery

items.explanationHtml:
Low T3 with high reverse T3 and normal-range TSH and free T4 during critical illness is nonthyroidal illness (euthyroid sick) syndrome: cytokines and stress reduce 5′-deiodinase activity, shifting T4 metabolism toward reverse T3. Thyroid hormone treatment has not shown benefit. Repeat tests after recovery, when values usually normalise; a brief TSH rise during recovery is expected.

Takeaway: in critical illness, low T3 with high reverse T3 needs no treatment; retest after recovery.

whyNot.A: Levothyroxine does not improve outcomes in nonthyroidal illness and he is not hypothyroid.
whyNot.B: T3 replacement in critical illness has not shown benefit and risks arrhythmia.
whyNot.C: Central hypothyroidism is unlikely with normal free T4; pituitary imaging is not indicated.
whyNot.E: There is no thyrotoxicosis to explain; TSH-receptor antibodies would not help.

items.objective: Recognise nonthyroidal illness syndrome and avoid treating it.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man who smokes 20 cigarettes a day has 3 months of tremor, weight loss and palpitations, and 6 weeks of eye irritation and double vision. Pulse is 110/min. He has a diffuse goiter with a bruit, bilateral proptosis, lid retraction, conjunctival redness and swelling of the eyelids. TSH is below 0.01 µU/mL (N = 0.5–5.0) and free T4 is 3.6 ng/dL (N = 0.8–1.8). Propranolol is started. Which of the following tests would best confirm the cause of his thyrotoxicosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Thyrotoxicosis with a diffuse goiter and orbitopathy is Graves disease clinically; TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb or TSI) confirm it, and are an accepted alternative to an uptake scan. They also help predict relapse after medical therapy.

Takeaway: confirm Graves disease with TSH-receptor antibodies (or radioiodine uptake when the picture is unclear).

whyNot.A: FNA evaluates nodules for cancer; it does not establish the cause of diffuse thyrotoxicosis.
whyNot.C: Calcitonin is a marker of medullary carcinoma.
whyNot.D: Thyroglobulin is high in most thyrotoxic states and does not identify Graves disease.
whyNot.E: Ultrasonography may show increased vascularity but is less specific than antibodies.

items.objective: Confirm Graves disease with TSH-receptor antibodies.

items.stemHtml: His TSH-receptor antibody titre is markedly raised. An ophthalmologist confirms active, moderate-to-severe orbitopathy without optic neuropathy. He wants to discuss treatment of his hyperthyroidism. Along with smoking cessation and treatment of the eye disease, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his hyperthyroidism?
items.explanationHtml:
Radioactive iodine can worsen active Graves orbitopathy, and it is avoided when orbitopathy is moderate to severe and active (glucocorticoid cover is used only for mild active disease). Appropriate choices are methimazole (or thyroidectomy). Methimazole is preferred over PTU outside the first trimester of pregnancy because PTU can cause severe liver injury. Stopping smoking improves the eye outcome.

Takeaway: with moderate-to-severe active Graves orbitopathy, treat hyperthyroidism with methimazole or surgery, not radioiodine.

whyNot.B: Iodine alone gives only temporary control and is used briefly before surgery or in storm.
whyNot.C: PTU is reserved for the first trimester of pregnancy and thyroid storm because of hepatotoxicity.
whyNot.D: Radioiodine can worsen active orbitopathy, especially in smokers.
whyNot.E: Glucocorticoid cover makes radioiodine acceptable for mild active orbitopathy, not moderate-to-severe active disease.

items.objective: Avoid radioiodine and choose methimazole or surgery when Graves orbitopathy is moderate to severe and active.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature. She has a round face, obesity and mild developmental delay. Her fourth and fifth fingers are short, and radiographs show shortened fourth and fifth metacarpals. Serum calcium is 7.2 mg/dL, phosphorus 6.4 mg/dL and intact PTH 210 pg/mL (N = 10–65). Infusion of synthetic PTH fails to raise urinary cyclic AMP. Her mother has the same hand findings but normal calcium and PTH. A variant in the gene encoding which of the following proteins is most likely?

options.label: C
options.html: Gs-alpha subunit of a heterotrimeric G protein

items.explanationHtml:
Low calcium, high phosphate and high PTH mean end-organ PTH resistance. Failure of PTH to raise urinary cyclic AMP localises the block between the receptor and adenylyl cyclase, which is coupled by Gs-alpha (encoded by GNAS). Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (short stature, round face, short fourth and fifth metacarpals) completes pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A. Because the kidney expresses only the maternal GNAS allele, the child who inherited the variant from her mother has hormone resistance, whereas the mother (who presumably inherited it from her father) has only the body habitus: pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism.

Takeaway: PTH resistance with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy is pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A, a maternally inherited GNAS (Gs-alpha) defect.

whyNot.A: Loss of CaSR function causes hypercalcemia with low urine calcium, not hypocalcemia.
whyNot.B: Excess FGF23 causes phosphate wasting with low phosphate; she has high phosphate.
whyNot.D: A receptor-binding defect is possible in theory, but the Albright phenotype and imprinting pattern fit a Gs-alpha defect.
whyNot.E: Vitamin D receptor defects cause hereditary vitamin D-resistant rickets with low phosphate and alopecia, not Albright features.

items.objective: Explain pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A as Gs-alpha (GNAS) loss with maternal imprinting.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy has a serum calcium of 10.9 mg/dL found during a sports physical. He has no symptoms, stones or fractures. Serum phosphorus is 3.2 mg/dL, and intact PTH is 58 pg/mL (N = 10–65). The 24-hour urine calcium is 40 mg, and the calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio is 0.004. His father and a sister have had similar calcium values for years without complications. Which of the following best explains the urine findings?

options.label: B
options.html: Increased PTH secretion from a parathyroid adenoma

options.label: C
options.html: Reduced sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor in parathyroid and kidney

options.label: D
options.html: Reduced tubular secretion of calcium caused by low GFR

options.label: E
options.html: Suppressed PTH from a PTH-related peptide

items.explanationHtml:
Mild lifelong hypercalcemia, normal PTH, very low urinary calcium (clearance ratio below 0.01) and affected relatives are familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, usually from a heterozygous inactivating CASR variant. The parathyroids need a higher calcium to suppress PTH, and in the thick ascending limb the less sensitive receptor allows more calcium reabsorption, so urine calcium is low.

Takeaway: Hypercalcemia with normal PTH and a calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01 in a family is FHH, a CaSR loss-of-function disorder.

whyNot.A: Calcitriol excess suppresses PTH and raises urinary calcium.
whyNot.B: Primary hyperparathyroidism usually raises urine calcium because the filtered load is high; the family history and low clearance ratio argue against it.
whyNot.D: Calcium is filtered and reabsorbed, not secreted, and his kidney function is normal.
whyNot.E: PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia suppresses intact PTH, which is normal here.

items.objective: Explain the hypocalciuria of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia through CaSR loss of function.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man has had dull pain in his right thigh for a year. His hat no longer fits, and he has noticed reduced hearing. Serum calcium and phosphorus are normal. Alkaline phosphatase is 640 U/L, and AST, ALT, GGT and bilirubin are normal. Radiographs show a thickened, bowed right femur with coarse trabeculae and a thickened skull. Which of the following is most likely seen on bone biopsy?

options.label: B
options.html: Fibrous tissue with hemosiderin-laden giant cells and cysts

options.label: C
options.html: Lamellar bone in a mosaic pattern with irregular cement lines

options.label: E
options.html: Woven bone trabeculae in fibrous stroma shaped like Chinese letters

items.explanationHtml:
An isolated high alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium, a growing skull, deafness and a bowed, thickened long bone is Paget disease of bone. Bursts of osteoclast resorption followed by disorganised osteoblast repair leave lamellar bone with haphazard cement lines in a mosaic pattern. The bone is thick but weak. Complications include fractures, nerve compression, high-output heart failure and, rarely, osteosarcoma.

Takeaway: Isolated high alkaline phosphatase with enlarging bones and mosaic lamellar bone is Paget disease.

whyNot.A: Wide osteoid seams are osteomalacia, which lowers phosphate and raises PTH.
whyNot.B: Brown tumours of hyperparathyroidism contain giant cells and hemosiderin but come with hypercalcemia.
whyNot.D: Thin, normally mineralised trabeculae are osteoporosis, which leaves alkaline phosphatase normal.
whyNot.E: Curvilinear woven bone in fibrous tissue is fibrous dysplasia, usually in younger patients.

items.objective: Recognise the histology and laboratory pattern of Paget disease of bone.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder who also takes omeprazole daily is admitted with muscle cramps and hand spasms. Serum calcium is 6.9 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, phosphorus 3.6 mg/dL, magnesium 0.6 mEq/L (N = 1.5–2.0) and intact PTH 14 pg/mL (N = 10–65). Intravenous calcium gluconate brings temporary relief, but calcium falls again within hours. Which of the following best explains the persistent hypocalcemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Autoimmune destruction of parathyroid chief cells

options.label: B
options.html: Hungry bone syndrome after alcohol withdrawal

options.label: C
options.html: Impaired PTH secretion and action due to magnesium deficiency

options.label: D
options.html: Loss-of-function variant in the Gs-alpha subunit

items.explanationHtml:
Severe hypomagnesemia (here from alcohol use and a proton pump inhibitor) blocks PTH release from the parathyroid and blunts the response of bone and kidney to PTH. PTH is therefore low or inappropriately normal despite hypocalcemia, and calcium replacement alone fails until magnesium is repleted.

Takeaway: Refractory hypocalcemia with low or normal PTH: check and replace magnesium.

whyNot.A: Autoimmune hypoparathyroidism does not explain the very low magnesium; with two clear causes of magnesium loss, the low PTH is best explained by magnesium depletion, which is reversible.
whyNot.B: Hungry bone syndrome follows parathyroidectomy or thyroidectomy for hyperthyroidism, not alcohol withdrawal.
whyNot.D: Gs-alpha loss causes PTH resistance with high PTH, not a low PTH.
whyNot.E: Vitamin D deficiency causes secondary hyperparathyroidism with high PTH and low phosphate.

items.objective: Explain how hypomagnesemia causes functional hypoparathyroidism.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman who had Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 8 years ago has had diffuse bone pain, difficulty climbing stairs and a waddling gait for 6 months. She stopped her supplements years ago. Serum calcium is 8.3 mg/dL, phosphorus 2.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 290 U/L, intact PTH 160 pg/mL (N = 10–65) and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 6 ng/mL (N = 20–50). Radiographs show bilateral linear lucencies perpendicular to the cortex of the femoral necks. Which of the following is the most likely histologic finding in her bone?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased osteoclast numbers with peritrabecular fibrosis only

options.label: B
options.html: Mosaic lamellar bone with prominent cement lines

options.label: C
options.html: Normal mineralised trabeculae that are reduced in number

options.label: D
options.html: Thick seams of unmineralised osteoid on bone surfaces

options.label: E
options.html: Woven bone produced by malignant osteoblasts

items.explanationHtml:
Malabsorption after gastric bypass has caused vitamin D deficiency with low calcium and phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase and secondary hyperparathyroidism: osteomalacia. Without enough calcium and phosphate, osteoid is laid down but not mineralised, leaving wide osteoid seams. The lucencies are pseudofractures (Looser zones). Proximal myopathy and bone pain are typical.

Takeaway: Low calcium and phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase and PTH, and pseudofractures mean osteomalacia: unmineralised osteoid.

whyNot.A: Peritrabecular fibrosis with osteoclast activity is the PTH effect, but on its own it does not explain the pseudofractures and defective mineralisation.
whyNot.B: Mosaic bone is Paget disease, which has normal calcium and phosphate.
whyNot.C: Reduced, normally mineralised trabeculae is osteoporosis, with normal laboratory values.
whyNot.E: Malignant osteoid is osteosarcoma, a focal tumour, not a diffuse metabolic process.

items.objective: Recognise osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency after bariatric surgery.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old woman with osteoporosis begins a weekly oral drug that must be taken fasting with a full glass of water while she stays upright for 30 minutes. The drug binds to hydroxyapatite and is taken up by bone-resorbing cells. Which of the following best describes its molecular action?

options.label: A
options.html: Binds RANKL and blocks its interaction with RANK

options.label: B
options.html: Binds sclerostin and releases inhibition of Wnt signalling

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibits farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in osteoclasts

options.label: D
options.html: Selectively activates estrogen receptors in bone

options.label: E
options.html: Stimulates the PTH type 1 receptor intermittently

items.explanationHtml:
Weekly oral dosing with strict fasting and upright instructions describes a nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate such as alendronate. It concentrates on bone surfaces, is ingested by osteoclasts and inhibits farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway; loss of protein prenylation disrupts the osteoclast ruffled border and causes apoptosis. The upright instruction prevents pill esophagitis.

Takeaway: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase and kill osteoclasts.

whyNot.A: Blocking RANKL is denosumab, a subcutaneous antibody given every 6 months.
whyNot.B: Sclerostin inhibition is romosozumab, a monthly injection.
whyNot.D: Selective estrogen receptor modulation is raloxifene, which has no fasting or upright requirement.
whyNot.E: Intermittent PTH receptor stimulation is teriparatide or abaloparatide, given by daily injection.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman has a serum calcium of 11.6 mg/dL (N = 8.4–10.2) on two occasions. She has no symptoms and no history of kidney stones or fractures. Phosphorus is 2.5 mg/dL, intact PTH 96 pg/mL (N = 10–65), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 34 ng/mL, eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m², and 24-hour urine calcium 290 mg. DXA shows a T-score of −2.7 at the distal radius and −1.6 at the lumbar spine. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Annual calcium and creatinine monitoring only

options.label: B
options.html: Begin hydrochlorothiazide to reduce urinary calcium

options.label: C
options.html: Referral for parathyroidectomy with preoperative localisation imaging

options.label: E
options.html: Start oral alendronate and repeat DXA in 2 years

items.explanationHtml:
She has primary hyperparathyroidism (high calcium, high PTH, normal vitamin D, urine calcium not low). Although asymptomatic, she meets criteria for surgery: calcium more than 1 mg/dL above the upper limit, and osteoporosis at the distal radius (a site PTH particularly affects). Parathyroidectomy is curative; localisation imaging (sestamibi, ultrasonography or 4D-CT) is done once surgery is planned.

Takeaway: Primary hyperparathyroidism with calcium >1 mg/dL above normal, osteoporosis, eGFR <60, stones or hypercalciuria, or age <50: refer for parathyroidectomy.

whyNot.A: Observation is for patients who meet no surgical criteria; she meets two.
whyNot.B: Thiazides raise serum calcium and are avoided in primary hyperparathyroidism.
whyNot.D: Cinacalcet lowers calcium but does not improve bone density or cure the disease; it is for patients who cannot have surgery.
whyNot.E: A bisphosphonate protects bone but leaves the hyperparathyroidism, and its calcium elevation, untreated.

items.objective: Apply surgical criteria in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer to the spine and pelvis is brought to the emergency department with 4 days of increasing confusion, thirst, constipation and poor oral intake. Blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg and pulse 110/min. Mucous membranes are dry. Serum calcium is 14.6 mg/dL, albumin 3.8 g/dL, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (baseline 0.8) and intact PTH 6 pg/mL (N = 10–65). ECG shows a short QT interval. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.html: Intravenous furosemide followed by oral alendronate

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous isotonic saline, subcutaneous calcitonin and intravenous zoledronic acid

options.label: C
options.html: Oral prednisone and a low-calcium diet

options.label: D
options.html: Subcutaneous denosumab alone without intravenous fluids

options.label: E
options.html: Urgent hemodialysis with a low-calcium bath

items.explanationHtml:
Severe, symptomatic hypercalcemia of malignancy with volume depletion and prerenal AKI is treated with intravenous isotonic saline to restore volume and calcium excretion, calcitonin for a rapid fall over hours, and an intravenous bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid, with the dose adjusted to kidney function) for a sustained effect over days. Suppressed PTH confirms a PTH-independent cause, here osteolytic metastases (with or without PTHrP).

Takeaway: Severe hypercalcemia: saline first, calcitonin for speed, a bisphosphonate (or denosumab) for durability.

whyNot.A: Furosemide before volume repletion worsens dehydration and kidney injury, and oral bisphosphonates act too slowly and absorb poorly.
whyNot.C: Glucocorticoids treat calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia (lymphoma, granulomas), not bone metastases from breast cancer.
whyNot.D: Denosumab is useful, especially when bisphosphonates cannot be used, but leaving the volume depletion untreated is unsafe.
whyNot.E: Dialysis is reserved for life-threatening hypercalcemia with severe kidney failure or failure of standard therapy.

items.objective: Manage severe hypercalcemia of malignancy with saline, calcitonin and a bisphosphonate.

items.stemHtml:
A 66-year-old man with newly diagnosed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma has fatigue and constipation. Laboratory studies after 2 L of intravenous saline show:

TestResult
Calcium12.4 mg/dL
Phosphorus4.1 mg/dL
Intact PTH5 pg/mL (N = 10–65)
PTH-related peptideUndetectable
25-hydroxyvitamin D28 ng/mL (N = 20–50)
1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D118 pg/mL (N = 18–72)

Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment to lower his calcium?
items.explanationHtml:
Suppressed PTH, absent PTHrP and a high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D with a normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D mean the lymphoma's macrophages are making calcitriol through unregulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase, raising gut calcium absorption. Glucocorticoids inhibit this enzyme activity and are effective, alongside treatment of the lymphoma. The same approach applies to sarcoidosis and other granulomatous disease.

Takeaway: Calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia (lymphoma, granulomas) responds to glucocorticoids.

whyNot.A: Cinacalcet lowers PTH, which is already suppressed.
whyNot.C: Thiazides reduce calcium excretion and would worsen hypercalcemia.
whyNot.D: Phosphate binders lower phosphate; they do not address calcitriol-driven calcium absorption.
whyNot.E: The parathyroids are suppressed and not the cause.

items.objective: Recognise calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia and treat it with glucocorticoids.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman developed permanent hypoparathyroidism after total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid cancer 1 year ago. She takes levothyroxine and calcium carbonate 1 g three times daily, but still has occasional tingling. Serum calcium is 7.6 mg/dL, phosphorus 5.2 mg/dL, magnesium 1.9 mEq/L, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 36 ng/mL and PTH undetectable. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Without PTH, the proximal tubule cannot adequately activate 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so ordinary vitamin D (already replete here) is not converted to the active hormone. Calcitriol, the active form, restores intestinal calcium absorption. The aim is a low-normal calcium, which limits hypercalciuria and kidney stones; urinary calcium is monitored, and a thiazide can be added if it is high.

Takeaway: Hypoparathyroidism needs calcium plus active vitamin D (calcitriol); target low-normal calcium.

whyNot.B: Her 25-hydroxyvitamin D is replete; the missing step is 1-alpha-hydroxylation, which needs PTH.
whyNot.C: Ergocalciferol also requires PTH-dependent activation and has the same limitation.
whyNot.D: A thiazide reduces urinary calcium losses but will not correct hypocalcemia on its own.
whyNot.E: Her magnesium is normal, so it is not limiting PTH or its action.

items.objective: Use calcitriol in chronic hypoparathyroidism.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman comes for a health maintenance visit. She has never had a fracture, takes no medications and drinks alcohol rarely. Her mother did not have a hip fracture. BMI is 24 kg/m². She has never had bone density testing. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding osteoporosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Bone density testing is not needed without a prior fracture

options.label: B
options.html: DXA of the hip and lumbar spine

options.label: C
options.html: Plain radiographs of the thoracic and lumbar spine

options.label: D
options.html: Serum alkaline phosphatase and calcium only

items.explanationHtml:
All women aged 65 years or older should be screened for osteoporosis with bone density testing, usually DXA of the hip and lumbar spine. Younger postmenopausal women are screened when a risk assessment shows increased risk.

Takeaway: Screen all women 65 and older for osteoporosis with DXA.

whyNot.A: Screening is aimed at finding osteoporosis before the first fracture.
whyNot.C: Radiographs detect fractures but are insensitive for low bone mass.
whyNot.D: Blood tests are normal in osteoporosis and do not measure bone density.
whyNot.E: Treatment decisions need a measured T-score or a fragility fracture.

items.objective: Screen women 65 and older for osteoporosis with DXA.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman with osteoporosis has received denosumab every 6 months for 5 years after a vertebral fracture. Her most recent DXA shows a lumbar spine T-score of −2.1, up from −3.0. She asks to stop treatment because she is tired of the injections. Creatinine clearance is 58 mL/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

options.label: A
options.html: Stop denosumab and give no further therapy

options.label: B
options.html: Stop denosumab and start a bisphosphonate around the time the next dose would be due

options.label: C
options.html: Stop denosumab and start calcium and vitamin D supplements only

options.label: E
options.html: Stop denosumab and repeat DXA in 5 years

items.explanationHtml:
Denosumab's effect wears off rapidly. Stopping it without follow-on therapy causes a rebound in bone turnover, rapid loss of the density gained and a risk of multiple vertebral fractures, especially in someone with a prior vertebral fracture. Transition to a bisphosphonate (often zoledronic acid or alendronate) timed to when the next denosumab dose would be due.

Takeaway: Never stop denosumab without starting a bisphosphonate.

whyNot.A: No follow-on therapy risks rebound vertebral fractures.
whyNot.C: Calcium and vitamin D are needed but are too weak to prevent rebound bone loss.
whyNot.D: Raloxifene has not been shown to prevent post-denosumab rebound and raises venous thromboembolism risk.
whyNot.E: Waiting 5 years without therapy is unsafe after stopping denosumab.

items.objective: Prevent rebound vertebral fractures when stopping denosumab.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old woman has a DXA T-score of −2.9 at the femoral neck. She has a peptic esophageal stricture that has required dilation twice and recurrent esophagitis. Creatinine clearance is 64 mL/min. She is otherwise independent. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her osteoporosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Daily oral calcium and vitamin D only

items.explanationHtml:
Oral bisphosphonates can cause pill esophagitis and are avoided in patients with esophageal stricture, achalasia or inability to stay upright. Intravenous zoledronic acid once a year avoids the esophagus and is effective; her kidney function permits it.

Takeaway: Use intravenous zoledronic acid (or denosumab) when oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated by esophageal disease.

whyNot.A: Calcium and vitamin D alone do not adequately reduce fracture risk at this T-score.
whyNot.C: Weekly alendronate is contraindicated with an esophageal stricture.
whyNot.D: Risedronate is also an oral bisphosphonate with the same esophageal risk.
whyNot.E: Anabolic therapy is limited to about 2 years and is reserved for very high risk; it is not lifelong.

items.objective: Choose intravenous zoledronic acid when oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated.

items.stemHtml: Before the planned zoledronic acid infusion, laboratory studies show serum calcium 8.1 mg/dL (albumin 4.0 g/dL), phosphorus 2.6 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 142 U/L, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 9 ng/mL (N = 20–50) and intact PTH 94 pg/mL (N = 10–65). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Give the infusion as planned and recheck calcium in 1 year

options.label: B
options.html: Give the infusion with a single dose of calcitriol

options.label: C
options.html: Replete vitamin D and calcium, then give the infusion once levels are corrected

options.label: E
options.html: Start cinacalcet to treat the high PTH

items.explanationHtml:
She has vitamin D deficiency with secondary hyperparathyroidism and low-normal calcium. A potent antiresorptive given now can cause symptomatic hypocalcemia, because bone can no longer release calcium to buffer the deficit. Replete vitamin D (cholecalciferol) and ensure adequate calcium first, then infuse. Untreated vitamin D deficiency also blunts the drug's benefit and may hide osteomalacia.

Takeaway: Correct vitamin D deficiency and hypocalcemia before zoledronic acid or denosumab.

whyNot.A: Infusing now risks hypocalcemia.
whyNot.B: One dose of calcitriol does not correct the deficiency and can cause hypercalciuria; the store of 25-hydroxyvitamin D needs replacing.
whyNot.D: Romosozumab also needs replete vitamin D and calcium, and the problem is the deficiency, not the drug class.
whyNot.E: The PTH rise is secondary to vitamin D deficiency; cinacalcet would worsen the hypocalcemia.

items.objective: Correct vitamin D deficiency before giving a potent antiresorptive.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman has 6 months of fatigue, a 5-kg weight loss, nausea and craving for salty food. She has vitiligo and takes levothyroxine for Hashimoto thyroiditis. Blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg supine. Her palmar creases, knuckles and gums are darkly pigmented. Serum sodium is 130 mEq/L and potassium 5.7 mEq/L. Which of the following best explains the change in her skin?

options.label: B
options.html: Increased cleavage of pro-opiomelanocortin in the pituitary

options.label: C
options.html: Increased conversion of cortisol to cortisone in the skin

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of aldosterone action on skin melanocytes

options.label: E
options.html: Loss of cortisol-mediated suppression of melanin degradation

items.explanationHtml:
Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex (with other autoimmune disease) removes cortisol feedback, so corticotrophs make much more pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC). POMC is cleaved into ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone, both of which stimulate melanocortin-1 receptors on melanocytes. Pigmentation, together with hyperkalemia from aldosterone loss, marks primary adrenal insufficiency.

Takeaway: hyperpigmentation in adrenal insufficiency comes from high POMC-derived peptides, so it occurs only in primary disease.

whyNot.A: Antibodies against melanocytes cause vitiligo (loss of pigment), not increased pigment.
whyNot.C: Skin 11β-HSD activity does not control pigmentation, and cortisol is low here.
whyNot.D: Aldosterone has no direct action on melanocytes; its loss explains the hyperkalemia and salt craving.
whyNot.E: Cortisol does not regulate melanin breakdown; the pigment comes from melanocortin receptor stimulation.

items.objective: Explain hyperpigmentation in primary adrenal insufficiency through increased POMC cleavage.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl has a firm, irregular abdominal mass that crosses the midline, bruising around both eyes and irritability. CT shows a calcified mass arising from the right adrenal gland. Urine homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid levels are raised. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells with rosettes around a central fibrillary core. Which of the following findings in the tumour cells would best predict aggressive behaviour?

options.label: E
options.html: Translocation of MYC to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus

items.explanationHtml:
An adrenal mass crossing the midline with orbital metastases ("raccoon eyes"), calcification, raised catecholamine metabolites and Homer Wright rosettes is neuroblastoma, a neural crest tumour. MYCN amplification is the key adverse prognostic marker and moves a child into the high-risk group.

Takeaway: in neuroblastoma, MYCN amplification predicts aggressive disease.

whyNot.B: WT1 loss is linked to Wilms tumour, which arises from the kidney, rarely crosses the midline and does not raise urine catecholamine metabolites.
whyNot.C: EWSR1-FLI1 fusion defines Ewing sarcoma, a bone tumour of older children.
whyNot.D: Biallelic RB1 loss causes retinoblastoma (and osteosarcoma).
whyNot.E: The MYC-immunoglobulin translocation defines Burkitt lymphoma.

items.objective: Identify neuroblastoma and its main adverse prognostic marker (MYCN amplification).

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man is seen for headaches, sweating and palpitations in brief attacks. Blood pressure is 168/104 mm Hg. Before any testing, a clinician starts propranolol for his tachycardia. Two hours after the first dose he has a severe headache and blood pressure of 236/132 mm Hg. Plasma free metanephrines are later found to be 9 times the upper limit of normal. Which of the following best explains the rise in blood pressure after propranolol?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of presynaptic beta receptors increased catecholamine release from sympathetic nerves

options.label: B
options.html: Loss of beta-1 inhibition of renin release

options.label: C
options.html: Loss of beta-2-mediated vasodilation left alpha-1-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed

options.label: D
options.html: Propranolol directly stimulated alpha-1 receptors on arterioles

options.label: E
options.html: Propranolol inhibited the breakdown of circulating catecholamines

items.explanationHtml:
The attacks and very high metanephrines indicate a pheochromocytoma. Circulating epinephrine and norepinephrine act on vascular alpha-1 receptors (vasoconstriction) and beta-2 receptors (vasodilation, mainly in skeletal muscle). A nonselective beta blocker removes the beta-2 vasodilation, leaving alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, and also removes some cardiac compensation, so blood pressure can surge. This is why alpha blockade must come first.

Takeaway: in pheochromocytoma, give alpha blockade before any beta blocker.

whyNot.A: Presynaptic receptor effects are minor; the catecholamines here come from the tumour, not from nerve terminals.
whyNot.B: Beta-1 blockade lowers renin, which would tend to lower, not raise, blood pressure.
whyNot.D: Propranolol has no alpha-agonist activity.
whyNot.E: Catecholamine breakdown by COMT and MAO is unaffected by propranolol.

items.objective: Explain why beta blockade without prior alpha blockade causes a hypertensive crisis in pheochromocytoma.

items.stemHtml:
A 26-year-old man is evaluated for new hypertension and muscle cramps. Over 3 months he has eaten several large bags of imported black licorice candy daily. He takes no medications.

TestResult
Blood pressure158/98 mm Hg
Serum sodium144 mEq/L
Serum potassium2.9 mEq/L
Serum bicarbonate32 mEq/L
Plasma renin activity0.2 ng/mL/h (N = 0.6–4.3)
Plasma aldosterone2 ng/dL (N = 4–31)

Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of the mineralocorticoid receptor by cortisol

options.label: B
options.html: Constitutive activation of the epithelial sodium channel

options.label: C
options.html: Excess 11-deoxycorticosterone from an adrenal enzyme block

options.label: D
options.html: Increased secretion of aldosterone by the zona glomerulosa

options.label: E
options.html: Increased secretion of renin by juxtaglomerular cells

items.explanationHtml:
Hypertension, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis with both renin and aldosterone suppressed mean a mineralocorticoid effect that is not aldosterone. Glycyrrhetinic acid in licorice inhibits 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 in the collecting duct, which normally inactivates cortisol to cortisone. Cortisol, present at far higher concentrations than aldosterone, then activates the mineralocorticoid receptor. It resolves after licorice is stopped.

Takeaway: low renin, low aldosterone hypertension with hypokalemia and a history of licorice is apparent mineralocorticoid excess.

whyNot.B: Liddle syndrome gives the same laboratory pattern, but it is inherited and not explained by licorice intake.
whyNot.C: 11β- and 17α-hydroxylase deficiencies are congenital and present earlier, with abnormal sex-steroid development.
whyNot.D: Primary aldosteronism would raise aldosterone, not suppress it.
whyNot.E: High renin would raise aldosterone; both are low here.

items.objective: Recognise licorice-induced apparent mineralocorticoid excess from a low-renin, low-aldosterone pattern.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man who smokes 40 cigarettes a day has 6 weeks of rapidly worsening proximal weakness, leg edema and new hyperglycemia. Blood pressure is 172/100 mm Hg. He is thin, with darkened skin but no striae. Serum potassium is 2.6 mEq/L and bicarbonate 34 mEq/L. Late-night salivary cortisol is markedly raised. Plasma ACTH is 310 pg/mL (N = 10–60). Cortisol does not suppress after 8 mg of dexamethasone. Pituitary MRI is normal. Which of the following is the most likely source of the ACTH?

options.label: D
options.html: Small cell carcinoma of the lung

options.label: E
options.html: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

items.explanationHtml:
A very high ACTH that does not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone, rapid onset, hyperpigmentation and severe hypokalemic alkalosis in a heavy smoker point to ectopic ACTH secretion, most often from small cell lung carcinoma (a neuroendocrine tumour). Such high cortisol levels saturate renal 11β-HSD2, so cortisol acts as a mineralocorticoid, causing hypokalemia and edema.

Takeaway: very high, nonsuppressible ACTH with rapid Cushing features and hypokalemia in a smoker suggests ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer.

whyNot.A: Adrenal carcinoma secretes cortisol autonomously, so ACTH would be suppressed.
whyNot.B: Pituitary adenomas usually give modestly raised ACTH that partly suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone, and the MRI is normal.
whyNot.C: CRH-secreting tumours are very rare and would usually show partial dexamethasone suppression; smoking points to the lung.
whyNot.E: Squamous cell lung cancer causes hypercalcemia through PTH-related peptide, not ACTH secretion.
