items.objective: Localise ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome with nonsuppressible ACTH to an ectopic small cell lung carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency diagnosed 3 years ago takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. For 2 days she has had vomiting and diarrhea and could not keep her tablets down. She is drowsy. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse 124/min and blood pressure 76/42 mm Hg. Serum sodium is 127 mEq/L, potassium 5.9 mEq/L and glucose 58 mg/dL. A blood sample for cortisol has been drawn. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Cosyntropin stimulation test before any treatment

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg and rapid intravenous normal saline with dextrose

options.label: C
options.html: Norepinephrine infusion and await the cortisol result

options.label: D
options.html: Oral fludrocortisone at double the usual dose

options.label: E
options.html: Oral hydrocortisone at triple the usual dose

items.explanationHtml:
This is an adrenal crisis in a patient with known Addison disease who could not absorb her medicine. Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at once (then 200 mg per 24 hours), rapid isotonic saline and dextrose for hypoglycemia, and look for the trigger. At this dose hydrocortisone has enough mineralocorticoid effect, so fludrocortisone is not needed acutely.

Takeaway: suspected adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone and saline immediately, never delayed for tests.

whyNot.A: The diagnosis is already established, and testing would delay life-saving treatment.
whyNot.C: Vasopressors without glucocorticoid work poorly in adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone restores vascular responsiveness.
whyNot.D: Fludrocortisone is not a treatment for crisis; she cannot absorb oral drugs and needs glucocorticoid.
whyNot.E: Sick-day oral dosing is for mild illness; she is vomiting and in shock.

items.objective: Treat adrenal crisis with immediate IV hydrocortisone and saline.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman has 4 months of fatigue, a 6-kg weight loss, light-headedness on standing and darkening of her elbows and an old scar. Blood pressure is 98/64 mm Hg supine and 84/56 mm Hg standing. She is otherwise stable and eating normally. Serum sodium is 131 mEq/L and potassium 5.4 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the adrenal glands with contrast

options.label: B
options.html: Morning cortisol and ACTH, then cosyntropin stimulation

options.label: D
options.html: Random cortisol, stopping if it is normal

items.explanationHtml:
Pigmentation, orthostatic hypotension, weight loss, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia suggest primary adrenal insufficiency. In a stable patient, measure early-morning cortisol with ACTH and confirm with a cosyntropin stimulation test; a high ACTH shows the problem is in the adrenal. Imaging comes after biochemical confirmation and antibody testing.

Takeaway: suspected adrenal insufficiency in a stable patient: morning cortisol and ACTH, then cosyntropin stimulation.

whyNot.A: Imaging is for after the diagnosis is confirmed, and only if 21-hydroxylase antibodies are negative.
whyNot.C: Pituitary imaging is for secondary insufficiency; pigmentation and hyperkalemia point to the adrenal.
whyNot.D: A random cortisol can be misleadingly normal; a single normal value does not exclude the diagnosis.
whyNot.E: Late-night salivary cortisol screens for cortisol excess, not deficiency.

items.objective: Choose morning cortisol, ACTH and cosyntropin stimulation to diagnose primary adrenal insufficiency.

items.stemHtml: Her 8 AM cortisol is 2.1 µg/dL and ACTH 480 pg/mL (N = 10–60). After 250 µg of cosyntropin, cortisol peaks at 2.6 µg/dL. Antibodies to 21-hydroxylase are positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term treatment?

options.label: D
options.html: Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone, with sick-day rules

items.explanationHtml:
The test confirms autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency, so both cortisol and aldosterone must be replaced: hydrocortisone in divided doses (largest on waking) and fludrocortisone, titrated to blood pressure, potassium and renin. Teach sick-day dose increases, emergency injectable hydrocortisone and medical identification, and screen periodically for other autoimmune endocrine disease.

Takeaway: primary adrenal insufficiency needs glucocorticoid plus mineralocorticoid replacement and sick-day education.

whyNot.A: Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid action and is long-acting, which raises the risk of overtreatment.
whyNot.B: Fludrocortisone alone leaves her cortisol deficient and at risk of crisis.
whyNot.C: Hydrocortisone alone at replacement doses does not adequately replace aldosterone in primary disease.
whyNot.E: Spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor and would worsen her salt loss and hyperkalemia.

items.objective: Replace glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid in primary adrenal insufficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman with HIV infection, well controlled on a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor regimen, has asthma treated with high-dose inhaled fluticasone for the past 5 months. She has gained 9 kg, mainly in her face and abdomen, and has new purple striae and easy bruising. She takes no oral or topical steroids. Her 8 AM serum cortisol is 1.4 µg/dL and ACTH is 4 pg/mL (N = 10–60). Which of the following is the most likely cause of her findings?

options.label: D
options.html: Excess fluticasone exposure from inhibited hepatic metabolism

items.explanationHtml:
Ritonavir strongly inhibits CYP3A4, which normally clears fluticasone. The inhaled steroid then accumulates systemically and causes iatrogenic Cushing syndrome. Exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses ACTH and the patient's own cortisol, so measured cortisol is low despite cushingoid features. Switch to an inhaled steroid less dependent on CYP3A4 (for example beclomethasone) or change the antiretroviral, and watch for adrenal insufficiency as the exposure falls.

Takeaway: cushingoid features with low cortisol and low ACTH mean exogenous glucocorticoid, including inhaled steroid boosted by ritonavir.

whyNot.A: A pituitary source would give a normal or high ACTH and a high cortisol.
whyNot.B: An adrenal adenoma suppresses ACTH but makes measured cortisol high, not low.
whyNot.C: Ectopic ACTH gives very high ACTH and cortisol.
whyNot.E: Lipodystrophy changes fat distribution but does not cause striae, bruising or a suppressed axis.

items.objective: Recognise iatrogenic Cushing syndrome from a ritonavir–inhaled fluticasone interaction.

items.stemHtml:
A 35-year-old woman has 18 months of weight gain, proximal weakness, purple striae and new hypertension. She takes no glucocorticoids or estrogen.

TestResult
24-hour urine free cortisol (two collections)3 and 4 times the upper limit of normal
Late-night salivary cortisol (two samples)Raised
Plasma ACTH, 9 AM58 pg/mL (N = 10–60)
Pituitary MRINo visible adenoma
Serum potassium3.9 mEq/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling with stimulation

options.label: D
options.html: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to look for a carcinoid

items.explanationHtml:
Cushing syndrome is confirmed by two different tests, and an unsuppressed ACTH shows it is ACTH-dependent. Most such cases are pituitary, but the MRI is negative, so inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH or desmopressin is needed to show a central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient before pituitary surgery. No gradient would send the search to an ectopic source.

Takeaway: ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome with a negative or equivocal pituitary MRI: petrosal sinus sampling.

whyNot.A: Adrenal imaging is for ACTH-independent disease, when ACTH is suppressed.
whyNot.B: Bilateral adrenalectomy is a last resort for uncontrollable disease, not a diagnostic step.
whyNot.D: Body imaging for an ectopic tumour comes only if sampling shows no pituitary gradient.
whyNot.E: Operating without localisation risks a failed exploration; the source must first be confirmed as pituitary.

items.objective: Use inferior petrosal sinus sampling for ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome with a negative pituitary MRI.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old man with hypertension on three drugs including a diuretic has a serum potassium of 3.2 mEq/L. Plasma aldosterone is 28 ng/dL with suppressed renin, and aldosterone fails to suppress after an intravenous saline load. Adrenal CT shows a 1.2-cm left adrenal nodule with a normal right adrenal. He wants a surgical cure if one is possible. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Primary aldosteronism is confirmed. At his age, small adrenal nodules are often nonfunctioning, and bilateral hyperplasia is common, so CT cannot reliably show which side is making aldosterone. Adrenal vein sampling compares aldosterone (corrected for cortisol) from each side; lateralisation to the left would justify adrenalectomy.

Takeaway: in primary aldosteronism, confirm the side with adrenal vein sampling before adrenalectomy in most patients who want surgery.

whyNot.B: FDG-PET assesses malignancy, which a small homogeneous nodule does not suggest, and it does not show aldosterone production.
whyNot.C: Removing the left gland on CT alone risks removing a nonfunctioning nodule while a bilateral or right-sided source remains.
whyNot.D: Waiting does not answer the question of which gland is secreting.
whyNot.E: A mineralocorticoid antagonist is appropriate if he declines surgery or has bilateral disease, but he wants a cure.

items.objective: Use adrenal vein sampling to lateralise primary aldosteronism before surgery.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman has episodic headaches, sweating and palpitations. Blood pressure is 172/102 mm Hg and pulse 104/min. Plasma free normetanephrine is 8 times the upper limit of normal. MRI shows a 4-cm left adrenal mass that is bright on T2-weighted images. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is planned. Which of the following is the most appropriate preoperative management?

options.label: A
options.html: Fine-needle biopsy of the mass to confirm the diagnosis

options.label: D
options.html: Phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin for 1–2 weeks with liberal salt and fluids

items.explanationHtml:
Before removing a pheochromocytoma, block alpha receptors for 1–2 weeks (phenoxybenzamine or a selective alpha-1 blocker), with a high-sodium diet and fluids to re-expand the contracted plasma volume. This prevents intraoperative hypertensive crises during tumour handling and reduces hypotension after removal. A beta blocker can be added only after alpha blockade if tachycardia persists.

Takeaway: prepare for pheochromocytoma surgery with alpha blockade and volume expansion.

whyNot.A: Biopsy of a pheochromocytoma can precipitate a hypertensive crisis and is not needed after biochemical confirmation.
whyNot.B: Unprepared surgery carries a high risk of severe intraoperative hypertension and arrhythmia.
whyNot.C: Beta blockade first leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed and can cause a crisis.
whyNot.E: MIBG therapy is for metastatic or unresectable disease, not routine preparation.

items.objective: Prepare a patient with pheochromocytoma for surgery with alpha blockade before beta blockade.

items.stemHtml:
A 61-year-old woman had CT for abdominal pain, which resolved. It showed a 3.1-cm right adrenal mass, which has been fully evaluated.

EvaluationResult
Noncontrast CTHomogeneous, smooth margins, 6 Hounsfield units
Blood pressure, potassium118/74 mm Hg; 4.3 mEq/L
Cortisol after 1 mg dexamethasone overnight1.1 µg/dL (normal below 1.8)
Plasma free metanephrinesNormal
Clinical features of cortisol or androgen excessNone

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: No further imaging or hormone testing for the mass

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat CT every 6 months for 5 years

items.explanationHtml:
The mass is a lipid-rich adenoma (homogeneous, 10 Hounsfield units or less) under 4 cm, and hormone testing shows no cortisol excess or pheochromocytoma; aldosterone testing is not needed with normal blood pressure and potassium. Current guidance says such a benign, nonfunctioning mass needs no further imaging or routine repeat testing unless new features appear.

Takeaway: a small, homogeneous, low-attenuation, nonfunctioning adrenal adenoma needs no follow-up imaging.

whyNot.A: Biopsy adds risk and no information for a typical adenoma.
whyNot.B: Surgery is for functioning masses or those with suspicious imaging.
whyNot.D: Serial CT scans add radiation and cost without benefit for a lipid-rich adenoma.
whyNot.E: There is no evidence of aldosterone excess to treat.

items.objective: Manage a benign-appearing, nonfunctioning adrenal incidentaloma without further follow-up.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy has had pubic hair and acne for 6 months and has grown 9 cm in the past year. Both testes measure 8 mL (prepubertal is under 4 mL), and the penis is enlarged. Bone age is 10.5 years. A GnRH-agonist stimulation test gives a pubertal LH rise. He has no headaches or visual symptoms, and neurologic examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Begin a GnRH agonist without imaging

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral testicular enlargement, advanced bone age and a pubertal LH response mean central precocious puberty. In boys a CNS cause (hypothalamic hamartoma, glioma, other tumours, hydrocephalus) is common enough that every boy needs brain MRI, even with a normal examination. Treatment with a GnRH agonist follows.

Takeaway: central precocious puberty in a boy requires brain MRI.

whyNot.A: A GnRH agonist is the treatment, but an underlying brain lesion must first be excluded.
whyNot.C: 17-hydroxyprogesterone screens for congenital adrenal hyperplasia, a peripheral cause in which the testes stay small.
whyNot.D: hCG-secreting tumours cause peripheral puberty with suppressed LH.
whyNot.E: Testicular ultrasonography is for a unilateral enlargement suggesting a Leydig cell tumour.

items.objective: Evaluate central precocious puberty in a boy with brain MRI.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy has had morning headaches for 4 months and has crossed from the 50th to the 10th percentile for height. Visual field testing shows loss of the outer (temporal) half of the visual field in both eyes. MRI shows a 3-cm cystic suprasellar mass with peripheral calcification. At surgery the cyst contains thick, dark-brown oily fluid. The tumour most likely arose from remnants of which of the following embryologic structures?

options.label: B
options.html: Neural crest of the skull base

items.explanationHtml:
A calcified, cystic suprasellar mass with oily fluid in a child with growth failure and bitemporal hemianopia is a craniopharyngioma. It arises from epithelial remnants of Rathke pouch, the outpouching of oral (surface) ectoderm that forms the anterior pituitary.

Takeaway: craniopharyngioma comes from Rathke pouch remnants and is typically calcified and cystic.

whyNot.A: The infundibulum of the diencephalon forms the posterior pituitary and stalk, which gives rise to pituicytomas and gliomas, not craniopharyngiomas.
whyNot.B: Neural crest gives rise to tumours such as schwannomas and neuroblastoma, not sellar cystic epithelial tumours.
whyNot.C: Notochord remnants give chordomas, usually at the clivus or sacrum, which destroy bone rather than form oily calcified cysts.
whyNot.E: Thyroglossal duct remnants form midline neck cysts, not intracranial masses.

items.objective: Relate craniopharyngioma to its Rathke pouch origin and typical imaging.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man with acromegaly still has an elevated IGF-1 after transsphenoidal surgery and a year of a somatostatin receptor ligand. He is started on a drug that is a modified growth hormone molecule which binds the GH receptor but prevents the receptor from signalling. Which laboratory test is most appropriate to monitor the effect of this drug?
items.explanationHtml:
Pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist. It does not act on the tumour, so GH secretion continues and often rises (loss of IGF-1 feedback). Its effect is seen as a fall in hepatic IGF-1 production, so IGF-1 guides dosing (along with liver tests and periodic MRI).

Takeaway: on pegvisomant, monitor IGF-1; GH levels are uninterpretable.

whyNot.A: Insulin sensitivity often improves, but insulin is not used to judge disease control.
whyNot.B: GH stays high or rises because the receptor, not secretion, is blocked.
whyNot.D: Prolactin is relevant to mixed GH-prolactin tumours but does not measure pegvisomant effect.
whyNot.E: Urine free cortisol is a screen for Cushing syndrome.

items.objective: Explain why IGF-1, not GH, is used to monitor GH receptor antagonist therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has 6 months of progressive difficulty seeing cars approaching from either side and low libido. MRI shows a 2.8-cm sellar mass compressing the optic chiasm and displacing the pituitary stalk. Serum prolactin is 58 ng/mL (N = 2–18). After resection, immunostaining of the tumour is negative for prolactin and all other pituitary hormones. Which of the following best explains his raised prolactin?

options.label: A
options.html: Ectopic prolactin secretion by tumour cells

options.label: B
options.html: Interrupted dopamine delivery to normal lactotrophs

options.label: D
options.html: Stimulation of lactotrophs by high TRH

options.label: E
options.html: Tumour secretion of an estrogen-like factor

items.explanationHtml:
A nonfunctioning macroadenoma compresses the stalk and its portal vessels. Dopamine from the arcuate (tuberoinfundibular) neurons, which tonically inhibits prolactin, no longer reaches the normal lactotrophs, so prolactin rises modestly (stalk effect). A true macroprolactinoma this size would usually raise prolactin into the hundreds or thousands.

Takeaway: mild hyperprolactinemia with a large nonsecreting mass is the stalk effect.

whyNot.A: The tumour stains negative for prolactin, so it is not the source.
whyNot.C: Kidney failure raises prolactin, but nothing suggests reduced kidney function here.
whyNot.D: High TRH raises prolactin in primary hypothyroidism, which is not suggested.
whyNot.E: Pituitary adenomas do not make estrogen-like factors.

items.objective: Explain the stalk effect on prolactin through loss of dopamine inhibition.

items.stemHtml:
A 64-year-old man who smokes heavily has 2 weeks of confusion and fatigue. He appears euvolemic, with normal skin turgor and no edema. Chest CT shows a central lung mass. Laboratory studies:

TestValue
Serum sodium122 mEq/L
Serum osmolality256 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality520 mOsm/kg
Urine sodium58 mEq/L
TSH2.1 μU/mL
Cortisol, 8 AM18 μg/dL

The cause of his hyponatremia acts mainly through which of the following cellular events?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of ENaC channels in principal cells

options.label: B
options.html: Inhibition of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb

options.label: C
options.html: Insertion of aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane of collecting duct cells

options.label: D
options.html: Opening of aquaporin-1 channels in the descending limb

options.label: E
options.html: Phospholipase C activation in vascular smooth muscle

items.explanationHtml:
Hypotonic hyponatremia with an inappropriately concentrated urine, high urine sodium and euvolemia, with normal thyroid and adrenal tests, is SIADH, here from ectopic ADH made by small cell lung cancer. ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells (Gs, cAMP, protein kinase A), which drives aquaporin-2 insertion into the apical membrane, so free water is reabsorbed.

Takeaway: SIADH retains free water through V2-mediated aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct.

whyNot.A: ENaC activation is the aldosterone effect; aldosterone is suppressed in SIADH.
whyNot.B: Blocking NKCC2 is the loop diuretic action, which impairs concentrating ability.
whyNot.D: Aquaporin-1 in the proximal tubule and descending limb is constitutive and not regulated by ADH.
whyNot.E: Phospholipase C activation through V1 receptors causes vasoconstriction, not water retention.

items.objective: Link SIADH to V2-receptor-mediated aquaporin-2 insertion.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman lost about 2 L of blood from uterine atony during delivery and needed transfusion of 4 units of red cells for hypotension. She is now 2 weeks postpartum and is otherwise recovering. Which of the following is most likely to be the earliest clinical sign of the injury she is at risk for?
items.explanationHtml:
The anterior pituitary enlarges during pregnancy without a matching rise in portal blood supply, so severe postpartum hemorrhage with hypotension can cause ischemic necrosis (Sheehan syndrome). Loss of prolactin makes failure to lactate the earliest sign; amenorrhea, fatigue, hypotension and hyponatremia follow.

Takeaway: postpartum hemorrhage followed by inability to breastfeed suggests Sheehan syndrome.

whyNot.B: Hyperpigmentation needs high ACTH (primary adrenal failure); in pituitary failure ACTH is low and skin is pale.
whyNot.C: Aldosterone is controlled by renin-angiotensin, so secondary adrenal insufficiency does not cause hyperkalemia.
whyNot.D: The posterior pituitary is usually spared, so diabetes insipidus is uncommon.
whyNot.E: Infarction of a normal-sized gland does not compress the chiasm.

items.objective: Recognise failure of lactation as the earliest sign of Sheehan syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has 1 year of reduced libido and erectile dysfunction, and 2 months of headaches. He bumps into door frames. Visual field testing shows bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a 2.6-cm sellar mass extending up to the optic chiasm. Laboratory studies show serum prolactin 2,400 ng/mL (N = 2–18), total testosterone 140 ng/dL (N = 300–1,000), and normal free T4 and 8 AM cortisol. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
A prolactin level in the thousands with a macroadenoma is a macroprolactinoma. A dopamine agonist (cabergoline) is first-line treatment even when vision is affected: it normalises prolactin and shrinks most tumours within days to weeks, often restoring vision and testosterone. Fields and prolactin are rechecked closely; surgery is for resistance, intolerance or apoplexy.

Takeaway: prolactinomas, including macroadenomas with field loss, are treated first with a dopamine agonist.

whyNot.B: Somatostatin analogs treat GH-secreting (and TSH-secreting) adenomas, not prolactinomas.
whyNot.C: Radiation is reserved for tumours that resist drugs and surgery.
whyNot.D: Testosterone does not shrink the tumour or protect vision, and hypogonadism usually resolves when prolactin falls.
whyNot.E: Surgery is second line for prolactinomas because cabergoline works so well.

items.objective: Start a dopamine agonist for a macroprolactinoma even with visual field loss.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman with schizophrenia has had no menstrual period for 4 months and has milky nipple discharge. Her psychosis has been well controlled on risperidone, started 6 months ago. Urine hCG is negative. Serum prolactin is 92 ng/mL (N = 3–25). TSH, creatinine and liver tests are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discuss with her psychiatrist a switch to aripiprazole, then recheck prolactin

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the pituitary before any change in medication

options.label: C
options.html: Start bromocriptine and continue risperidone unchanged

options.label: D
options.html: Start cabergoline and stop risperidone today

options.label: E
options.html: Stop risperidone without a replacement and recheck prolactin

items.explanationHtml:
Her hyperprolactinemia began after starting a dopamine (D2) antagonist, and risperidone is one of the antipsychotics most likely to raise prolactin. When it is safe, the best step is to switch to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic such as aripiprazole (a partial agonist), in agreement with her psychiatrist, and recheck prolactin. MRI is needed if prolactin stays high, or if the drug cannot be changed and onset does not match the drug.

Takeaway: suspected drug-induced hyperprolactinemia: change the drug safely and recheck before imaging.

whyNot.B: Imaging first is reasonable only when the drug cannot be changed or the timeline does not fit; it risks finding an incidental microadenoma.
whyNot.C: Dopamine agonists can oppose the antipsychotic effect and worsen psychosis; remove the cause instead.
whyNot.D: Stopping her antipsychotic abruptly risks relapse, and cabergoline is unnecessary if the cause is the drug.
whyNot.E: Stopping an antipsychotic without a replacement risks a psychotic relapse.

items.objective: Manage antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia by switching to a prolactin-sparing drug.

items.stemHtml:
A 38-year-old woman has 8 months of irregular menses, fatigue, weight gain, constipation and dry skin. Pregnancy test is negative.

TestValue
TSH64 μU/mL
Free T40.4 ng/dL
Prolactin48 ng/mL (N = 3–25)
Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodiesStrongly positive

MRI shows a symmetrically enlarged pituitary gland without a discrete adenoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Cabergoline, then repeat MRI in 3 months

options.label: B
options.html: Levothyroxine, then recheck prolactin and MRI

items.explanationHtml:
Long-standing primary hypothyroidism (Hashimoto thyroiditis) raises TRH, which stimulates thyrotrophs and lactotrophs. The pituitary enlarges from thyrotroph hyperplasia, and prolactin rises. Levothyroxine corrects both; the gland shrinks and prolactin normalises, so reassess after treatment.

Takeaway: check TSH in every patient with hyperprolactinemia; hypothyroidism can mimic a pituitary tumour.

whyNot.A: A dopamine agonist treats the prolactin but not the cause, and the gland enlargement is not a prolactinoma.
whyNot.C: Intravenous thyroid hormone is for myxedema coma; she is stable.
whyNot.D: Octreotide is for GH- or TSH-secreting adenomas; her TSH is high because the thyroid has failed.
whyNot.E: Biopsy is unnecessary; the enlargement is expected to regress with treatment.

items.objective: Treat pituitary hyperplasia and hyperprolactinemia caused by primary hypothyroidism with levothyroxine.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman has noticed that her rings no longer fit and her shoe size has increased over 3 years. She has new snoring, heavy sweating and bilateral hand numbness at night. Blood pressure is 152/94 mm Hg. She has frontal bossing, a widened nose and spaces between her lower teeth. Fasting glucose is 118 mg/dL. Serum IGF-1 is 3 times the upper limit of normal for her age. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Oral glucose tolerance test with serum GH measurements

items.explanationHtml:
She has the clinical picture of acromegaly with a high IGF-1. The confirmatory test is an oral glucose load: in healthy people glucose suppresses GH, but in acromegaly GH fails to fall below about 1 ng/mL. Pituitary MRI follows confirmation.

Takeaway: screen acromegaly with IGF-1, confirm with GH non-suppression after oral glucose, then MRI.

whyNot.A: Insulin-induced hypoglycemia is a stimulation test for GH deficiency, not excess.
whyNot.C: GH is secreted in pulses, so a random level can be high in healthy people and is not diagnostic.
whyNot.D: GHRH is measured only when ectopic GHRH secretion (for example a neuroendocrine tumour) is suspected after a pituitary cause is excluded.
whyNot.E: Somatostatin receptor imaging is not part of the routine diagnosis.

items.objective: Confirm acromegaly with failure of GH suppression after an oral glucose load.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man had transsphenoidal resection of a 1.8-cm GH-secreting macroadenoma 3 months ago. He feels better, but serum IGF-1 remains 1.8 times the upper limit of normal. MRI shows residual tumour invading the right cavernous sinus, which the surgeon considers unresectable. Visual fields are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Persistent acromegaly after surgery, with residual tumour in the cavernous sinus that cannot be removed, is treated medically. A long-acting somatostatin receptor ligand (octreotide or lanreotide) is the usual first choice; pegvisomant or combinations are added if IGF-1 stays high, and focused radiotherapy is reserved for resistant disease.

Takeaway: persistent acromegaly after surgery: start a somatostatin receptor ligand.

whyNot.A: Dopamine agonists help only mild disease, usually with modest IGF-1 elevation, and are not first choice here.
whyNot.C: Repeat surgery cannot reach tumour that invades the cavernous sinus.
whyNot.D: Untreated GH excess raises cardiovascular, metabolic and cancer risk; it should be controlled.
whyNot.E: Whole-brain radiation is not used; focused radiotherapy is a later option for resistant tumours.

items.objective: Treat persistent acromegaly after surgery with a somatostatin receptor ligand.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man has sudden, severe headache that started 3 hours ago, with vomiting and double vision. He has had low energy and reduced libido for a year. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), blood pressure 86/54 mm Hg and pulse 112/min. He has a right third nerve palsy and reduced visual acuity in both eyes. Noncontrast CT of the head shows a sellar mass with hemorrhage. Blood is drawn for cortisol, free T4 and electrolytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Sudden headache, ophthalmoplegia and visual loss with hemorrhage into a sellar mass is pituitary apoplexy. Hypotension suggests acute ACTH deficiency, which can be fatal. Give stress-dose intravenous hydrocortisone immediately after drawing blood, with fluids, then arrange urgent neurosurgical review for decompression given the visual deficit.

Takeaway: in pituitary apoplexy, give IV hydrocortisone first.

whyNot.A: Cabergoline treats prolactinomas over weeks; it does nothing for acute adrenal crisis.
whyNot.C: Thyroid hormone before cortisol can precipitate or worsen adrenal crisis.
whyNot.D: The CT already shows the cause; lumbar puncture adds nothing and delays treatment.
whyNot.E: Waiting for results while he is hypotensive risks death from adrenal crisis.

items.objective: Give stress-dose hydrocortisone first in pituitary apoplexy.

items.stemHtml:
A 44-year-old woman had radiation therapy for a nasopharyngeal cancer 6 years ago. She now has fatigue, cold intolerance and weight gain. Blood pressure is 102/66 mm Hg.

TestValue
Sodium132 mEq/L
Potassium4.2 mEq/L
TSH1.1 μU/mL
Free T40.5 ng/dL
Cortisol, 8 AM2.1 μg/dL
ACTH8 pg/mL (N = 10–60)

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Hydrocortisone, with levothyroxine started after it

options.label: C
options.html: Levothyroxine, with hydrocortisone if she remains tired

options.label: D
options.html: Levothyroxine and hydrocortisone started at the same high dose

items.explanationHtml:
Low free T4 with an inappropriately normal TSH, and low cortisol with a low ACTH, mean secondary hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency from radiation-induced hypopituitarism. Glucocorticoid replacement comes first: thyroid hormone raises metabolic rate and cortisol clearance and can trigger adrenal crisis if cortisol is not replaced. Levothyroxine is then started and dosed by free T4, not TSH.

Takeaway: in hypopituitarism, replace cortisol before thyroid hormone.

whyNot.A: Aldosterone is preserved in pituitary disease (renin-angiotensin control), so fludrocortisone is not needed; her potassium is normal.
whyNot.C: Starting levothyroxine first risks precipitating adrenal crisis.
whyNot.D: Starting both together still exposes her to the risk of crisis; cortisol should be established first.
whyNot.E: GH replacement is considered only after the other axes are replaced, and it is not urgent.

items.objective: Replace glucocorticoid before thyroid hormone in central hypothyroidism with ACTH deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy is brought for evaluation because he is the shortest boy in his class. He has always been at the 5th percentile for height, and his height velocity over the past 2 years has been 5 cm/year. He has no pubic hair and testicular volumes are 3 mL each. His father did not start shaving until age 17 and reached a normal adult height. Bone age radiograph shows a bone age of 12 years. Thyroid function and celiac serology are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
A steady growth velocity, delayed bone age, delayed puberty and a father who matured late are constitutional delay of growth and puberty. He has more time to grow, and adult height is usually normal. Reassurance and follow-up are appropriate; a short course of low-dose testosterone can be offered if delay causes distress.

Takeaway: normal growth velocity with delayed bone age and a family history of late puberty is constitutional delay.

whyNot.A: Stimulation testing is for children with low growth velocity or low IGF-1, not this pattern.
whyNot.B: A karyotype is mainly for girls (Turner syndrome) or boys with features of a chromosomal disorder.
whyNot.C: Pituitary imaging is for suspected GH deficiency or other features of a sellar lesion.
whyNot.E: GH is not indicated for constitutional delay.

items.objective: Recognise constitutional delay of growth and puberty and reassure.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman has 3 months of intense thirst and urinating about 7 L/day, including several times at night. She takes no medications. She has no history of psychiatric illness. Laboratory studies show serum sodium 146 mEq/L, serum osmolality 298 mOsm/kg, glucose 88 mg/dL, calcium 9.3 mg/dL, potassium 4.1 mEq/L and urine osmolality 110 mOsm/kg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Restriction of fluid intake to 1.5 L/day at home

items.explanationHtml:
Dilute polyuria with a high-normal serum sodium and no osmotic or electrolyte cause suggests diabetes insipidus rather than primary polydipsia. The next step is a supervised water deprivation test (with desmopressin at the end), or stimulated copeptin where available, to separate central from nephrogenic DI and confirm the diagnosis before treatment.

Takeaway: confirm and classify diabetes insipidus with a supervised water deprivation test (or stimulated copeptin) before treating.

whyNot.A: Thiazides are a treatment for nephrogenic DI; giving one before a diagnosis is premature.
whyNot.B: Empiric desmopressin in someone who may have primary polydipsia risks dangerous hyponatremia.
whyNot.C: Kidney imaging does not distinguish the causes of dilute polyuria.
whyNot.D: Unsupervised fluid restriction in true DI can cause severe hypernatremia.

items.objective: Choose a supervised water deprivation test to evaluate dilute polyuria.

items.stemHtml: During the supervised test, after 7 hours without fluids she has lost 3% of her body weight. Serum sodium is 149 mEq/L and plasma osmolality 304 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality has risen only to 150 mOsm/kg. One hour after desmopressin, urine osmolality is 480 mOsm/kg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Her urine stayed dilute despite a rising plasma osmolality (no ADH effect), then concentrated by more than 50% after desmopressin, showing that her kidneys respond to ADH. That is central diabetes insipidus (AVP deficiency).

Takeaway: no concentration with dehydration plus a large rise after desmopressin means central DI.

whyNot.B: In nephrogenic DI the kidney does not respond to desmopressin, so urine stays dilute.
whyNot.C: In primary polydipsia, ADH release is intact and urine concentrates during deprivation.
whyNot.D: SIADH causes hyponatremia with concentrated urine, the opposite pattern.
whyNot.E: Osmotic diuresis gives urine osmolality near or above plasma, not 150 mOsm/kg.

items.objective: Interpret a water deprivation test showing central diabetes insipidus.

items.stemHtml: She is started on desmopressin and her symptoms resolve. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her evaluation?

options.label: A
options.html: Genetic testing for AVP receptor 2 variants

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the hypothalamus and pituitary

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat water deprivation test in 6 months

items.explanationHtml:
Central DI that appears in adulthood without trauma or surgery needs MRI of the hypothalamus and pituitary to look for a cause: tumours (craniopharyngioma, germinoma, metastasis), infiltration (sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis), or lymphocytic infundibulohypophysitis. Anterior pituitary function should be tested too. Advise her to drink only to thirst to avoid hyponatremia on desmopressin.

Takeaway: new central DI needs sellar and hypothalamic MRI to find the cause.

whyNot.A: AVPR2 variants cause congenital nephrogenic DI, not central DI.
whyNot.B: Lithium causes nephrogenic DI, and she takes no medications.
whyNot.D: Repeating the test adds nothing once the diagnosis is clear and does not reveal the cause.
whyNot.E: The kidneys respond normally to desmopressin, so a kidney lesion is excluded.

items.objective: Image the hypothalamus and pituitary after diagnosing central diabetes insipidus.

items.stemHtml: A 12-year-old girl had subtotal resection of a craniopharyngioma 8 months ago. She now eats constantly, takes food from classmates and has gained 18 kg. She takes hydrocortisone, levothyroxine and desmopressin, and her doses are adequate on laboratory testing. Damage to which of the following hypothalamic regions most likely explains her weight gain?
items.explanationHtml:
The ventromedial nucleus (with the arcuate and paraventricular circuits) mediates satiety. Destruction, as with craniopharyngioma or its surgery, removes satiety signalling, giving relentless hyperphagia and hypothalamic obesity that responds poorly to diet.

Takeaway: ventromedial hypothalamic damage causes hyperphagia and obesity; lateral damage causes anorexia.

whyNot.A: Lateral hypothalamic damage removes the hunger drive and causes weight loss.
whyNot.B: Posterior hypothalamic damage impairs heat conservation, causing poikilothermia.
whyNot.C: Supraoptic damage causes central diabetes insipidus, which she has, but not hyperphagia.
whyNot.D: Suprachiasmatic damage disturbs the circadian rhythm.

items.objective: Relate ventromedial hypothalamic damage to hyperphagia and obesity.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy has not started puberty. He has never been able to smell coffee or smoke. He is 168 cm tall with eunuchoid proportions, sparse pubic hair and testicular volumes of 2 mL. Serum LH, FSH and testosterone are all low. Karyotype is 46,XY. Which of the following best explains his condition?

options.label: C
options.html: Failure of neuronal migration from the olfactory placode

options.label: D
options.html: Nondisjunction producing an extra X chromosome

items.explanationHtml:
Delayed puberty with low LH and FSH and anosmia is Kallmann syndrome. GnRH neurons arise in the olfactory placode and migrate with olfactory axons into the hypothalamus; defects in this migration (for example ANOS1 or FGFR1 variants) leave both the olfactory bulbs and GnRH secretion deficient.

Takeaway: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism plus anosmia means failed GnRH neuron migration (Kallmann syndrome).

whyNot.A: Androgen insensitivity gives a female phenotype with high testosterone and high LH.
whyNot.B: Primary testicular failure raises LH and FSH.
whyNot.D: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes primary hypogonadism with high gonadotropins, and his karyotype is normal.
whyNot.E: Gonadotroph adenomas are usually nonfunctioning macroadenomas in older adults and do not cause anosmia.

items.objective: Explain Kallmann syndrome as failed migration of GnRH neurons from the olfactory placode.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man is in the intensive care unit 5 days after a subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm, with ischemia in the region just above the optic chiasm. His temperature has been 40.2°C (104.4°F) for 2 days without shivering. Blood, urine and sputum cultures, chest radiography and cerebrospinal fluid analysis show no infection. Acetaminophen has little effect. Injury to which of the following regions best explains his fever?
items.explanationHtml:
The anterior (preoptic) hypothalamus drives heat loss through sweating and cutaneous vasodilation. Damage there leaves heat production unopposed and causes central hyperthermia, which is typically high, sustained, without sweating, and poorly responsive to antipyretics because it does not run through prostaglandin E2.

Takeaway: anterior hypothalamic damage causes hyperthermia; posterior damage causes poikilothermia.

whyNot.B: Lateral damage causes loss of appetite, not fever.
whyNot.C: Posterior damage removes heat conservation, so the patient cools with the environment.
whyNot.D: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the circadian clock, not the thermoregulatory centre.
whyNot.E: Ventromedial damage causes hyperphagia and obesity.

items.objective: Relate anterior hypothalamic injury to central hyperthermia.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy has been extremely hungry since infancy and is above the 99th percentile for weight. He is tall for his age, developmentally normal and has no dysmorphic features. Serum leptin is high, in proportion to his fat mass. Genetic testing finds a heterozygous loss-of-function variant in a G protein-coupled receptor expressed on paraventricular hypothalamic neurons that signals satiety. The normal ligand of this receptor is derived from which of the following precursors?
items.explanationHtml:
The receptor is the melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R). Leptin stimulates arcuate POMC neurons, which cleave pro-opiomelanocortin into alpha-MSH; alpha-MSH activates MC4R in the paraventricular nucleus to produce satiety. MC4R variants are the commonest monogenic cause of severe early-onset obesity, often with increased linear growth.

Takeaway: leptin → POMC → alpha-MSH → MC4R is the satiety pathway; its defects cause monogenic obesity.

whyNot.A: AgRP is an MC4R antagonist released by hunger-promoting neurons, not the activating ligand.
whyNot.B: Ghrelin acts on the growth hormone secretagogue receptor to stimulate hunger.
whyNot.C: Neuropeptide Y promotes feeding through Y receptors, not MC4R.
whyNot.D: Orexins act on orexin receptors to promote wakefulness and feeding.

items.objective: Trace the leptin-POMC-alpha-MSH-MC4R satiety pathway.

items.stemHtml:
A 20-year-old woman who runs about 110 km per week has had no menstrual period for 7 months. Her BMI is 17.8 kg/m². She has had a metatarsal stress fracture. Pregnancy test is negative. Prolactin and TSH are normal.

OptionGnRH pulse frequencyLHEstradiol
AIncreasedHighHigh
BIncreasedHighLow
CNormalHighLow
DReducedLow or normalLow
EReducedLowHigh

Which of the following sets of findings is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Energy deficit from intense training and low intake lowers leptin and raises cortisol, which slows GnRH pulses. LH and FSH fall to low or low-normal levels, and estradiol is low (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea). Low estrogen and low energy availability reduce bone formation, explaining the stress fracture.

Takeaway: functional hypothalamic amenorrhea is low GnRH pulsatility with low or normal gonadotropins and low estradiol.

whyNot.A: High gonadotropins and estradiol would suggest a gonadotropin-secreting tumour, not energy deficiency.
whyNot.B: Fast GnRH pulses favour LH, as in polycystic ovary syndrome, where estrogen is not low.
whyNot.C: High LH with low estradiol is primary ovarian insufficiency, in which gonadotropins rise because feedback is lost.
whyNot.E: Low gonadotropins cannot sustain a high estradiol without an autonomous estrogen source.

items.objective: Describe the hormonal pattern of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy has drunk large amounts of water and has wet his bed every night for 2 months. He has a scaly, greasy rash on his scalp and a tender swelling of his skull. Radiographs show several punched-out lytic skull lesions. Serum sodium is 147 mEq/L and urine osmolality is 90 mOsm/kg. A biopsy of a skull lesion is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Cells positive for CD1a and langerin, with rod-shaped cytoplasmic granules on electron microscopy

options.label: C
options.html: Plasma cells producing a monoclonal light chain

options.label: D
options.html: Sheets of small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes

options.label: E
options.html: Spindle cells arranged in a storiform pattern

items.explanationHtml:
Lytic skull lesions, seborrheic-like scalp rash and central diabetes insipidus in a young child point to Langerhans cell histiocytosis. The lesional cells are dendritic cells that express CD1a and langerin (CD207) and contain Birbeck granules (rod- or tennis-racket-shaped); many carry BRAF V600E. Infiltration of the stalk and hypothalamus causes the DI.

Takeaway: lytic bone lesions plus central DI in a child suggests Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

whyNot.B: Sarcoidosis can cause central DI but is rare at this age and does not cause punched-out skull lesions with this rash.
whyNot.C: Myeloma causes lytic lesions in older adults, not toddlers with central DI.
whyNot.D: Small round blue cells with rosettes fit neuroblastoma, which can metastasise to the skull but does not cause this rash or DI pattern.
whyNot.E: A storiform spindle-cell pattern describes fibrous histiocytic tumours, not this disease.

items.objective: Recognise Langerhans cell histiocytosis as a cause of central diabetes insipidus.

items.stemHtml: A 5-year-old girl has had breast development and pubic hair for 6 months and has grown 9 cm in the past year. She has brief episodes of unprovoked laughter that her parents call "giggling spells". Bone age is 8 years. After a GnRH agonist is injected, serum LH rises into the pubertal range. MRI shows a small, nonenhancing mass attached to the floor of the third ventricle. The mass most likely causes her puberty by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Activating mutation of the LH receptor in the ovary

options.label: B
options.html: Autonomous estrogen secretion by the mass

options.label: E
options.html: Pulsatile GnRH release from neurons within the mass

items.explanationHtml:
Gelastic (laughing) seizures and central precocious puberty with a nonenhancing mass on the tuber cinereum is a hypothalamic hamartoma. It contains GnRH-producing neurons (and glia that stimulate GnRH release), so pulsatile GnRH activates the pituitary-gonadal axis early; the LH rise after stimulation confirms a central process.

Takeaway: hypothalamic hamartoma causes central precocious puberty through its own GnRH release, often with gelastic seizures.

whyNot.A: Activating LH receptor variants cause gonadotropin-independent puberty in boys (familial male-limited precocious puberty), with suppressed LH.
whyNot.B: An estrogen-secreting source would suppress LH, not give a pubertal LH response.
whyNot.C: hCG-secreting germ cell tumours cause precocious puberty mainly in boys, and they enhance on MRI.
whyNot.D: Loss of dopamine inhibition raises prolactin, which suppresses, rather than starts, puberty.

items.objective: Explain central precocious puberty from a hypothalamic hamartoma.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college student has had no menstrual period for 5 months. Over the past year she has trained for a triathlon and lost 6 kg. Her BMI is 18.1 kg/m². She has no galactorrhea, hirsutism or acne. Urine hCG is negative. Prolactin and TSH are normal; FSH is 3.1 mIU/mL, LH 1.8 mIU/mL and estradiol 18 pg/mL (all low). Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.html: Clomiphene citrate for 5 days each month

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the pituitary with contrast

items.explanationHtml:
Amenorrhea with low gonadotropins and estradiol in a young woman with weight loss and heavy training, and normal prolactin and TSH, is functional hypothalamic amenorrhea. First-line treatment corrects the energy deficit: more calories, less training, nutrition (and psychological) support, plus screening for an eating disorder. Menses usually return as energy availability improves.

Takeaway: treat functional hypothalamic amenorrhea by restoring energy balance.

whyNot.A: Ovulation induction is for women seeking pregnancy and does not fix the cause.
whyNot.B: Oral contraceptives give withdrawal bleeds but do not restore the axis, protect bone poorly here and mask recovery.
whyNot.D: MRI is not needed when the history explains low gonadotropins and there are no headaches or visual symptoms.
whyNot.E: Bisphosphonates are avoided in young women who may become pregnant and do not address the cause.

items.objective: Treat functional hypothalamic amenorrhea by correcting energy deficit.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old woman has had functional hypothalamic amenorrhea for 2 years. Over the past 9 months she has worked with a dietitian and therapist, reduced her running and regained 3 kg, but her BMI is still 18.4 kg/m² and menses have not returned. Estradiol remains low. DXA shows a lumbar spine Z-score of −2.3. She takes calcium and vitamin D and does not want pregnancy now. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Transdermal estradiol with cyclic oral progestin

items.explanationHtml:
When menses do not return after an adequate trial of nutritional and behavioural treatment and bone density is low, short-term transdermal estradiol with cyclic oral progestin is suggested to protect bone, while energy restoration continues. Transdermal estradiol avoids the hepatic first-pass reduction of IGF-1 seen with oral estrogen, and the progestin protects the endometrium.

Takeaway: for persistent functional hypothalamic amenorrhea with low bone density, use transdermal estradiol plus cyclic progestin, not the combined pill or bisphosphonates.

whyNot.A: The combined pill has not been shown to improve bone density in this condition and masks the return of menses.
whyNot.B: Denosumab is not studied for this use in young women and has rebound bone loss when stopped.
whyNot.C: Bisphosphonates persist in bone for years and are avoided in women of reproductive age.
whyNot.D: Teriparatide is not indicated for young women with this cause of low bone mass.

items.objective: Choose transdermal estradiol with cyclic progestin for bone protection in persistent functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man with Kallmann syndrome has been treated with intramuscular testosterone since age 16. He and his partner now want to have a child. Semen analysis shows no sperm. Which of the following is the most appropriate change in therapy?

options.label: C
options.html: Start clomiphene citrate and stop testosterone

options.label: D
options.html: Stop testosterone and start hCG injections, adding FSH if needed

items.explanationHtml:
His problem is GnRH deficiency, so the testes are normal but unstimulated. Exogenous testosterone does not raise intratesticular testosterone enough and further suppresses LH and FSH. To induce spermatogenesis, stop testosterone and give hCG (an LH analogue that stimulates Leydig cells), adding FSH (recombinant FSH or menotropins) if sperm do not appear; pulsatile GnRH is an alternative in specialist centres.

Takeaway: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with a wish for fertility needs gonadotropins, not testosterone.

whyNot.A: Aromatase inhibition cannot restore gonadotropins when the hypothalamus makes no GnRH.
whyNot.B: More testosterone suppresses the axis further and does not produce sperm.
whyNot.C: Clomiphene works by raising endogenous GnRH and gonadotropin release, which he cannot do.
whyNot.E: Any testosterone preparation suppresses spermatogenesis.

items.objective: Use gonadotropins to induce spermatogenesis in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man has had reduced libido, erectile dysfunction and fatigue for a year. He has taken oxycodone, now about 120 mg daily, for chronic back pain since a spinal fusion 4 years ago. BMI is 27 kg/m². Two fasting morning total testosterone levels are 190 and 205 ng/dL (N = 300–1,000). LH is 2.0 mIU/mL (N = 2–12), prolactin and ferritin are normal, and he has no headaches or visual symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hypogonadism?

options.label: D
options.html: Opioid suppression of hypothalamic GnRH release

items.explanationHtml:
Low testosterone with a low-normal LH is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Long-term high-dose opioids act on hypothalamic opioid receptors to suppress GnRH pulses; this is common and often unrecognised. Management is to discuss tapering the opioid, with testosterone replacement as an option if that is not possible and there are no contraindications.

Takeaway: chronic opioid use is a common reversible cause of secondary hypogonadism.

whyNot.A: Hemochromatosis can cause secondary hypogonadism, but his ferritin is normal.
whyNot.B: Klinefelter syndrome causes primary hypogonadism with high LH and small firm testes from adolescence.
whyNot.C: A macroadenoma is possible, but with a clear functional cause, normal prolactin and no mass symptoms, the opioid is the most likely explanation.
whyNot.E: Testicular failure would raise LH.

items.objective: Identify opioid-induced suppression of GnRH as a cause of secondary hypogonadism.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman has 2 months of excessive thirst and urinating about 6 L/day. For a year she has had a dry cough, and she had tender red nodules on her shins last spring. Serum sodium is 147 mEq/L and urine osmolality 120 mOsm/kg, rising to 430 mOsm/kg after desmopressin. Chest radiography shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. MRI shows a thickened, enhancing pituitary stalk and hypothalamic enhancement. Serum calcium is 10.8 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Central diabetes insipidus from a thickened stalk and hypothalamic enhancement, with hilar lymphadenopathy, prior erythema nodosum, cough and mild hypercalcemia, is neurosarcoidosis involving the hypothalamus. Confirm with tissue (usually from a more accessible site such as a lymph node) showing noncaseating granulomas, and test anterior pituitary function.

Takeaway: central DI plus a thickened stalk and systemic granulomatous disease suggests neurosarcoidosis.

whyNot.A: Germinomas thicken the stalk in children and young adults but do not explain hilar nodes, erythema nodosum or hypercalcemia.
whyNot.B: Langerhans cell histiocytosis causes stalk thickening and DI, but with lytic bone or lung cystic disease rather than hilar adenopathy and erythema nodosum.
whyNot.C: Lymphocytic hypophysitis is often peripartum and lacks systemic features.
whyNot.D: Metastases can cause DI but there is no known primary and the systemic picture fits sarcoidosis.

items.objective: Recognise neurosarcoidosis as a cause of central diabetes insipidus.

items.stemHtml:
A 45-year-old man had transsphenoidal resection of a large craniopharyngioma 30 hours ago. Over the past 8 hours his urine output has been 350–450 mL/hour. He is alert and thirsty. He receives hydrocortisone per protocol.

TestBefore surgeryNow
Serum sodium140 mEq/L151 mEq/L
Serum osmolality288 mOsm/kg310 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality—95 mOsm/kg
Glucose96 mg/dL124 mg/dL

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Large volumes of dilute urine with a rising sodium after surgery near the stalk are central diabetes insipidus from injury to ADH-producing axons. Give desmopressin, let him drink to thirst, and check sodium often, because a SIADH-like phase may follow about a week later (the triphasic response) and continued desmopressin can then cause hyponatremia.

Takeaway: postoperative central DI: desmopressin with close sodium monitoring, watching for a triphasic course.

whyNot.B: Restricting fluids in DI worsens hypernatremia.
whyNot.C: Thiazides are a long-term option for nephrogenic DI, not acute central DI.
whyNot.D: Hypertonic saline treats hyponatremia and would raise his sodium further.
whyNot.E: Tolvaptan blocks V2 receptors and would increase water loss.

items.objective: Treat postoperative central diabetes insipidus with desmopressin and monitor for a triphasic response.

items.stemHtml: A 5-year-old girl is brought because of breast development over the past 5 months. She has grown 8 cm in the past year (previously 5–6 cm/year). She has Tanner stage 3 breasts and sparse pubic hair. There are no café-au-lait macules, and she has no headaches. Bone age is 7.5 years. A basal LH on a sensitive assay is in the pubertal range, and pelvic ultrasonography shows an enlarged uterus without an ovarian mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Rapid progression, accelerated growth, advanced bone age and a pubertal LH mean central precocious puberty. In a girl this young (under 6), the chance of an intracranial lesion such as a hypothalamic hamartoma or tumour is high enough that MRI of the brain is indicated before treatment.

Takeaway: central precocious puberty in a young girl or any boy needs brain MRI.

whyNot.A: 17-hydroxyprogesterone screens for congenital adrenal hyperplasia, a peripheral cause with suppressed LH.
whyNot.B: hCG-secreting tumours cause peripheral precocious puberty, mostly in boys, with suppressed LH.
whyNot.D: Progressive puberty with advanced bone age at age 5 needs evaluation and treatment, not watchful waiting.
whyNot.E: Medroxyprogesterone is an outdated treatment that does not preserve adult height and does not address the cause.

items.objective: Order brain MRI for central precocious puberty in a young girl.

items.stemHtml: MRI shows a 9-mm hypothalamic hamartoma. She has had no seizures. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Central precocious puberty from a hypothalamic hamartoma without refractory seizures is treated medically with a long-acting GnRH agonist. Continuous receptor stimulation desensitises gonadotrophs, LH and FSH fall, puberty stops progressing and adult height is preserved. Treatment usually continues until a normal age for puberty.

Takeaway: central precocious puberty, including from a hamartoma, is treated with a depot GnRH agonist; surgery is for refractory seizures.

whyNot.A: Aromatase inhibitors are used for some peripheral causes; they do not stop the central axis.
whyNot.C: Ketoconazole blocks steroid synthesis and is used for some peripheral causes in boys, not central puberty.
whyNot.D: Radiosurgery is a seizure treatment for hamartomas, not first-line for precocious puberty.
whyNot.E: Resection carries significant risk and is reserved for drug-resistant gelastic epilepsy.

items.objective: Treat central precocious puberty with a long-acting GnRH agonist.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man has had two calcium kidney stones. Serum calcium is 11.3 mg/dL and PTH is elevated. His mother had surgery for a pituitary tumour, and his maternal aunt had a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour. Germline testing shows a pathogenic variant inherited from his mother; DNA from one of his tumours later shows loss of the remaining normal allele. The protein encoded by the affected gene normally has which of the following functions?

options.label: A
options.html: A cell-adhesion molecule that anchors epithelial cells

options.label: B
options.html: A GTPase-activating protein that turns off RAS

options.label: C
options.html: A nuclear protein that restrains proliferation by regulating transcription

options.label: D
options.html: A receptor tyrosine kinase for glial-derived neurotrophic factor ligands

options.label: E
options.html: A ubiquitin ligase subunit that degrades hypoxia-inducible factor

items.explanationHtml:
Hyperparathyroidism with relatives who had pituitary and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours is MEN1. The MEN1 gene encodes menin, a nuclear tumour suppressor that restrains cell proliferation through effects on transcription and chromatin. Tumours arise when the second, normal allele is lost (two hits).

Takeaway: MEN1 is caused by loss of the menin tumour suppressor, following the two-hit model.

whyNot.A: Loss of E-cadherin, an adhesion molecule, causes hereditary diffuse gastric and lobular breast cancer.
whyNot.B: Neurofibromin is the RAS GTPase-activating protein lost in neurofibromatosis type 1.
whyNot.D: RET is the receptor tyrosine kinase activated in MEN2, which does not cause pituitary or pancreatic tumours.
whyNot.E: The VHL protein targets hypoxia-inducible factor; its loss causes renal cell carcinoma, hemangioblastomas and pheochromocytoma.

items.objective: Identify menin as the tumour suppressor lost in MEN1.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old girl has a tall, thin build with long limbs, everted eyelids, and small pink nodules on the tip of her tongue and along her lips. She has had chronic constipation since childhood. A 2-cm firm thyroid nodule is found. Her lenses are normally positioned and echocardiography shows a normal aortic root. In addition to the thyroid tumour, she is at greatest risk of which of the following?

options.label: D
options.html: Hyperplasia of all four parathyroid glands

options.label: E
options.html: Papillary carcinoma of the contralateral thyroid lobe

items.explanationHtml:
Mucosal neuromas, a marfanoid habitus without lens or aortic disease, constipation from intestinal ganglioneuromatosis and a thyroid nodule (medullary thyroid carcinoma) are MEN2B. About half of patients develop pheochromocytoma, which must be excluded before thyroid surgery.

Takeaway: MEN2B = MTC, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus, without hyperparathyroidism.

whyNot.B: Pituitary adenomas belong to MEN1.
whyNot.C: Gastrinomas belong to MEN1.
whyNot.D: Parathyroid hyperplasia occurs in MEN1 and MEN2A but not in MEN2B.
whyNot.E: Papillary carcinoma is not part of MEN2; the thyroid cancer of MEN2 is medullary.

items.objective: Recognise MEN2B and its association with pheochromocytoma.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has had itchy, brown, rippled plaques between her shoulder blades for years. She now has a thyroid nodule, and her serum calcitonin is markedly elevated. Her serum calcium is 9.6 mg/dL. From which embryologic tissue do the cells that form her thyroid tumour derive?

options.label: A
options.html: Endoderm of the floor of the primitive pharynx

options.label: B
options.html: Mesoderm of the second pharyngeal arch

options.label: C
options.html: Neural crest cells that migrate to the ultimobranchial body

options.label: E
options.html: Third pharyngeal pouch endoderm that forms the inferior parathyroids

items.explanationHtml:
Cutaneous lichen amyloidosis with a calcitonin-secreting thyroid tumour suggests MEN2A with medullary thyroid carcinoma. MTC arises from parafollicular C cells, which come from neural crest cells that migrate into the ultimobranchial body (from the fourth pharyngeal pouch) and are incorporated into the thyroid. Follicular cells, by contrast, come from endoderm of the pharyngeal floor.

Takeaway: C cells, and therefore medullary thyroid carcinoma, are of neural crest origin, like the adrenal medulla.

whyNot.A: Floor-of-pharynx endoderm forms the follicular cells, the source of papillary and follicular carcinomas.
whyNot.B: Second-arch mesoderm forms muscles of facial expression and parts of the hyoid, not thyroid cells.
whyNot.D: Stomodeal ectoderm forms Rathke's pouch (anterior pituitary) and oral epithelium.
whyNot.E: Third pouch endoderm forms the inferior parathyroids and thymus, not C cells.

items.objective: Trace medullary thyroid carcinoma to neural crest-derived parafollicular C cells.

items.stemHtml: A 6-week-old boy has failed to pass meconium normally and has abdominal distension. Rectal suction biopsy shows absent ganglion cells. His father had a total thyroidectomy for medullary thyroid carcinoma and a left adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma at age 31. A single germline variant in which of the following genes best explains the disorders in both the father and the son?
items.explanationHtml:
The father has MEN2A (MTC and pheochromocytoma), caused by an activating germline RET variant. RET signalling is also needed for enteric neural crest cells to colonise the distal bowel. Some MEN2A variants, especially at certain cysteine codons, also lower RET function at the cell surface, so the same variant can cause Hirschsprung disease.

Takeaway: RET gain of function causes MEN2; reduced RET function causes Hirschsprung disease, and some MEN2A families have both.

whyNot.A: APC causes familial adenomatous polyposis (and is linked to cribriform-morular thyroid cancer), not MTC or Hirschsprung disease.
whyNot.B: MEN1 causes parathyroid, pancreatic and pituitary tumours, not MTC.
whyNot.C: NF1 can cause pheochromocytoma but not MTC or aganglionosis.
whyNot.E: VHL causes pheochromocytoma with renal cell carcinoma and hemangioblastomas, not MTC.

items.objective: Link RET variants to both MEN2A and Hirschsprung disease.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman has asymptomatic hypercalcemia (calcium 11.0 mg/dL) with an elevated PTH and osteopenia on DXA. Her brother has a prolactinoma, and germline testing has confirmed that she carries the family's MEN1 variant. Neck ultrasonography shows two enlarged parathyroid glands. Which of the following is the most appropriate operation?

options.label: A
options.html: Excision of the two enlarged glands only

options.label: B
options.html: Excision of the larger gland guided by sestamibi scanning

options.label: C
options.html: Radiofrequency ablation of the enlarged glands

options.label: D
options.html: Subtotal (three-and-a-half gland) parathyroidectomy with cervical thymectomy

items.explanationHtml:
Hyperparathyroidism in MEN1 is multigland hyperplasia, even when imaging shows only one or two large glands. Limited excision leads to persistent or recurrent disease, so the operation is subtotal parathyroidectomy (leaving a remnant of about half a gland), or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation, together with transcervical thymectomy to remove supernumerary glands and reduce the risk of thymic carcinoid.

Takeaway: MEN1 hyperparathyroidism needs subtotal or total parathyroidectomy with thymectomy, not single-gland surgery.

whyNot.A: All four glands are abnormal; leaving two hyperplastic glands guarantees recurrence.
whyNot.B: Focused single-gland surgery suits a sporadic adenoma, not MEN1.
whyNot.C: Ablation is not a standard treatment for MEN1 hyperparathyroidism.
whyNot.E: The thyroid is normal in MEN1, and removing it adds risk without benefit.

items.objective: Choose subtotal parathyroidectomy with thymectomy for MEN1 hyperparathyroidism.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man was found to have MEN1 after resection of a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour; germline testing identified a pathogenic MEN1 variant. His 19-year-old daughter is healthy, with normal serum calcium, and asks what she should do. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Annual pancreatic MRI starting now, without genetic testing

options.label: B
options.html: Genetic counselling and targeted testing for her father's variant

options.label: C
options.html: No evaluation unless she develops symptoms

options.label: E
options.html: Testing only if she plans a pregnancy

items.explanationHtml:
MEN1 is autosomal dominant, so each child of a carrier has a 50% chance of inheriting the variant. First-degree relatives are offered genetic counselling and targeted testing for the known familial variant. A carrier then begins biochemical and imaging surveillance; a non-carrier needs no further screening, which spares years of tests.

Takeaway: offer first-degree relatives targeted testing for a known MEN1 variant; only carriers need surveillance.

whyNot.A: Imaging everyone without knowing carrier status exposes non-carriers to needless tests.
whyNot.C: Tumours in MEN1 are often silent until advanced; waiting for symptoms loses the benefit of surveillance.
whyNot.D: Parathyroid surgery is done only for established hyperparathyroidism, not prophylactically.
whyNot.E: Her risk does not depend on pregnancy plans; testing is relevant now.

items.objective: Offer cascade genetic testing to relatives in a family with a known MEN1 variant.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman with known MEN1 (treated by subtotal parathyroidectomy 2 years ago) has had amenorrhea for 6 months and milky nipple discharge. She is not pregnant. Serum prolactin is 168 ng/mL (N below 20). TSH and calcium are normal. MRI shows a 7-mm pituitary adenoma without mass effect. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Bromocriptine only if she wishes to conceive

items.explanationHtml:
A microprolactinoma causing hypogonadism and galactorrhea is treated first with a dopamine agonist, and cabergoline is preferred because it is more effective and better tolerated. Prolactinomas in MEN1 are treated the same way as sporadic ones, though they can be more resistant.

Takeaway: symptomatic prolactinoma, including in MEN1: cabergoline first.

whyNot.A: Treatment is indicated now for hypogonadism and galactorrhea, regardless of pregnancy plans; bromocriptine is mainly chosen around conception.
whyNot.C: Somatostatin analogues treat GH-secreting adenomas and some neuroendocrine tumours, not prolactinomas.
whyNot.D: Radiation is reserved for rare tumours resistant to drugs and surgery.
whyNot.E: Surgery is for dopamine agonist failure or intolerance.

items.objective: Treat a prolactinoma in MEN1 with cabergoline.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has a 2.4-cm thyroid nodule. Fine-needle aspiration shows medullary thyroid carcinoma, and serum calcitonin and CEA are elevated. He has no relatives known to have endocrine tumours, and his blood pressure is normal. In addition to staging neck ultrasonography, which of the following tests should be offered to every patient with this diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: BRAF V600E testing of the aspirate

items.explanationHtml:
About a quarter of medullary thyroid carcinomas are hereditary, and a family history may be absent (new variants, small families, unrecognised disease). Every patient with MTC is therefore offered germline RET testing; a positive result changes surgery (pheochromocytoma screening first, parathyroid assessment) and triggers testing of relatives. Plasma metanephrines are also measured before surgery.

Takeaway: all patients with MTC get germline RET testing, whatever the family history.

whyNot.A: BRAF testing helps in indeterminate follicular-cell nodules, not in diagnosed MTC.
whyNot.C: C cells do not concentrate iodine, so radioiodine imaging has no role.
whyNot.D: Thyroglobulin is made by follicular cells and is a marker for differentiated (papillary and follicular) cancer, not MTC.
whyNot.E: Thyroid antibodies identify autoimmune thyroiditis and do not affect MTC care.

items.objective: Offer germline RET testing to every patient with medullary thyroid carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has a 1.8-cm left thyroid nodule. Fine-needle aspiration shows medullary thyroid carcinoma, and serum calcitonin is high. Germline testing shows a RET codon 634 variant. She has occasional headaches; blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. Thyroidectomy is being planned. Which of the following should be done first?

options.label: D
options.html: Start a beta-blocker for her blood pressure

items.explanationHtml:
A RET codon 634 variant means MEN2A, in which pheochromocytoma is common. Before any surgery, pheochromocytoma must be excluded with plasma free metanephrines (or urine fractionated metanephrines); an unsuspected tumour can cause a fatal hypertensive crisis during anaesthesia.

Takeaway: in MTC or a RET carrier, check metanephrines before any operation.

whyNot.B: Radioiodine has no role in MTC.
whyNot.C: Thyroglobulin is not a marker for MTC.
whyNot.D: A beta-blocker alone in a possible pheochromocytoma can precipitate a hypertensive crisis from unopposed alpha stimulation.
whyNot.E: Operating before excluding pheochromocytoma risks an intraoperative crisis.

items.objective: Exclude pheochromocytoma before thyroidectomy in MEN2.

items.stemHtml: Plasma normetanephrine and metanephrine are both more than four times the upper reference limit. CT shows a 3.5-cm right adrenal mass and a normal left adrenal gland. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

options.label: A
options.html: Alpha-blockade, then right adrenalectomy, then total thyroidectomy

options.label: B
options.html: Beta-blockade, then simultaneous adrenalectomy and thyroidectomy

options.label: C
options.html: Bilateral adrenalectomy at the time of thyroidectomy

options.label: D
options.html: Total thyroidectomy first, then adrenalectomy in 3 months

options.label: E
options.html: Total thyroidectomy now, with surveillance of the adrenal mass

items.explanationHtml:
The pheochromocytoma is treated first. She needs alpha-adrenergic blockade for 1–2 weeks (with a beta-blocker added only afterwards, if needed for tachycardia) and volume expansion, then laparoscopic right adrenalectomy. Once she has recovered and catecholamines have normalised, total thyroidectomy with appropriate neck dissection follows. The normal left adrenal is preserved and kept under surveillance.

Takeaway: in MEN2 with pheochromocytoma and MTC: alpha-block, remove the pheochromocytoma, then the thyroid.

whyNot.B: Starting with a beta-blocker risks unopposed alpha vasoconstriction, and combining both major operations is not preferred.
whyNot.C: Removing a normal left adrenal gland causes lifelong adrenal insufficiency without benefit.
whyNot.D: Thyroid surgery with an active pheochromocytoma risks a hypertensive crisis.
whyNot.E: A functioning pheochromocytoma must be removed, not watched, and it must come first.

items.objective: Sequence alpha-blockade, adrenalectomy and then thyroidectomy in MEN2.

items.stemHtml: She recovers well from both operations. Her 3-year-old son is tested and carries the same RET codon 634 variant. He is well, his neck examination is normal, and his serum calcitonin is within the age-appropriate reference range. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for his thyroid?

options.label: A
options.html: Annual neck ultrasonography, with surgery if a nodule appears

options.label: C
options.html: Total thyroidectomy at or before about age 5, timed by calcitonin

options.label: D
options.html: Thyroid surgery only if calcitonin exceeds the adult cutoff

options.label: E
options.html: Total thyroidectomy at age 18, when he can consent

items.explanationHtml:
Nearly all RET carriers develop MTC. For high-risk variants such as codon 634, prophylactic total thyroidectomy is recommended at or before about 5 years of age, with the exact timing guided by serum calcitonin, so that the thyroid is removed while disease is at most microscopic. He will also be screened for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism later in childhood.

Takeaway: a child with a high-risk RET variant (codon 634) has prophylactic thyroidectomy by about age 5.

whyNot.A: By the time a nodule appears, MTC may already have spread to lymph nodes.
whyNot.B: C cells do not take up iodine, so ablation would not prevent MTC.
whyNot.D: Waiting for a high calcitonin means waiting for established cancer.
whyNot.E: Waiting until adulthood allows MTC to develop and spread in a high-risk carrier.

items.objective: Time prophylactic thyroidectomy by RET risk class in a child carrier.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man had total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection for sporadic medullary thyroid carcinoma 3 months ago (germline RET testing negative; plasma metanephrines normal). He feels well and takes levothyroxine. Which of the following serum tests are most appropriate for detecting persistent or recurrent cancer?
items.explanationHtml:
MTC cells secrete calcitonin and CEA. Postoperative levels, and later their doubling times, show whether disease persists and how fast it is growing, and guide imaging.

Takeaway: follow medullary thyroid carcinoma with calcitonin and CEA, not thyroglobulin.

whyNot.B: Chromogranin A and serotonin are used for carcinoid and other neuroendocrine tumours, not as MTC markers.
whyNot.C: Free T4 and TSH guide levothyroxine dosing, not cancer surveillance.
whyNot.D: Thyroglobulin tracks differentiated follicular-cell cancers.
whyNot.E: Calcium and PTH check parathyroid function after neck surgery but do not detect MTC.

items.objective: Use calcitonin and CEA to monitor medullary thyroid carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman with MEN2A had total thyroidectomy for medullary thyroid carcinoma 6 weeks ago. Postoperative calcitonin is undetectable. She takes levothyroxine, and her TSH is now 0.05 µU/mL with a free T4 at the upper limit of normal. She asks whether her dose should stay this high to prevent recurrence. Which of the following is the most appropriate levothyroxine goal?

options.label: A
options.html: Dose high enough to keep TSH suppressed below 0.1 µU/mL

options.label: B
options.html: Dose high enough to keep free T4 above the reference range

options.label: C
options.html: Replacement dose that keeps TSH within the reference range

options.label: D
options.html: Stop levothyroxine and give liothyronine until radioiodine is given

options.label: E
options.html: Stop thyroid hormone, because her remaining C cells will make it

items.explanationHtml:
TSH suppression helps in differentiated thyroid cancer because follicular cells grow in response to TSH. C cells are not TSH-dependent, so after thyroidectomy for MTC levothyroxine is given only as replacement, aiming for a normal TSH. Her current over-replacement risks atrial fibrillation and bone loss without benefit, so the dose should be lowered.

Takeaway: after thyroidectomy for MTC, replace thyroid hormone to a normal TSH; do not suppress.

whyNot.A: Suppression gives no benefit in MTC and adds cardiac and skeletal harm.
whyNot.B: Deliberate hyperthyroxinemia has no role and causes harm.
whyNot.D: Radioiodine is not used in MTC, so there is no reason to withdraw levothyroxine.
whyNot.E: C cells make calcitonin, not thyroid hormone; after total thyroidectomy she needs lifelong levothyroxine.

items.objective: Replace levothyroxine to a normal TSH after thyroidectomy for MTC.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old adolescent raised as a girl is evaluated because over the past year her voice has deepened, her muscle mass has increased and her clitoris has enlarged markedly.
